The same current had fed the Sabbatean movement of Sabbatai Zevi, who declared himself Messiah in 1665. Israel ben Eliezer, about 1698 to 1760, called the Baal Shem Tov, is regarded as the founder. He was a folk healer who became wealthy and well known, and most of what is told of him comes from hagiographic accounts. His follower Dov Ber, the Maggid of Mezhirichi, succeeded him and turned his ideas into a movement.

Hasidic thought draws heavily on Lurianic Kabbalah and to an extent popularises it. Its most basic theme is the immanence of God in the universe. Its defining doctrine is that of the tzadik, the Righteous One, also called the Rebbe, as an inspiration and the figure around whom followers are organised. Hasidim are organised in independent groups called courts or dynasties, each headed by a hereditary Rebbe, and these often keep the name of the Eastern European town where they began, as Satmar, Belz and Vizhnitz do.

Worship stresses devotion, and wordless melodies called nigunim are a means of reaching devekut, cleaving to God, in prayer and communal gatherings. Many Hasidim use Galician Yiddish among themselves. Hasidic tales, a genre of hagiographies and anecdotes, were often passed on orally, and the earliest collection dates from 1815.

Early in the 19th century the tzaddiqim became a leading power across most of Eastern Europe, even in Lithuania, a stronghold of the opposing Misnagdic camp. Less than three generations after the Baal Shem Tov's death the movement had hundreds of thousands of followers by 1830. In the early 20th century emigration to America, urbanisation, World War I and the Russian Civil War uprooted the shtetls that had been its base. In the Soviet Union repression of religion brought rapid secularisation, though a few Hasidim, especially of Chabad, practised in secret for decades. Today most Hasidim live in Israel and the United States.
hassan-ii-of-morocco: Hassan was born on 9 July 1929 at the Dar al-Makhzen in Rabat, during the French protectorate, the eldest son of Sultan Mohammed V and his second wife, Lalla Abla bint Tahar. He studied Islamic sciences in Fez and then at the Royal College in Rabat, and took a law degree in 1951 and a master's degree in public law in 1952 at the University of Bordeaux.

French authorities exiled the royal family on 20 August 1953, first to Corsica and then to Madagascar. Hassan advised his father during the exile, returned with him on 16 November 1955 and took part in the negotiations of February 1956 that led to independence. In April 1956 his father named him commander-in-chief of the new Royal Moroccan Armed Forces.

Hassan became king on 26 February 1961, after his father died following surgery, and also held the office of prime minister. In 1962 he and his aides wrote Morocco's first constitution. It defined a constitutional monarchy with several parties, made Islam the state religion and gave the king the title Amir al-Mu'minin, with a person described as inviolable and sacred.

The opposition parties, among them the UNFP and the Istiqlal, protested against it. Morocco fought the Sand War with Algeria in 1963, and student protests in Casablanca in March 1965 became riots whose repression left hundreds dead. In June he dissolved parliament and suspended the constitution, ruling directly for more than five years under a state of exception. In 1969 Morocco recovered Sidi Ifni from Spain.

He survived two coup attempts. On 10 July 1971, during his birthday party at Skhirat, army cadets stormed the palace; about 400 people were reportedly killed by the rebels and loyal troops killed more than 150. On 16 August 1972 air force jets fired on his aircraft over Tétouan, killing eight people. Later he organised the Green March of 1975 into the former Spanish Sahara, after which Morocco controlled much of the territory and the conflict with the Polisario Front began.

The decades from the 1960s to the late 1980s are called the Years of Lead, when thousands of dissidents were jailed, killed, exiled or forcibly disappeared. The opposition leader Mehdi Ben Barka disappeared in Paris in October 1965. In 1990 Hassan set up the Consultative Human Rights Council, and in 1991 he pardoned two thousand prisoners, including political prisoners held in secret prisons such as Tazmamart.

The first opposition-led government was elected in 1998. Hassan died in Rabat on 23 July 1999 and was succeeded by his eldest son, Mohammed VI, who in 2004 created the Equity and Reconciliation Commission to investigate abuses committed during his father's reign.
hasselt: Hasselt lies between the Campine region, north of the Demer, and the Hesbaye region to the south. The name derives from the Germanic word Hasaluth, which refers to the common hazel.

Hasselt was founded in about the 7th century on the Helbeek, a tributary of the Demer. In the Middle Ages it became one of the free cities of the county of Loon, whose borders were roughly those of the present province of Limburg. It is first named in a document in 1165. In 1232 Arnold IV, Count of Loon, gave the city the same freedoms as those enjoyed in Liège. From 1366 the county was ruled directly by the Prince-Bishopric of Liège, until annexation by France in 1794.

Under the First French Empire Maastricht was the capital of the Department of the Lower Meuse. After the defeat of Napoleon in 1815 the area became part of the United Kingdom of the Netherlands, and King William I renamed the department after the medieval Duchy of Limburg, a duchy that had never included Hasselt or Maastricht. Belgium split from the Netherlands in 1830, but the status of Limburg was settled only in 1839, when it was divided into Belgian and Dutch parts. Hasselt became the provisional capital of the Belgian province. In ecclesiastical terms Belgian Limburg became independent of the Diocese of Liège only in 1967, when Hasselt became the seat of a new diocese.

Hasselt is known for jenever, a gin. It escaped the ban on the production and sale of the drink imposed in 1601 by Albert VII, Archduke of Austria, and Isabella Clara Eugenia, because it belonged to the Prince-Bishopric of Liège. Jenever production was the most important industry in Limburg in the 19th century, with most distilleries in Hasselt.

Hasselt is the capital and largest city of the province of Limburg in the Flemish Region of Belgium and the seat of the Catholic diocese of Hasselt. The Gothic St Quentin's Cathedral, begun in the 11th century, and the Refuge of Herkenrode Abbey, of 1542, the city's oldest civic building, stand there, and Hasselt University was established in 1971.
hastings-banda: Hastings Kamuzu Banda was born Akim Kamnkhwala Mtunthama Banda near Kasungu, to Mphonongo Banda and Akupingamnyama Phiri. No birth was registered, so his date of birth is unknown. After attending village and mission schools he was baptised in 1910. He studied at the Wilberforce Institute in Ohio, graduating from its high school section in 1928, and later at the University of Edinburgh, which awarded him the Scottish Triple Qualification in 1941.

He became an elder of a parish in the Church of Scotland. In 1951 he moved to the Gold Coast, and Malawian Congress leaders, among them Henry Chipembere and Kanyama Chiume, later asked him to return and lead their cause.

Banda opposed the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland, formed in 1953, because he feared it would cost Nyasaland's Africans further rights. He reached Nyasaland on 6 July 1958 after an absence of about 42 years and toured the country speaking against the federation. By February 1959 Rhodesian troops had been flown in and a state of emergency declared. On 3 March he was arrested in Operation Sunrise and held in Gwelo in Southern Rhodesia.

He was released in April 1960 and invited to London for talks on independence. After elections in August 1961 he became de facto prime minister, a title formally granted on 1 February 1963. In December 1962 the British Secretary of State R. A. Butler essentially agreed to end the federation.

A month after independence Banda dismissed four ministers who had proposed limits on his powers, and the dissidents fled the country. The constitution of 6 July 1966 made Malawi a republic and Banda its first president, the only candidate, and formally made the Malawi Congress Party the sole legal party. The party made him president for life in 1970, and the legislature did the same for the country in 1971. His title included the word Ngwazi, meaning saviour or conqueror in Chichewa.

In 1983 three ministers and a member of parliament who had favoured multiparty politics died in what was officially a traffic accident. Adult citizens had to carry party cards, the Malawi Young Pioneers acted as the party's paramilitary wing, and films and books were censored. Human rights groups estimate that at least 6,000 people were killed, tortured or jailed without trial. With the end of the Cold War, donors pressed for reform, and in 1993 Banda agreed to a referendum that ended the one-party system. He was defeated in the elections that followed and died in South Africa on 25 November 1997.
hatay-province: Hatay lies mostly outside Anatolia, along the eastern coast of the Levantine Sea, and borders Syria to the south and east. Its second-largest city is İskenderun, formerly Alexandretta. About 46 per cent of the land is mountain, 33 per cent plain and 20 per cent plateau and hillside. The Orontes River runs through it and reaches the Mediterranean at a delta in Samandağ.

The area has been settled since the early Bronze Age. It belonged in turn to the Akkadian Empire, the Amorite kingdom of Yamhad and the kingdom of Mitanni, and was then ruled by Hittites and Neo-Hittite peoples, from whom the modern name derives. It was the centre of the Seleucid Empire, home to the four Greek cities of the Syrian tetrapolis, and from 64 BCE Antioch was an important centre of the Roman Empire. The Rashidun Caliphate conquered the region in 638, and the Crusaders took it in 1098 and made it the centre of the Principality of Antioch. The Ottoman sultan Selim I took it from the Mameluks in 1516.

Under the Ottomans the area was the sanjak of Alexandretta. After the First World War it was placed under the French mandate for Syria. A French-Turkish treaty of 20 October 1921 made the sanjak autonomous, and it then had 220,000 inhabitants, 87,000 of them Turks, alongside Arabs, Jews, Assyrians, Kurds and Armenians. In 1936 Turkey complained to the League of Nations about the treatment of the Turkish community, and the sanjak was given autonomy in November 1937.

Hatay State, a transitional entity, existed from 7 September 1938 to 29 June 1939. France was willing to return the area to Turkey in exchange for a pact against possible European aggression. On 29 June 1939, after a referendum that has been called rigged, Hatay became a Turkish province. Syria disputed both the separation and the annexation, and about 50,000 people, among them 22,000 Armenians, are estimated to have left for Syria.

Hatay is Turkey's southernmost province, with its capital at Antakya, the ancient Antioch, and a population of 1,686,043 in 2022. Its people include Sunni Muslims and Alawites, with Syriac Orthodox, Maronite, Antiochian Greek and Armenian communities. Its sites include Alalakh, Tell Tayinat and the Hatay Archaeology Museum at Antakya, with a large collection of Roman mosaics. The province was heavily damaged by the earthquakes of 2023.
hathor: Cattle imagery is frequent in the art of Predynastic Egypt, as are images of women with upraised, curved arms like horns, and both may represent goddesses connected with cattle. The Gerzeh Palette, from the Naqada II period, shows a cow's head with inward-curving horns surrounded by stars, which suggests a link with the sky.

Hathor herself is not unambiguously mentioned or depicted until the Fourth Dynasty, c. 2613 to 2494 BCE, although some objects that refer to her may be earlier. When she does clearly appear, her horns curve outward. Her Egyptian name, ḥwt-ḥr, is usually translated as house of Horus, but it can also mean my house is the sky.

The Egyptologist Robyn Gillam calls Hathor a type of deity rather than a single entity, and suggests that the royal goddess promoted by the Old Kingdom court absorbed many local goddesses, who were then treated as her manifestations. Texts speak of Seven Hathors, and sometimes of as many as 362.

As a sky goddess she was mother or consort of Horus and Ra, and so the symbolic mother of the pharaohs. She was also one of the goddesses who acted as the Eye of Ra. Her other concerns were music, dance, love, sexuality and motherhood, and the sistrum, a rattle, was important in her worship. The Seven Hathors appear in New Kingdom tales at births, foretelling how the characters will die.

She was shown as a cow, as a woman with a cow's head, and most often as a woman wearing a headdress of cow horns and a sun disk. Hathor also helped the dead cross into the Duat, and the Theban necropolis was portrayed as a mountain with her cow emerging from it.

From the Fourth Dynasty Hathor was the goddess most closely linked with the king, and late Old Kingdom rulers promoted her cult in the provinces to bind those regions to the court. More temples were dedicated to her than to any other Egyptian goddess. At Dendera, her oldest temple in Upper Egypt, which dates to at least the Fourth Dynasty, kings made additions across Egyptian history, and the last version, from the Ptolemaic and Roman periods, is among the best preserved of that time.

Many festivals involved drinking and dancing, such as the Festival of Drunkenness on the twentieth day of the month of Thout. In households women prayed to her for children, and the only known surviving birth brick is decorated with an image of a woman holding her child between images of Hathor. Isis increasingly overshadowed her after the New Kingdom, but she continued to be venerated until the early centuries CE.
hatikvah: Imber emigrated to Ottoman-ruled Palestine in 1882 and read his poem to the pioneers of the early Jewish villages: Rishon LeZion, Rehovot, Gedera and Yesud Hama'ala. Shmuel Cohen, a very young resident of Rishon LeZion with a musical background, sang the poem to a melody he knew from Romania, after seeing the emotional response of the farmers who had heard it. His adaptation helped the poem spread quickly through the Zionist communities of Palestine, and it was adopted as an anthem by the Hovevei Zion and later by the Zionist Movement.

The melody is based on "La Mantovana", a 16th-century Italian song composed by Giuseppe Cenci (Giuseppino del Biado) around 1600. It circulated widely in Renaissance Europe under other titles, among them the Polish "Pod Krakowem" and the Romanian "Cucuruz cu frunza-n sus". Its best-known earlier use was by Bedřich Smetana in Vltava, from Má vlast. The tune follows a minor scale, which is uncommon in national anthems and often heard as mournful, although the title and words are optimistic. The first line of the refrain, "Our hope is not yet lost", has been compared with the openings of the Polish and Ukrainian anthems, and may allude to the vision of the dried bones in Ezekiel 37.

The Zionist Organization held anthem competitions in 1898 and 1900 and judged all the entries unsatisfactory. Imber's poem was popular nonetheless, and at the Sixth Zionist Congress in 1903 it was sung by those opposed to the proposal for a Jewish state in Uganda. Only at the Eighteenth Congress in Prague in 1933 did a motion formally adopt it as the movement's anthem. The British Mandate government briefly banned its public performance from 1919.

In 1948 the song was unofficially proclaimed the anthem of the State of Israel. It became official only in November 2004, when the Knesset sanctioned an abbreviated version, the first stanza and refrain. Some religious Jews have objected that it never mentions God or the Torah, and some non-Jewish citizens of Israel, particularly Arab citizens, find that its focus on Jewish aspirations makes it hard to identify with.
hatshepsut: Hatshepsut was the eldest daughter of Thutmose I and his great royal wife Ahmose. After her father's death she was married to her half-brother Thutmose II, when she was fourteen or fifteen. The couple had at least one daughter, Princess Neferure. When Thutmose II died, his son Thutmose III inherited the throne as a child of two, and Hatshepsut ruled first as his regent.

By the seventh year of the reign of Thutmose III, around 1472 BCE, she had assumed the position of pharaoh beside him, taking the full royal titulary and sharing his regnal count, which backdated her accession to Year 1. Thutmose III became junior coregent. She is depicted in statues with the regalia of the office, including a false beard, and the images are seen as symbolic. Priests told a story of divine birth in which Amun conceived her through her mother, and the Oracle of Amun proclaimed her pharaoh.

She re-established trade networks disrupted during the Hyksos occupation and funded an expedition to the Land of Punt, around Year 9, which returned with 31 living myrrh trees and frankincense. She was one of the most prolific builders in Egypt. She erected twin obelisks at Karnak and built the Red Chapel and the Temple of Pakhet, which the Greeks called the Speos Artemidos. Her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari, with its focal point Djeser-Djeseru, is considered a masterpiece of ancient architecture. Her last dated attestation is Year 20, and she no longer appears in Year 22.

Her death is presumed in Year 22 of Thutmose III. She was probably buried in KV20 in the Valley of the Kings with her father, though Thutmose I was later moved to another tomb. A mummy from tomb KV60 was proposed in 2007 as hers, partly because a molar found in a canopic box seemed to fit its jaw, but in 2011 the tooth was identified as a lower molar while the mummy lacked an upper one, casting doubt on the identification.

Late in the reign of Thutmose III and into that of his son Amenhotep II, her cartouches and images were chiselled from walls and her statues at Deir el-Bahari were torn down and buried in a pit. Why this was done is not clear; scholars have proposed political necessity, the securing of Amenhotep II's uncertain claim, and a ritual deactivation of statues. The erasure confused nineteenth-century Egyptologists such as Jean-Francois Champollion, who found feminine verbs beside a bearded king. James Henry Breasted called her the first great woman in history of whom we are informed.
hattusa: The earliest traces of settlement on the site date from the 6th millennium BCE. Toward the end of the 3rd millennium BCE the Hattian people settled there and called the place Hattush. Assyrian merchants set up a trading post there in the 19th and 18th centuries BCE. A burned layer shows the city was destroyed around 1700 BCE; King Anitta of Kussara took credit and erected an inscribed curse on anyone who resettled it. The city was nevertheless rebuilt. Around 1650 BCE the Hittite king Labarna moved the capital from Neša to Hattusa and took the name Hattusili, the man from Hattusa.

The capital later moved north to Sapinuwa under Tudhaliya I after attacks by the Kaskians, and south to Tarhuntassa under Muwatalli II. In the mid-13th century BCE Mursili III returned the seat to Hattusa, where it remained until the end of the Hittite kingdom in the 12th century BCE.

At its peak the city covered 1.8 square kilometres, in an inner and an outer part surrounded by massive walls erected under Suppiluliuma I, c. 1344 to 1322 BCE. The inner city held a citadel with large administrative buildings and temples, and the royal residence stood on a high ridge called Büyükkale. The outer city to the south had elaborate gateways decorated with reliefs of warriors, lions and sphinxes, and four temples. Modern estimates put the population at around 10,000. Houses of timber and mud brick have vanished, leaving only the stone walls of temples and palaces.

The city was destroyed with the Hittite state around 1200 BCE, as part of the Late Bronze Age collapse. Excavations suggest it was abandoned gradually over several decades, and a regional drought has been suggested. The final burning probably came after the royal family, elites and state apparatus had left, and agricultural communities with a different material culture settled in the ruins as early as the 12th century BCE.

The French archaeologist Charles Texier brought attention to the ruins after his visit in 1834. In 1905 and 1906 Hugo Winckler of the German Oriental Society began excavating the royal fortress. Thousands of tablets were recovered, mostly in the then unreadable Hittite language, and a few Akkadian texts identified the site as Hattusa. Systematic German excavations continue, and the site was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1986.

About 30,000 clay tablets from Hattusa form the main corpus of Hittite literature, among them official correspondence, contracts, legal codes, cult procedures and oracles. One tablet records the terms of a peace between the Hittites and Egypt under Ramesses II after the Battle of Kadesh, in 1259 or 1258 BCE.
haut-rhin: Haut-Rhin, meaning Upper Rhine, is one of the original 83 departments of the French Revolution. It was created on 4 March 1790, by the law of 22 December 1789, from the southern half of the province of Alsace, known as Haute-Alsace. In 1798 it absorbed Mulhouse, formerly a free city and the last Swiss enclave in the south of Alsace, and in 1800 it took in the whole department of Mont-Terrible. In 1814 it lost the territories that had belonged to Mont-Terrible, which were returned to Switzerland except for the former County of Montbéliard, and in 1816 Montbéliard was transferred to Doubs.

In 1871 most of it was annexed by the German Empire under the Treaty of Frankfurt, and the remaining French part later formed the Territoire de Belfort, so named since 1922. The department returned to France in 1919 under the Treaty of Versailles but remains administratively separate from Belfort. In 1940 it was annexed de facto by Nazi Germany, and France recovered it in 1944.

Haut-Rhin borders the Territoire de Belfort and the Vosges department and the Vosges Mountains to the west, Bas-Rhin to the north, Switzerland to the south and Germany to the east, where the frontier follows the Rhine. A fertile plain lies at its centre. The population was 770,738 in 2023. Mulhouse is the most populous commune and Colmar, the prefecture, the second.

Alsace and the neighbouring Moselle department keep a legal system slightly different from the rest of France. Its statutes date from the period 1871 to 1919, when the area belonged to the German Empire, and Paris accepted after 1919 that some local laws would remain. Notably, there is no formal separation of church and state there. On 1 January 2021 Bas-Rhin and Haut-Rhin were merged into the European Collectivity of Alsace.
haute-loire: Haute-Loire, which means Upper Loire, is a landlocked department surrounded by the departments of Loire, Ardèche, Lozère, Cantal and Puy-de-Dôme. The Loire rises in its southern part and flows north, creating a wide valley with ranges of the Massif Central on either side. The highest point is Mont Mézenc at 1,753 metres, and the average elevation is 719 metres. Part of the north lies in the Livradois-Forez Regional Natural Park, a protected area of farmland and woodland.

The first known inhabitants were hunter-gatherers, later followed by pastoralists. The Gaulish tribe of the Vellavi later controlled the region. Between 462 and 477 it was incorporated into the Visigothic Kingdom, ending Roman political control. After Clovis I won the Battle of Vouillé in 507, Velay came under Frankish rule. In about 928 the area became a fiefdom of the Count of Toulouse and later came under the Count of Poitiers.

Haute-Loire is one of the original 83 departments created during the French Revolution, on 4 March 1790. Two thirds of it, centred on Le Puy-en-Velay, is the old Velay, and its distance from Toulouse had allowed it a great deal of autonomy. During the Second World War French partisans, aided by Allied supply drops, liberated the department. Le Puy-en-Velay was besieged by mid-August 1944, and on 18 August Germans trying to escape in a convoy of fifty trucks were ambushed. The town fell the next day.

Le Puy-en-Velay is the prefecture and the largest town, and the department had 228,654 inhabitants in 2023. The cathedral of Le Puy is a gathering place for pilgrims before they set out for Santiago de Compostela, and it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1998. Another pilgrimage site is a 12th-century chapel on a rocky pinnacle, reached by 268 steps. Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette, was born in 1757 at the Château de Chavaniac.
haute-savoie: Haute-Savoie takes its name from the historical region of Savoy, as does the neighbouring department of Savoie to the south. To the north it borders the Swiss canton of Geneva and Lake Geneva, to the east the canton of Valais and Italy's Aosta Valley, and to the west the department of Ain. It has the largest range of elevations of any French department: its lowest point is 250 m in the Rhône Valley and its highest is Mont Blanc, at 4,810 m. Because the country is mountainous, passes matter to trade and economic life, among them the Col de la Forclaz and the Mont Blanc Tunnel, which links Chamonix to Courmayeur.

Savoy was governed by the House of Savoy from 1032 to 1860, and the Dukes of Savoy ruled the region from 1416 to 1720. After the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713 the territory of modern Haute-Savoie and neighbouring Savoie became part of the Kingdom of Sardinia. France annexed the region by the Treaty of Turin, formalised on 24 March 1860.

From November 1942 to September 1943 Haute-Savoie was under military occupation by Fascist Italy. The Maquis des Glières, a band of Free French Resistance fighters, operated from the department. In the winter of 1943–1944 German troops burned down around 500 farms in response to Resistance activity. The first Winter Olympic Games were held at Chamonix in 1924.
havana: Havana lies on the northern coast of Cuba along the Straits of Florida, south of the Florida Keys, where the Gulf of Mexico joins the Atlantic Ocean. The city extends mostly westward and southward from a bay, which is entered through a narrow inlet and divides into three main harbours. The Almendares River crosses the city from south to north.

The city stands mostly on low hills. A limestone ridge about 60 metres high slopes up from the east and culminates in the heights of La Cabaña and El Morro, where the Spanish built fortifications overlooking the eastern bay.

In the early 16th century Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar founded the town of San Cristóbal de la Habana on the southern coast of Cuba, at the mouth of the Mayabeque River, now the town of Batabanó. The low and swampy land caused the settlement to fail. In those years the Spanish established settlements on the northern coast, among them La Chorrera, at the mouth of the Almendares River. The town that became Havana grew up beside Puerto de Carenas, the Careening Port, in 1519, and the quality of the harbour led to the change of location.

Havana overtook Santiago in the mid-16th century because of the advantages of its harbour and became the capital of the island. It became a fundamental place for the Spanish colonial empire in the Americas and a stopping point for galleons returning to the Iberian Peninsula, and walls and forts were built to protect it from naval attacks. After the Cuban War of Independence a new constitution was adopted in 1901.

Havana is the capital and largest city of Cuba and the seat of its government. It is the country's main port. The population in 2021 was 2,142,939. Its economy first developed on its location as one of the early great trade centres of the New World, and sugar and a slave trade first brought riches to the city.

Old Havana, Habana Vieja, contains the core of the original city and was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982. Its landmarks include the Fortress San Carlos de la Cabaña, El Morro Castle, built because of the threat to the harbour from pirates, and the Fortress San Salvador de la Punta, built in the 16th century. The University of Havana was established in 1728.
havel: The Havel flows through four German states: Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Brandenburg, Berlin and Saxony-Anhalt. It is a right tributary of the Elbe, which it joins at Havelberg. The direct distance from its source to its mouth is only 94 kilometres, far less than the river's own length. South of Spandau, where the Spree joins it, the river widens into a broad lake that extends, through some narrower reaches, to Potsdam. Among its features there are the Großer Wannsee, the island of Schwanenwerder and the island of Pfaueninsel, and the river passes Brandenburg an der Havel before reaching the Elbe.

Earlier Greek and Latin sources, such as the Germania of Tacitus, wrote the river's name as Habola, Habula or Havela. The name is related to German words such as Haff and Hafen, meaning a harbour or port. The Slavic people who later moved into the Havel area were called Heveller in German sources, and occasionally Havolane.

In the twentieth century the river became part of a political frontier. During the partition of Germany, the stretch where the Havel enters Berlin formed the border between East Germany and West Berlin, and border control points were set up for vessels on it. In the 1950s the Havel Canal was built, joining the river at Hennigsdorf and running to Paretz, so that East German vessels could avoid the stretch of river under the political control of West Berlin.

The Havel is navigable from the Mecklenburg Lake District to its confluence with the Elbe. Its upper reaches carry little other than leisure traffic, but further downstream it is an important link in the German commercial waterway network, carrying traffic from the Rhine and the North Sea to Berlin and Poland. Canals connect it to the Oder and to the Elbe, among them the Oder-Havel Canal and the Elbe-Havel Canal.

In its lower course the Havel passes through a series of locks, for example at Spandau, Rathenow and Havelberg. At Potsdam the navigation splits into two channels, and at Brandenburg an der Havel commercial shipping uses a separate canal north of the city centre, while leisure craft pass through the town itself.
hawaii: Hawaii consists of 137 volcanic islands that make up almost the entire Hawaiian archipelago, spanning 1,500 miles in the Pacific Ocean about 2,000 miles southwest of the U.S. mainland. The eight main islands, from northwest to southeast, are Niʻihau, Kauaʻi, Oʻahu, Molokaʻi, Lānaʻi, Kahoʻolawe, Maui and Hawaiʻi, after which the state is named. The archipelago is physiographically and ethnologically part of Polynesia. The name Hawaiʻi is very similar to Proto-Polynesian *Sawaiki, reconstructed as meaning homeland, and one explanation names it for Hawaiʻiloa, a figure of oral tradition said to have discovered the islands.

The date of human arrival is debated. Early archaeological studies suggested Polynesians from the Marquesas or Society Islands arrived as early as the 3rd century CE. Some archaeologists think a later wave from Tahiti around 1100 CE introduced a new line of high chiefs, the kapu system, human sacrifice and the building of heiau, as Hawaiian tradition tells of Paʻao. Others say no evidence supports a later influx and treat Paʻao as myth, and more recent studies place the first settlement at around 900 to 1200 CE. The islands were home to numerous independent chiefdoms.

In 1778 the British explorer James Cook was the first known non-Polynesian to arrive. European and American explorers, traders and whalers followed, and introduced diseases such as syphilis, tuberculosis, smallpox and measles. The indigenous population fell from an estimated 300,000 in the 1770s to 60,000 in the 1850s and 24,000 in 1920, though estimates of the pre-contact figure range from 150,000 to 1.5 million. Hawaii became a unified, internationally recognised kingdom in 1810.

Sugar plantations had a strong foothold by the 1840s and were tightly controlled by American missionary families and businessmen known as the Big Five. In 1893 resident American and European capitalists and landholders overthrew the monarchy. Hawaii was an independent republic from 1894 until 12 August 1898, when it became a U.S. territory. It was attacked by Japan on 7 December 1941 and admitted as a state on 21 August 1959. In 1993 the U.S. government formally apologised for its role in the overthrow.

Hawaii is the 50th state of the United States, with its capital and largest city, Honolulu, on Oʻahu, where two thirds of residents live. Hawaiian was added to the state constitution in 1978 as an official language alongside English. Kamehameha III chose Honolulu as capital for its natural harbour, the present-day Honolulu Harbor, and the previous capitals were Lahaina on Maui and Kailua-Kona on Hawaiʻi. The aboriginal culture is Polynesian, and lūʻau and hula have spread in modified form to the wider United States.
hawiye: The Hawiye trace their lineage to Sheikh Ahmed bin Abdulrahman bin Uthman, known as Sheikh Hawiye. Oral tradition and Arabic hagiologies remember him as a saint called Hawi al-Ulum, conservator of knowledge, a name shortened in time to Hawiye, and carry his genealogy back to Aqeel bin Abu Talib. Some scholars regard such claims as historically untenable. The anthropologist Ioan Lewis held that traditions of descent from noble Arab families are most probably figurative expressions of the importance of Islam in Somali society. Tradition places his tomb at Qundhuro in the Haraghe region, where his eldest son Karanle is buried beside him.

The 12th-century writer Al-Idrisi placed the Hawiye on the coast between Ras Hafun and Merca and in the lower basin of the Shabelle river, the first documentary reference to a specific Somali group. Ibn Sa'id, who lived from 1214 to 1274, called Merca their capital.

In the 13th century the Hawiye, with the Rahanweyn, came under the Ajuran Empire, whose domain reached from Hobyo in the north to Qelafo in the west and Kismayo in the south. The Ajuran are themselves said to descend from the Jambelle branch of the Hawiye, and Lee Cassanelli describes Ajuran power as resting on spiritual pre-eminence and Hawiye kinship solidarity.

According to local oral tradition as Cassanelli reports it, the Hiraab Imamate was an alliance of closely related groups of the Gorgaarte division. Its founders rebelled because the Ajuran rulers had grown proud, neglected sharia law and imposed heavy taxes. With Mogadishu as its capital, the imamate ruled from the Shabelle valley and the Benadir to the arid lands of Mudug for at least two centuries. The explorer John Kirk, visiting in 1873, met Imam Mahmood at Mogadishu and saw about twenty large dhows there and at Merca loading grain, much of it for Zanzibar.

At independence in 1960 the first president, Aden Adde, the first prime minister, Abdullahi Issa, and the founder of the army, Daud Abdulle Hirsi, were all Hawiye. Hawiye leaders formed the United Somali Congress in opposition to President Siad Barre, whom General Mohamed Farrah Aidid, of the Habar Gidir, overthrew in 1991. From late 1991 Mogadishu was divided between the factions of Aidid and of President Ali Mahdi Muhammad, of the Abgaal. The stalemate lasted until 2006, when the Islamic Courts Union, a predominantly Hawiye organisation, ended the rule of the factional warlords, before an Ethiopian intervention overthrew it. The Hiraab hereditary leadership survives to this day.
hayreddin-barbarossa: Hayreddin was born on Lesbos, and was called Khizr or Hızır as a child. His father, Yakup Ağa, was a sipahi who had taken part in the Ottoman conquest of the island in 1462 and became an established potter. His mother, Katerina, was a Greek Orthodox woman from Lesbos. Of the four sons, Oruç, Ilyas and Khizr all became seamen. The brothers turned privateers against the Knights Hospitaller based on Rhodes. The Knights killed Ilyas in a fight, and Oruç rowed as a galley slave for the Order for four years until his father paid a ransom.

In 1503 Oruç made the island of Djerba his base, and Khizr joined him. The brothers were later allowed to use the port of La Goulette, near Tunis, on condition of giving one third of their spoils to its sultan. Between 1504 and 1510 Oruç carried Muslim Mudéjars from Spain to North Africa, and the title Baba Oruç, meaning Father Oruç, is said to have become Barbarossa in Spain, France and Italy.

In 1516 the brothers took Jijel and Algiers from the Spaniards. In 1517 Oruç offered Algiers to the Ottoman sultan Selim I, who accepted it as a province. Oruç and his brother Ishak were killed in combat near Tlemcen in 1518.

Khizr then offered his allegiance to Selim and in 1519 received the title of beylerbey, with janissaries, galleys and cannons. He defeated a Spanish and Italian army that tried to retake Algiers in 1519 and raided the coasts of Provence and Spain. In 1533 Sultan Suleiman appointed him Kapudan Pasha. In 1534 he sailed with 80 galleys, raided Calabria and the Gulf of Naples, and captured Tunis, forcing the Hafsid sultan Mulay Hassan to flee.

Barbarossa retired to Constantinople in 1545, leaving his son Hasan Pasha in charge in Algiers, and dictated his memoirs, five hand-written volumes known as the Gazavat-ı Hayreddin Paşa. He died in 1546 in his seaside palace at Büyükdere on the Bosphorus. He is buried in a mausoleum built in 1541 by the architect Mimar Sinan near the ferry port of Beşiktaş, at the site where his fleet used to assemble. The Ottoman supremacy in the Mediterranean that he established lasted until the Battle of Lepanto in 1571.
hebei: Hebei means north of the river, from its position north of the Yellow River on the North China Plain. In the Yu Gong the region is recorded as Jizhou, which gave it the abbreviation Ji, and its nickname Yanzhao comes from the states of Yan and Zhao that held it in antiquity. The west of the province rises into the Taihang Mountains and the Yan Mountains run through the north, beyond which lie the grasslands of Inner Mongolia. The Bohai Sea lies to the east, and the province entirely surrounds Beijing and Tianjin on land.

In the Warring States period Jin was partitioned and much of its territory in Hebei went to Zhao. Under the Han dynasty the area was ruled as You Prefecture in the north and Ji Province in the south. At the end of the Han, Yuan Shao overcame Gongsun Zan there but was defeated by Cao Cao at the Battle of Guandu in 200. The northern frontier position made Hebei change hands often in the age of the Sixteen Kingdoms. The Northern Qi had its capital at Ye, near modern Linzhang. During the Tang dynasty the area was officially called Hebei for the first time, and a Great Yan State existed there from 756 to 763 during the An Lushan Rebellion.

Emperor Gaozu of the Later Jin ceded much of northern Hebei to the Khitan Liao dynasty. These Sixteen Prefectures of Yanyun, which lay within the Great Wall, became a weakness in Chinese defence for the next century. After the Jingkang Incident of 1127 the Southern Song gave up all of North China to the Jurchen Jin dynasty. Between 1048 and 1128 the Yellow River ran directly through the province. Under the Yuan the area was administered directly from the capital Dadu. In the Ming it became Beizhili, and the Yongle Emperor moved the capital to Beijing in 1421. The Qing called it Zhili, meaning directly ruled, and the Republic of China created the province of Hebei in 1928, when the capital moved to Nanjing.

Hebei is a province of North China with Shijiazhuang as its capital and largest city; its population was 74.6 million at the 2020 census. After the founding of the People's Republic, the regions around Chengde and Zhangjiakou were merged into it. The Tangshan earthquake of 28 July 1976 killed about 242,000 people by the official count. Five UNESCO World Heritage Sites lie there, among them the Great Wall, the Chengde Mountain Resort and the Qing imperial tombs. The Zhaozhou Bridge, built during the Sui dynasty, is the oldest standing bridge in China.
hebrew: Hebrew is a Northwest Semitic language and belongs to the Canaanite languages. It was the spoken language of the Iron Age kingdoms of Israel and Judah from about 1200 to 586 BCE, and epigraphic evidence supports the view that the earlier layers of biblical literature reflect their language. The earliest examples of written Paleo-Hebrew date to the 10th century BCE. Two claims for older inscriptions are disputed: Amihai Mazar called a shard from Khirbet Qeiyafa, which its discoverer Yossi Garfinkel thought might be the earliest Hebrew writing, proto-Canaanite, and a claimed curse tablet from Mount Ebal is rejected by practically all professional epigraphers apart from its discoverer's team.

Nearly all the Hebrew Bible is written in Biblical Hebrew, much of it in a dialect that scholars believe flourished around the 6th century BCE. For this reason Jews have called it Lashon Hakodesh, 'the holy tongue', since ancient times. The Bible itself calls it Yehudit, 'Judean', and the name Ivrit appears in the Mishnah. Hebrew is written from right to left in an abjad of 22 letters. The ancient Paleo-Hebrew alphabet resembled the Canaanite and Phoenician ones, while the modern 'square' script, Ashurit, developed from the Aramaic script.

Scholars debate how far Hebrew remained a spoken vernacular after the Babylonian exile, when Old Aramaic was the predominant international language. It ceased to be a regular spoken language between 200 and 400 CE, as it declined after the unsuccessful Bar Kokhba revolt against the Roman Empire. It survived as the language of Jewish liturgy, rabbinic literature, commerce between Jews of different native languages and poetry. The first dated book printed in Hebrew was published by Abraham Garton in Reggio in 1475. With the rise of Zionism in the 19th century it was revived as a spoken language, led by Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, and Modern Hebrew became the main language of the Yishuv in Palestine and then the official language of the State of Israel.
hebrides: The Hebrides are the largest archipelago in Scotland and the British Isles, with a combined area of 7,285 square kilometres. The Inner Hebrides, closer to the mainland, include Islay, Jura, Skye, Mull, Raasay, Staffa and the Small Isles. The Outer Hebrides form a chain of more than 100 islands and skerries about 70 kilometres west of the mainland, among them Lewis and Harris, North Uist, Benbecula, South Uist and Barra. Their rocks range from Precambrian strata, among the oldest in Europe, to Paleogene igneous intrusions. Pliny the Elder, around 77 CE, wrote that there were 30 Hebudes.

The islands were settled in the Mesolithic era around 6500 BCE or earlier. The standing stones at Callanish date to the 3rd millennium BCE, and Cladh Hallan, a Bronze Age settlement on South Uist, is the only site in the UK where prehistoric mummies have been found. Scottish Gaelic arrived from Ireland with the growing influence of the kingdom of Dál Riata from the 6th century CE.

Viking raids began towards the end of the 8th century, and in the following decades the Hebrides came under Norse control and settlement, especially after Harald Fairhair's victory at Hafrsfjord in 872. The Norse called the islands Suðreyjar, the Southern Isles. In 1098 Edgar of Scotland formally signed the islands over to Magnus III of Norway, who had conquered Orkney, the Hebrides and the Isle of Man in a swift campaign. His skald Bjorn Cripplehand recorded that in the Uists the king dyed his sword red in blood.

As the Norse era closed, Norse-speaking princes gave way to Gaelic-speaking clan chiefs, including the MacLeods of Lewis and Harris and Clan Donald. By the early 14th century the MacDonald Lords of the Isles, based on Islay, were in theory their feudal superiors. James IV forfeited their lands in 1493. Many islesmen supported the Jacobite risings of 1715 and 1745, and after Culloden the clan system was broken up and the islands became a series of landed estates.

The culture of the inhabitants has been successively influenced by Celtic-speaking, Norse-speaking and English-speaking peoples, and the names of the islands derive from the different languages spoken there. Much of Scottish Gaelic literature and music has historically originated in the Hebrides. The economy depends on crofting, fishing, tourism, the oil industry and renewable energy. The islands have less biodiversity than mainland Scotland, but a significant number of seals and seabirds.
hebron: Hebron lies in the Judaean Mountains at 930 metres above sea level, 30 kilometres south of Jerusalem and about 43 kilometres north-east of Beersheba. It is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the Levant. Excavations around Tel Rumeida reveal strong fortifications from the Early Bronze Age, and the city flourished in the 17th and 18th centuries BCE before a fire destroyed it. In Arabic the city is al-Khalil, from the epithet Khalil al-Rahman, Friend of the Merciful, given to Abraham.

Genesis says the city was formerly called Kiryath-arba. After the destruction of the First Temple most Jewish inhabitants were exiled, and Edomite presence is attested in the Persian and Hellenistic periods. The settlement at Tel Rumeida was destroyed, probably during John Hyrcanus's conquest of Idumaea around 112 or 107 BCE, and later layers show a population with Jewish characteristics, though the evidence cannot say whether this was settlers or converted Idumaeans. Herod the Great built the wall that still surrounds the Cave of the Patriarchs. During the First Jewish-Roman War the town was laid waste by Sextus Vettulenus Cerialis.

The Rashidun Caliphate took Hebron in 638 and turned the Byzantine church over Abraham's tomb into a mosque. The Crusader Godfrey de Bouillon captured the city in 1099 and renamed it Castellion Saint Abraham; the sanctuary became a church until Muslim rule returned. In 1260, after Baibars defeated the Mongol army, minarets were added, and six years later he barred Christians and Jews from the sanctuary. Sephardi Jews settled in Hebron after the expulsion from Spain. The British occupied the city on 8 December 1917. Jordan held it from 1948 and Israel from the Six-Day War of 1967; under the Hebron Agreement of 1997 Israel withdrew from 80 percent of the city, which passed to the Palestinian Authority.

Hebron is the capital of the Hebron Governorate, with 201,063 people inside the city limits. It is a commercial and industrial centre, known for limestone, grapes, ceramics, glass and metalworking. The Cave of the Patriarchs is said to hold the tombs of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and their wives; its Isaac Hall serves as the Ibrahimi Mosque and the Abraham and Jacob Hall as a synagogue. The Old City, with narrow winding streets and stone houses, is one of the best preserved sites of the Mamluk era and was inscribed by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site in 2017.
hecataeus-of-miletus: Hecataeus was the son of Hegesander and came from a very wealthy family of Miletus, a city then under Persian rule in the satrapy of Lydia. He was active at the time of the Greco-Persian Wars. After travelling widely he settled in his native city, where he held a high position and devoted himself to writing geographical and historical works.

When Aristagoras, acting tyrant of Miletus, called a council of leading Ionians to organise a revolt against Persian rule, Hecataeus tried without success to dissuade his fellow citizens. In 494 BCE, when the defeated Ionians had to sue for terms, he was one of the ambassadors sent to the Persian satrap Artaphernes, whom he persuaded to restore the constitutions of the Ionian cities.

Two works are known, both surviving only in fragments. The Periodos ges, meaning Journey round the Earth or World Survey, was written in two books, the first on Europe and the second on Asia, which included Africa. It began at the Straits of Gibraltar and ran clockwise round the coasts of the Mediterranean and Black Sea, giving the peoples and places met on a coastal voyage. More than 300 fragments are preserved, mostly as citations for place names in the work of Stephanus of Byzantium.

His other work, the Genealogies, was a book on mythography in four books, of which fewer than forty fragments remain. It took a sceptical view of the traditions of families who claimed descent from gods. He is also credited with improving the map of Anaximander, which showed the world as a disc encircled by Oceanus.

Hecataeus is the first known Greek historian and was one of the first classical writers to mention the Celtic and Illyrian peoples. He was probably the first of the logographers to attempt a serious prose history and to use a critical method to separate myth from historical fact, although he accepted Homer and other poets as trustworthy authorities. Herodotus, though he contradicts Hecataeus at least once, owes him the concept of a prose history.
hecate: Hecate's earliest appearance in literature is in Hesiod's Theogony in the 8th century BCE, where she is described as a goddess of great honour with domains in sky, earth and sea. Evidence suggests she originated among the Carians of Anatolia, where most names invoking her, such as Hecataeus and Hecatomnus, are attested, and where her unrivalled cult site stood at Lagina. She may derive from local sun goddesses. The earliest evidence of her cult comes from Selinunte in Sicily, where she had a temple in the 6th and 5th centuries BCE.

Hecate was associated with borders, city walls, doorways and crossroads, and so with realms beyond the world of the living. Her cult titles reflect this role: Enodia, on the way; Propylaia, before the gate; Triodia, who frequents crossroads; and Klêidouchos, holding the keys. She was expected to avert harmful spirits from the house or city she guarded, and so could also refuse to avert them. As holder of the keys between realms she is recognized as a chthonic goddess. In the 3rd century BCE Theocritus describes her unlocking the gates of death, and she appears with Hermes guiding Persephone back from the underworld.

By the 1st century CE her chthonic and nocturnal character had made her a goddess heavily associated with witchcraft; in Lucan's Pharsalia the witch Erichtho invokes her. She was also tied to plant lore, medicines and poisons, and Apollonius of Rhodes says Medea was taught medicine by her. Dogs were among her most important attributes, and garlic was a favoured offering. Her lunar role rests on late evidence: no artwork before the Roman period connects her to the Moon.

Hecate's cult became established in Athens about 430 BCE, when the sculptor Alcamenes made the earliest known triple-formed statue for her new temple. Home shrines often took the form of a Hekataion, a carving of a triple Hecate facing three directions around a central pillar, and larger ones stood at public crossroads, such as on the road to the Acropolis.

Athenians honoured her at the Deipnon, a meal served to Hecate and the restless dead once a lunar month at the dark moon. It was set out at a small shrine by the front door, since the street and the doorway form a crossroads where she dwelled, and might include cake or bread, fish, eggs and honey. The Romans often knew her as Trivia, an epithet shared with Diana, and in the Roman era she was closely identified with Diana and Artemis.
hector-berlioz: Hector Berlioz was born on 11 December 1803 at La Côte-Saint-André, in the département of Isère, the eldest child of Louis Berlioz, a physician. He moved to Paris in 1821, aged seventeen, and at his father's insistence enrolled in the School of Medicine, forcing himself to continue despite his revulsion at dissecting bodies. In 1824 he composed a Messe solennelle, which was performed twice and then suppressed; a copy was found in 1991. His first opera, Les Francs-juges, was never performed and survives in fragments, the best known being its overture.

Berlioz won the Prix de Rome in 1830 with the cantata La Mort de Sardanapale, having modified his natural style to please the judges after his Cléopâtre of the previous year had been thought to betray dangerous tendencies. In the same year he wrote the Symphonie fantastique, in which an idealised portrait of the Irish actress Harriet Smithson recurs as an idée fixe. After a concert on 9 December 1832 she finally met him, and they married; the marriage foundered, and she died in June 1862.

In the 1840s he struggled as a composer, completing the song cycle Les Nuits d'été to poems by Théophile Gautier and publishing articles on orchestration that became his Treatise on Instrumentation. After the failure of La Damnation de Faust he turned increasingly to conducting, appearing in London from 1851 and in Germany.

Berlioz called four large works symphonies, but his idea of the genre differed greatly from the classical German pattern, since he used the symphony to tell a story. His three completed operas were never written to commission. Benvenuto Cellini was an outright failure, and Les Troyens, a five-act, five-hour work, was too large for the Opéra: only its last three acts were staged in Paris, in November 1863, and were cut further during a run of 22 performances. The experience demoralised him, and he wrote almost no more music.

Opinion was divided for many years between those who thought him an original genius and those who found his music lacking in form. When Richard Strauss revised the Treatise on Instrumentation in 1905 he added new material but left Berlioz's text unchanged. Berlioz died in Paris on 8 March 1869, aged 65.
heidelberg: Heidelberg lies on the eastern edge of the Upper Rhine Plain, where the Neckar leaves its narrow valley between the Odenwald and the Little Odenwald and begins its last stretch towards Mannheim, about 20 kilometres downstream, where it joins the Rhine. The old town lies in the valley on the south bank, dominated by the ruins of the castle, 80 metres above the river on the slopes of the Königstuhl. On the north bank rises the Heiligenberg, or Holy Mountain, along which runs the Philosophers' Walk.

Between 600,000 and 200,000 years ago, Heidelberg Man died at nearby Mauer; his jaw bone, found in 1907, is the earliest evidence of human life in Europe. In the 5th century BCE a Celtic refuge and place of worship was built on the Heiligenberg, and a fort followed around 40 CE. The first reference to Heidelberg itself is in a document of Schönau Abbey dated 1196, taken as the town's founding date. In 1156 the castle and its settlement passed to the house of Hohenstaufen, and in 1214 the Palatinate passed to Ludwig I, Duke of Bavaria. In 1356 the Golden Bull confirmed far-reaching rights for the counts palatine, who were also electors.

The university played a leading part in scholasticism, Renaissance humanism and the German Reformation, and in April 1518 Martin Luther was received there to defend his Ninety-five Theses. The library, founded in 1421, is the oldest existing public library in Germany. The castle on the higher slope was destroyed by a gunpowder explosion in 1537. Heidelberg fell to the Grand Duchy of Baden in 1803, and Grand Duke Charles Frederick re-founded the university, naming it Ruperto-Carola after its two founders. The university reopened in 1945 on the initiative of a small group of professors, among them Alfred Weber and Karl Jaspers.

Heidelberg is the fifth-largest city in Baden-Württemberg, with about 163,000 inhabitants, roughly a quarter of them students. It belongs to the Rhine-Neckar Metropolitan Region, centred on Mannheim. It is a scientific centre, home to the European Molecular Biology Laboratory and four Max Planck Institutes, and has been named a City of Literature by UNESCO's Creative Cities Network.
heidelberg-university: Heidelberg University was founded in 1386 on the instruction of Pope Urban VI and was the third university established in the Holy Roman Empire, after Prague (1347) and Vienna (1365). The Great Schism of 1378, which produced rival popes in Avignon and Rome, made it possible for Heidelberg, a relatively small city and capital of the Electorate of the Palatinate, to gain a university of its own. German rulers and churchmen supported the pope in Rome, and the German students and teachers in Paris lost their stipends and had to leave.

Between 1414 and 1418 professors of theology and law took part in the Council of Constance as counsellors to Louis III. It first taught the nominalism known as the via moderna. In 1412 realism and the teachings of John Wycliffe were forbidden, but around 1454 the university decided that realism would also be taught, so that two ways were taught in parallel.

Martin Luther's disputation at Heidelberg in April 1518 made a lasting impression, and his followers among the masters and scholars became leading Reformationists in south-west Germany. When the Electorate of the Palatinate turned to the Reformed faith, Otto Henry, Elector Palatine, made the university a Calvinist institution, and members of its divinity school took part in creating the Heidelberg Catechism in 1563. In 1803 Karl Friedrich of Baden, to whom the part of the Palatinate on the right bank of the Rhine had been allotted, reestablished it as a state institution. He divided it into five faculties, and it has borne his name together with that of Ruprecht I ever since.

After the Nazi seizure of power in 1933 the university supported the regime like other German universities. It dismissed many staff and students for political and racial reasons, and members of the faculty and students took part in book burnings on 17 May 1933. The inscription over the New University, The Living Spirit, was changed to The German Spirit.

Women have been admitted since 1899. Modern scientific psychiatry, psychopharmacology, experimental psychology, mathematical statistics and modern sociology were introduced as disciplines by Heidelberg students or faculty. Among its historical scientific achievements are the invention of spectroscopy and of the Bunsen burner and the discovery of the elements caesium and rubidium.
heilongjiang: Heilongjiang is the northernmost and easternmost province of China, with the country's northernmost point at Mohe along the Amur and its easternmost at the confluence of the Amur and Ussuri rivers. It borders Jilin to the south, Inner Mongolia to the west and five regions of Russia to the north and east. Its name means black dragon river, the Chinese name of the Amur. Mountain ranges, among them the Greater and Lesser Khingan, cover much of the province, and the Greater Khingan holds China's largest remaining virgin forest. The east and southwest are flatter and drained by tributaries of the Amur, including the Songhua, Nen and Mudan rivers. Winters are long and bitter, and the far north is subarctic.

Ancient Chinese records name the Sushen, Buyeo, Mohe and Khitan among the peoples of the region, and Mongolic Donghu lived in its west. The eastern portion was ruled by the Bohai Kingdom, then by the Khitan Liao dynasty. The Jurchen Jin dynasty (1115 to 1234), which later ruled much of north China, arose within the borders of modern Heilongjiang.

Heilongjiang was created as an administrative unit in 1683, in the Kangxi era of the Qing dynasty, from the northwestern part of Jilin. It was supervised by the General of Heilongjiang, whose seat moved from Aigun to Nenjiang in 1690 and to Qiqihar in 1699, probably for reasons of supply. Manchuria was closed to Han Chinese migration. In 1858 and 1860 the Qing were forced to give up all land beyond the Amur and Ussuri rivers to the Russian Empire, which gave the province its present northern and eastern borders. Manchuria was then opened to Han settlement, and by the early twentieth century the Han had become the dominant group.

Japanese forces invaded in 1931 and completed their conquest in 1932, and the province became part of the puppet state of Manchukuo. After the Soviet Army defeated Japan in Manchuria in 1945, Heilongjiang became the first province, and Harbin the first major city, to be wholly controlled by the communists. Heilongjiang and Songjiang provinces were merged in 1954.

Heilongjiang's capital and largest city is Harbin. Most residents are Han Chinese, many descended from migrants during the Qing dynasty, from from Shandong and Hebei, and ten indigenous minorities are officially recognised, among them the Manchu, Daur, Oroqen and Hezhen. The Daqing oilfields are an important source of petroleum, and the province has China's largest plantations of rice, corn and soybeans, on fertile black soil.
heinrich-heine: Heine was born on 13 December 1797 in Düsseldorf, then in the Duchy of Berg, the eldest of four children of the textile merchant Samson Heine and Peira, née van Geldern. He was called Harry in childhood. His uncle Salomon realised that he had no talent for trade, and it was decided that he should study law, so in 1819 he went to the University of Bonn. There he was a radical liberal, but he was more interested in history and literature, heard the critic August Wilhelm Schlegel lecture, and began to acquire a reputation as a poet. He also wrote two tragedies, Almansor and William Ratcliff, which had little success in the theatre.

It was extremely difficult to make a living as a writer in Germany, and Heine never had enough money. In Hamburg in January 1826 he met Julius Campe, who remained his chief publisher for the rest of his life. Books under 320 pages had to be submitted to censorship, so Campe printed dissident works in large type to run longer. Heine's travel writings, the Reisebilder, were a success. He left for France in 1831, drawn by the July Revolution, by freedom from German censorship and for a time by Saint-Simonianism. In Paris he became a celebrity, counting Victor Hugo, Frederic Chopin and Franz Liszt among his acquaintances, and wrote everything in German, translating it into French with a collaborator.

After the German Diet banned the Young Germany writers in November 1835, his name was added at Metternich's insistence, but he went on commenting on German politics from a distance. In the 1840s his verse became more political and satirical. The most popular of his political poems was The Silesian Weavers, based on the weavers' uprising of 1844.

In May 1848 Heine fell paralysed and did not leave what he called his mattress-grave until his death on 17 February 1856. A hair analysis in 1997 confirmed chronic lead poisoning. Many composers set his poems, among them Robert Schumann in the song cycle Dichterliebe and Friedrich Silcher in his setting of Die Lorelei. The Nazis removed or destroyed all monuments to him and, from 1940, banned his books. His line from Almansor, spoken after the burning of the Quran at Granada, was engraved at the site of the 1933 book burning on Berlin's Opernplatz.
heinrich-himmler: Heinrich Luitpold Himmler was born in Munich on 7 October 1900 into a conservative middle-class Catholic family. His father, Joseph Gebhard Himmler, was a teacher, and his godfather, Prince Heinrich of Bavaria, had been tutored by his father. He attended a grammar school in Landshut, did well in his schoolwork but struggled in athletics, and suffered lifelong stomach complaints. He served in a reserve battalion in the First World War without seeing combat and joined the Nazi Party on 1 August 1923. As a member of Ernst Röhm's paramilitary unit he took part in the Beer Hall Putsch, was questioned but not charged, and lost his job.

Himmler joined the SS in 1925. On the resignation of its commander Erhard Heiden in January 1929 he became Reichsführer-SS with Hitler's approval and over the next year grew the force from about 290 men to about 3,000. Early in 1934, as Hitler and other leaders feared a coup by Röhm, Hermann Göring handed control of the Prussian secret police, the Gestapo, to Himmler on 20 April, and Hitler appointed him chief of all German police outside Prussia. Reinhard Heydrich became head of the Gestapo two days later. From 1943 he was also chief of the Kriminalpolizei and Minister of the Interior, and he controlled the Waffen-SS.

In 1939 Himmler, Heydrich and Heinrich Müller carried out a false flag operation to give a pretext for the invasion of Poland, and the Einsatzgruppen, repurposed as death squads, murdered some 65,000 intellectuals and other civilians by the end of that year. At the Wannsee meeting of 20 January 1942 Heydrich told the attendees that Hitler had placed Himmler in charge of the plan for the final solution. In speeches at Poznań in October 1943 Himmler referred explicitly to the extermination of the Jewish people. As Reich Commissioner for the Consolidation of German Nationhood he was deeply involved in Generalplan Ost, whose aim was to enslave, expel or exterminate the native population of the east.

After the 20 July 1944 plot against Hitler, Himmler formed a commission that arrested over 5,000 suspected opponents, and Hitler's reprisals brought the execution of more than 4,900 people. In March 1945 he tried without Hitler's knowledge to open peace talks with the western Allies. Hitler learned of this on 28 April, dismissed him from all his posts and ordered his arrest. British forces captured him, and he committed suicide in British custody on 23 May 1945. He played a central role in the genocide of an estimated 5.5 to 6 million Jews and in the deaths of millions of other victims.
heinrich-schliemann: Heinrich Schliemann was born on 6 January 1822 in Neubukow in Mecklenburg-Schwerin, the fifth of nine children of a poor Lutheran pastor. His mother died when he was nine. His father had schooled him in the tales of the Iliad and the Odyssey, but the family's poverty made university impossible, and at fourteen he became a grocer's apprentice. Later he said his passion for Homer began when he heard a drunken miller recite Homeric verses. In 1841 a ship on which he sailed as a cabin boy foundered in a gale, and he came ashore in the Netherlands and became a bookkeeper in Amsterdam.

In 1846 the firm B. H. Schröder & Co. sent him to St Petersburg as its general agent. He learned languages by a system of his own, and by the end of his life could converse in a dozen besides German. In 1851 he went to California, where his brother had grown rich in the gold fields, and bought and resold gold dust in Sacramento.

Several of the stories in his autobiography of 1881 about this time, including his meeting with President Millard Fillmore and the date of his American citizenship, are contradicted by other evidence. He returned to Russia in 1852, married Ekaterina Petrovna Lyschin and made a profit trading in indigo dye. By 1858 he was wealthy enough to retire.

In 1868 Schliemann visited sites in the Greek world and published Ithaka, der Peloponnesus und Troja, arguing that Hissarlik was Troy. The English amateur Frank Calvert had identified Hissarlik and persuaded him to dig on land his family owned, after Schliemann's soundings at Pınarbaşı disappointed him. By 1873 his trench had revealed nine buried cities.

On 15 June 1873 he found gold that he took to be Priam's Treasure, and later admitted that his story of his wife Sophia carrying it away in her shawl was untrue, since she was in Athens. He smuggled the treasure out of the Ottoman Empire and, after being sued, paid compensation. His collections reached Berlin in 1881 and were taken to Moscow by Soviet forces in 1945.

In 1876 he began digging at Mycenae, under the supervision of Panagiotis Stamatakis, and found the Shaft Graves with their skeletons and gold, among them the so-called Mask of Agamemnon. He later excavated at Orchomenus, at Tiryns with Wilhelm Dörpfeld and again at Troy. The layer he took for Homeric Troy is now dated to between 3,000 and 2,000 BCE, too early for the Trojan War. His excavation of nine layers has been criticised as destructive of significant remains, and he died on 26 December 1890.
heinrich-von-kleist: Bernd Heinrich Wilhelm von Kleist was born on 18 October 1777 in Frankfurt an der Oder, in the Margraviate of Brandenburg. After a scanty education he entered the Prussian Army in 1792, served in the Rhine campaign of 1796 and retired in 1799 as a lieutenant. He studied law, philosophy, natural sciences and Latin at the Viadrina University, and in 1800 took a post in the Ministry of Finance in Berlin. The next year he visited Paris and settled in Switzerland, where he read his first drama, the tragedy The Schroffenstein Family, to Heinrich Zschokke and Ludwig Wieland.

In 1807, on a journey to Dresden, Kleist was arrested by the French as a spy and held in the Fort de Joux. In 1808 he published the journal Phöbus with Adam Heinrich Müller, and in 1810 and 1811 he edited the Berliner Abendblätter. Penthesilea (1808) takes its Amazon queen from a Greek source and shows wild passion. The romantic play Käthchen of Heilbronn (1808) kept its popularity for many years, and the comedy The Broken Jug (1808) made his name in that genre. Die Hermannsschlacht (1809) is anti-Napoleonic propaganda, and The Prince of Homburg, one of his best works, was first published by Ludwig Tieck in 1821.

His Collected Stories of 1810 and 1811 include Michael Kohlhaas, about a Brandenburg horse dealer in Martin Luther's day, as well as The Earthquake in Chile and The Marquise of O. His essays on aesthetics and psychology touch on questions discussed by Kant, Fichte and Schelling.

Kleist met Henriette Vogel in 1809 through Adam Müller. According to the autopsy report she had cancer. On 21 November 1811 they travelled from Berlin to the Wannsee, left farewell letters, and Kleist shot her and then himself on the shore of the Kleiner Wannsee near Potsdam. They were buried in a common grave there. The Eleventh Edition of the Encyclopædia Britannica called him by far the most important North German dramatist of the Romantic movement. The Kleist Prize for German literature is named after him.
hejaz: The name comes from the Arabic verb meaning to separate, because the region divides the Najd in the east from the Tihamah in the west. It lies along the Red Sea Rift, bordered by the Red Sea on the west and Jordan and the Gulf of Aqaba on the north. Its volcanic landscape includes lava fields known as harrat, among the largest alkali basalt regions on earth. Its history has often centred on oasis cities such as Yathrib, later Medina, Fadak, Khaybar, Taymah and Al-Ula, which grew rich on trade, especially the incense trade that carried goods north from South Arabia.

In antiquity the Thamud, attested from the 8th century BCE to the 5th century CE, were based in the north-west around Hegra, and the Kingdom of Lihyan ruled from Dedan in the Al-Ula oasis. The Nabataeans occupied the north-west from the 1st century BCE until the Roman Empire annexed their kingdom in 106 CE. The Quraysh, a tribe of the Mudar confederation, ruled Mecca and cared for the Kaaba. In 622 Muhammad brokered a treaty between pagan Arab and Jewish tribes at Medina, the Constitution of Medina.

The Hejaz was at the centre of the first Islamic state and the Rashidun Caliphate, whose capital was Medina from 622 to 656. Mecca was the capital of the Zubayrid Caliphate from 683 to 692, after which Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan brought the region back under the Umayyads. From 967 to 1916 the local sharifs governed the semi-sovereign Sharifate of Mecca, acknowledging the suzerainty of various dynasties, among them the Ayyubid Sultanate, the Mamluk Sultanate and, from 1517, the Ottoman Empire. On 23 December 1925 Sharif Hussein surrendered to the Saudis, and in 1932 the kingdoms of Hejaz and Nejd were renamed the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

The Hejaz forms the western region of Saudi Arabia and includes Mecca, Medina, Jeddah, Tabuk, Yanbu, Taif and Al-Bahah. Jeddah is its largest city, and Hejazi Arabic is the most widely spoken dialect. Mecca and Medina are the first and second holiest sites in Islam. Al-Hijr, with rock-cut structures credited to the Thamud, was the first World Heritage Site in Saudi Arabia.
helen-of-troy: Helen is a figure of Greek mythology said to have been the most beautiful woman in the world. She was believed to be the daughter of Zeus by Leda or Nemesis, and the sister of Clytemnestra, Castor and Pollux. In her youth she was abducted by Theseus, who left her with his mother Aethra or an associate at Aphidnae or Athens, until her brothers Castor and Pollux invaded Athens and returned her to Sparta.

When she came to marry, kings and princes from around the world sought her hand. Her father Tyndareus feared giving offence to those he rejected, and Odysseus proposed that all the suitors swear to defend the chosen husband against anyone who quarrelled with him. This was the Oath of Tyndareus. Menelaus was chosen because he had offered the most gifts, and he and Helen ruled Sparta after Tyndareus and Leda abdicated. They had a daughter, Hermione.

Paris, a Trojan prince, came to Sparta on a supposed diplomatic mission. Aphrodite had promised him the most beautiful woman in the world as a reward for judging her the most beautiful of the goddesses. Most ancient sources, following Homer, hold that Helen fell in love with him and went to Troy willingly, though she is sometimes shown as abducted. Menelaus called on the other suitors to honour their oaths, and the Trojan War began.

Accounts of her time in Troy contradict one another. Homer shows her as ambivalent, regretful of her choice yet sly in restoring her reputation, while Virgil's Aeneid has her feign Bacchic rites and signal to the Greeks from a tower. Euripides, Stesichorus and Herodotus denied that she went to Troy at all and placed her in Egypt for the war.

In Homer's account Helen returned to Sparta with Menelaus. In another version, used by Euripides in Orestes, Apollo saved her and she was taken up to Mount Olympus, becoming a sea goddess who watched over sailors with Castor and Pollux. Her major cult centres were in Laconia, and at Therapne she shared a shrine with Menelaus. She was also worshipped in Attica and on Rhodes. Images of her appear from the 7th century BCE, and the elopement or abduction was a popular motif in Classical Greece.
helicopter: The fourth-century Daoist book Baopuzi by Ge Hong reportedly describes some of the ideas inherent to rotary-wing aircraft. Designs similar to the Chinese toy appeared in some Renaissance paintings, and in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries Western scientists developed flying machines based on it. The word helicopter is adapted from the French hélicoptère, coined by Gustave Ponton d'Amécourt in 1861 from the Ancient Greek helix, spiral, and pteron, wing.

Engines held back the early machines. Rubber bands and similar devices limited them to toys and small models, and steam engines lacked the power for manned flight. The internal combustion engine at the end of the nineteenth century made lifting humans possible. In the early 1920s the Argentine Raúl Pateras-Pescara de Castelluccio demonstrated one of the first successful applications of cyclic pitch.

A helicopter's rotor consists of a mast, hub and blades. The torque of a single main rotor must be countered, and the design Igor Sikorsky settled on for his VS-300 was a smaller tail rotor at the end of a tail boom. Between 1939 and 1943 the VS-300 went through four iterations and became the basis for modern helicopters. Twin-rotor designs carry more payload, and coaxial, tiltrotor and compound helicopters also fly. The pilot works the cyclic, the collective, the anti-torque pedals and the throttle, and hovering is the most demanding task. If the engine fails, the helicopter can enter autorotation.

Heinrich Focke designed the transverse twin-rotor Fw 61, which first flew in June 1936. Hanna Reitsch flew it inside the Deutschlandhalle in Berlin in February 1938, and it set records between 1937 and 1939. On 11 December 1951 Charles Kaman's K-225 became the first turbine-powered helicopter. Because it can take off and land vertically and hover, a helicopter does work that was impossible or slow for other aircraft, including transport, military roles, firefighting, search and rescue, medical transport and aerial observation.
heliocentrism: Heliocentrism was opposed to geocentrism, which placed the Earth at the centre. The sphericity of the Earth was widely recognised in Greek and Roman astronomy from at least the 4th century BCE, but its daily rotation and yearly orbit around the Sun were not universally accepted until the Copernican Revolution. The first non-geocentric model was proposed by the Pythagorean Philolaus, who taught that a central fire lay at the centre of the universe, with the Earth, Sun, Moon and planets revolving around it. Aristarchus of Samos developed a fully heliocentric model in the 3rd century BCE. It did not replace the view of a stationary Earth, and from the 2nd century CE the predominant model was the geocentric one of Ptolemy's Almagest.

Other traditions came close to it. Aryabhata, in the Aryabhatiya of 499, proposed that the Earth spins on its axis and gave the planets' periods with respect to the Sun, though most scholars hold that his system was not explicitly heliocentric. In India, Nilakantha Somayaji, in the Tantrasamgraha of 1501, revised a planetary system in which the planets orbit the Sun and the Sun orbits the Earth, similar to the one Tycho Brahe later proposed. Copernicus's De revolutionibus orbium coelestium elaborated the heliocentric model in geometrical detail, derived its parameters from observations and provided tables for computing the positions of stars and planets. In reality his system did not predict the planets' positions any better than the Ptolemaic system.

In 1533 Johann Albrecht Widmannstetter lectured on the theory in Rome, and Pope Clement VII and several cardinals listened with interest. In 1539 Martin Luther remarked that someone wanted to turn the whole of astronomy upside down, and cited Joshua, who bade the sun and not the earth stand still. Giordano Bruno was the only known person to defend Copernicus during his own lifetime, and was condemned by the Roman Inquisition and burned in Rome in 1600. Galileo Galilei reported with his telescope that Jupiter has moons and that Venus shows a full range of phases.

The Galileo affair did little to slow the spread of heliocentrism, and by 1686 Fontenelle's Conversations on the Plurality of Worlds was introducing it to the general public. After the observations of William Herschel, Friedrich Bessel and others it was realised that the Sun, though near the barycenter of the Solar System, is not central in the universe, and modern astronomy distinguishes no universal centre.
heliopolis-ancient-egypt: Heliopolis was the capital of the Heliopolite or 13th nome of Lower Egypt. Its Egyptian name, Iunu, meant "the Pillars", and the Pyramid Texts of the Old Kingdom call it the "House of Ra". The Greeks called it Hēlioúpolis, "City of the Sun", because they identified Ra and Atum, whose principal cult stood there, with their own sun god Helios. It appears in the Hebrew Bible as On. The city was occupied from prehistoric times, when it was a settlement of Stone Age farmers, and it expanded greatly under the Old and Middle Kingdoms.
