Heliopolis was the chief cult centre of Atum, who came to be identified with Ra and then with Horus as Ra-harakhty. Its main temple was the "Great House" or "House of Atum". Its priests held that Atum or Ra was the first being, rising self-created from the primeval waters. A decline in the importance of Ra's cult in the Fifth Dynasty led to the Ennead, a group of nine major deities that placed the others below Ra-Atum. Under Akhenaten in the Eighteenth Dynasty a temple of the Aten was built here, and the cult of the Mnevis bull, another embodiment of the Sun, kept its altar in the city.

Herodotus states that the priests of Heliopolis were the best informed of all the Egyptians in matters of history, and Ptolemy II had Manetho, the chief priest, draw his history of the ancient kings from its archives. Alexander the Great halted here on his march from Pelusium to Memphis. The Ptolemies favoured the cult of Serapis, and Alexandria eclipsed Heliopolis as a seat of learning. By the first century BCE Strabo found the temples deserted and the town almost uninhabited, though priests were still present.

Under Roman rule many of its obelisks were taken away. The taller Vatican obelisk was removed by Caligula, and Augustus took the Obelisk of Montecitorio to Rome. Two smaller ones, called Cleopatra's Needles, later went to London and New York. In the Middle Ages the growth of Cairo and Fustat created a demand for building stone, and builders stripped the ruins of the temples.

The ancient city lies 15 to 20 metres below the streets of Al-Matariyyah, Ain Shams and Tel Al-Hisn in northern Cairo. The obelisk of Senusret I of the Twelfth Dynasty still stands where it was raised, marking the site of the great Temple of Ra-Atum. It is 21 metres high and is believed to be the oldest surviving obelisk in the world. Some crude brick walls can be seen in fields, and a few granite blocks bear the name of Ramesses II. Tombs were excavated in 2004, and parts of a colossal statue of Psamtik I were found in 2017.
helios: Helios most likely has Proto-Indo-European origins. His name is the inherited Greek word for the Sun, cognate with Latin sol, Sanskrit surya and Old Norse sól. Walter Burkert wrote that Helios and the dawn goddess Eos are of impeccable Indo-European lineage in both etymology and status, and the imagery of a chariot-driving solar deity is likely Indo-European too. In Greek mythology Helios is the son of the Titans Hyperion and Theia and the brother of Eos and Selene. He was not among the regular and more prominent deities but a more shadowy member of the Olympian circle, though among the most ancient.

Helios was pictured driving a chariot from east to west each day, rising from the river Oceanus and setting under the earth in the west. At night he was said to travel east in a golden boat. Because the Sun sees everything, he was invoked as a witness to oaths, and he was among the three deities called on in the Iliad to witness the truce between Greeks and Trojans. The best-known story is that of his son Phaethon, who asked to drive the chariot for a day and failed with disastrous results.

In the Odyssey, Odysseus's men kill and eat the sacred cattle that Helios kept at Thrinacia, and at his request Zeus strikes their ship with a thunderbolt. According to Pindar, Helios received no land when the gods divided the earth, and he asked for an island he had seen rising from the sea. This was Rhodes, his major cult centre, where the Colossus of Rhodes, a gigantic statue of the god, stood at the port until an earthquake destroyed it.

Helios was a relatively minor deity in Classical Greece. In late antiquity his worship grew, as he took on elements of Apollo and the Roman sun god Sol and was equated with Mithras. On 25 December 274 the emperor Aurelian instituted a state cult of Sol Invictus, or Helios Megistos, and in the 4th century the emperor Julian made Helios the central divinity of a short-lived revival of traditional Roman religion.

The earliest humanoid images of Helios, from the late sixth and early fifth centuries BCE, show a bearded man on a chariot; later art shows him young and beardless with a radiant crown. The element helium takes its name from him.
hellenistic-period: The Greek world was fragmented after the Peloponnesian War and the battles of Leuctra in 371 BCE and Mantinea in 362 BCE, which let the northern kingdom of Macedon rise to predominance under Philip II. When Alexander the Great died on 10 June 323 BCE he left a sprawling empire made up of largely autonomous satrapies and no chosen successor. His generals, the Diadochi, or Successors, disputed who should be king of Macedon, and the empire broke apart in the Wars of the Diadochi. Greek kingdoms arose across West Asia, northeast Africa and South Asia, including the Seleucid Empire, the Ptolemaic Kingdom, Pergamon, the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom and the Indo-Greek Kingdom.

The Hellenistic states of Asia and Egypt were run by an occupying elite of Greco-Macedonian administrators backed by a standing army of mercenaries. Monarchs ran their kingdoms as royal estates and were expected to lead their armies in the field and act as patrons of the people. Ptolemy, who had been appointed satrap of Egypt, declared himself king in 305 BCE and made Alexandria his capital. Seleucus I received Babylonia and built an empire that at its height held central Anatolia, the Levant, Mesopotamia and Persia, though Pergamon, Bactria and Parthia later broke away.

Greek colonists and the Greek language spread to these realms, which also adopted local practice, so Hellenistic culture was a fusion. A Greek dialect called Koine became the common language of the ancient world. The age saw the rise of New Comedy, the Septuagint translation of the Hebrew Bible and the philosophies of Stoicism, Epicureanism and Pyrrhonism, and the mathematician Euclid and the polymath Archimedes belong to it. Alexandria, with its Library and Mouseion, was the centre of the preservation of earlier Greek literature.

Rome took over the Hellenistic world piece by piece. Attalus III bequeathed Pergamon to the Roman Republic in 133 BCE, Rome conquered Greece in 146 BCE, and Pontus fell in 63 BCE. The Battle of Actium in 31 BCE and the conquest of Ptolemaic Egypt the following year eliminated the last major Hellenistic kingdom. Scholars have proposed other end dates, but most accept 31 or 30 BCE. Nineteenth-century scholars often held the period to be a decline from classical Greece, a comparison now regarded as unfair.
helmand-river: The Helmand, historically also called the Etymandros, is the longest river in Afghanistan and the main watershed of the Sistan Basin, which has no outlet to the sea. It rises in the Sanglakh Range of the Hindu Kush, in the north-east of Maidan Wardak Province, about 40 kilometres west of Kabul, where the Unai Pass separates it from the watershed of the Kabul River. It flows south-westward for 1,150 kilometres through Daykundi and Uruzgan provinces and past the city of Lashkargah in Helmand Province.

Beyond Lashkargah it enters the desert of Dasht-e Margo and then reaches the Sistan marshes and the Hamun-i-Helmand lake region around Zabol, on the border between Afghanistan and Iran. Smaller rivers such as the Tarnak and the Arghandab flow into it. The Arghandab is its chief tributary and has a major dam north of Kandahar, and the Kajaki Dam stands on the Helmand itself.

The name comes from the Avestan Haētumant, meaning dammed or having a dam, which referred to the river and the irrigated areas around it. The word is related to the Sanskrit Setumatī. The Avesta mentions the Helmand valley by name as the Aryan land of Haetumant, one of the early centres of the Zoroastrian faith in what is now Afghanistan.

By the late first millennium BCE and the early first millennium CE, communities of Hindus and Buddhists were so numerous in the Helmand and Kabul valleys that the Parthians referred to the region as India. From 1758 to 1842 the Helmand formed the northern border of the Brahui Khanate of Kalat.

The river is managed by the Helmand and Arghandab Valley Authority and is used extensively for irrigation, although a build-up of mineral salts has reduced its usefulness for watering crops. For much of its length it is free of salt. Its waters are essential to farmers in Afghanistan, and they also matter to farmers in the south-east of Iran, in the province of Sistan and Baluchistan.
helmut-kohl: Helmut Kohl was born on 3 April 1930 in Ludwigshafen, the third child of Hans Kohl, a Bavarian army veteran and civil servant, and Cäcilie Kohl. He joined the Christian Democratic Union in 1946, at the age of 16. In 1958 he took a doctorate in history at Heidelberg University, and then worked for a foundry and for the Industrial Union for Chemistry.

He was elected the youngest member of the Rhineland-Palatinate parliament in 1959. On 19 May 1969 he became minister-president of that state. As a reformer he focused on schools and education: his government abolished school corporal punishment and the parochial school, and he founded the University of Trier-Kaiserslautern. In 1973 he was elected national chairman of the CDU.

Kohl led the opposition under Chancellor Helmut Schmidt. The Free Democratic Party broke with its coalition partner in 1982, and on 1 October 1982 a constructive vote of no confidence deposed Schmidt, the only time a chancellor has been removed in that way. Three days later the Bundestag elected Kohl chancellor of a CDU/CSU-FDP coalition. His government stationed NATO mid-range missiles despite strong opposition from the peace movement.

On 22 September 1984 Kohl met the French president François Mitterrand at Verdun, and their long handshake became a symbol of Franco-German reconciliation. After the revolutions of 1989 his government acted decisively, and reunification followed in 1990. With Mitterrand he was an architect of the Maastricht Treaty, which established the European Union and the euro. He moved the federal capital from Bonn back to Berlin, though government offices relocated only in 1999. He lost the 1998 election to Gerhard Schröder and resigned as party leader.

In 1999 it emerged that the CDU had received and kept illegal donations during Kohl's leadership; Der Spiegel reported that he had not benefited personally but had run the party's finances outside the legal boundaries. His reputation suffered in Germany, though abroad he was still regarded as a European statesman. In 1998 the European heads of state or government named him Honorary Citizen of Europe, an honour previously given only to Jean Monnet. Kohl died on 16 June 2017 in Ludwigshafen, aged 87, and was buried in Speyer after a European act of state in Strasbourg.
helmut-schmidt: Helmut Schmidt was born on 23 December 1918 in Barmbek, a working-class district of Hamburg. He graduated from the Lichtwark School in 1937 and volunteered for military service that year, joining an anti-aircraft battery of the Luftwaffe. After brief service on the Eastern Front in 1941, including the Siege of Leningrad, he worked from 1942 at the Ministry of Aviation. From December 1944 he served as an Oberleutnant in the Flak artillery on the Western Front, and he was captured by the British in April 1945. He joined the Social Democratic Party in 1946 and read economics at the University of Hamburg.

Schmidt entered the Bundestag in 1953, and his sharp speeches won him the nickname Schmidt-Schnauze, Schmidt the Lip. From 1961 to 1965 he was Hamburg's senator of the interior. During the flood of 1962, in which 300 people drowned, he used all means at his disposal, including federal police and army units, even where that overstepped his legal authority. He is credited with saving a further 1,000 lives and rehousing thousands of homeless people, which gave him a reputation as a Macher, someone who gets things done. In Willy Brandt's government he served as defence minister from 1969 to 1972 and finance minister from 1972 to 1974.

He became chancellor on 16 May 1974, after Brandt resigned in an espionage scandal. The worldwide recession was his main problem, and he held to a tough line on public spending. With the French president Valéry Giscard d'Estaing he helped begin the world economic summits in 1975, signed the Helsinki Accords that year and helped set up the European Monetary System in 1978. He was re-elected in 1976 and 1980, but his coalition fell apart in 1982 when its partner, the Free Democratic Party, changed sides.

After leaving the Bundestag in 1986 Schmidt remained a public voice, as co-publisher of the weekly Die Zeit from 1983 and as the author of memoirs such as Men and Powers. He was a gifted pianist and recorded Mozart and Bach concertos. He died at his Hamburg home on 10 November 2015, aged 96, and a state funeral was held on 23 November. The University of the Federal Armed Forces in Hamburg bears his name.
helmuth-von-moltke-the-elder: Helmuth Karl Bernhard von Moltke was born on 26 October 1800 in Parchim, Mecklenburg-Schwerin, the son of Generalleutnant Friedrich Philipp Victor von Moltke, a German in Danish service. In 1806 French troops burned his father's country house and plundered his townhouse in Lübeck, leaving the family impoverished. At twelve he entered the Royal Danish Military Academy at Copenhagen, and in 1818 he became a page to King Frederick VI of Denmark and a second lieutenant. At twenty-one he left Denmark for the Prussian army, despite the loss of seniority, and after the general war school he graduated in 1826.

As a young officer Moltke worked on the military survey in Silesia and Posen and in 1832 was seconded to the general staff at Berlin. He wrote a short romance, The Two Friends, in 1827, and studies of Holland and Belgium and of Poland. In 1835 he took leave to travel in south-eastern Europe, and Sultan Mahmud II asked him to help modernise the Ottoman army. He stayed two years at Constantinople, learned Turkish and surveyed the city, the Bosporus and the Dardanelles.

On 29 October 1857 the new king appointed him Chief of the Prussian General Staff, a post he held for thirty years. He changed armament and communications, introduced staff rides, revised mobilisation and began a formal study of European politics for campaign planning. In 1860 he added a Railway Section; a contemporary wrote that he never made an important decision without consulting the railway timetables. He also commanded in the Second Schleswig War and the Austro-Prussian War.

In the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–1871 his plans for a railway deployment south of Mainz, revised every year, were adopted without dispute. Five days after the mobilisation order he was made Chief of Staff of the Army for the war, with the right to issue orders equivalent to royal commands. He was made a count in October 1870 after Sedan and a field marshal in June 1871.

Moltke sat in the Reichstag from 1871 to 1891 and oversaw the General Staff's official histories of the wars, the history of the Franco-Prussian War appearing between 1874 and 1881. After the war he was a national hero, and more than fifty monuments to him were raised in Germany. He married Marie Burt in 1842 and remained devoted to her after her death in 1868. He died on 24 April 1891. He was the earliest-born person whose recorded voice survives: two wax cylinders made on 21 October 1889 hold a line of Hamlet and a passage of Faust.
helsingborg: Helsingborg stands at the narrowest part of the Øresund, the strait between Sweden and Denmark, about 4 km from the Danish city of Helsingør on the opposite shore. It is one of the oldest cities of what is now Sweden and has been the site of permanent settlement officially since 21 May 1085. Its position was very important for Denmark, which at that time controlled both sides of the strait.

From 1429 Eric of Pomerania introduced the Sound Dues, a levy on trading vessels passing through the sound between Helsingør and Helsingborg. The dues were one of the main sources of income for the Danish Crown. They were first directed against the Hanseatic League, and crossing traffic such as fishermen did not pay them.

After the Dano-Swedish War of 1657 to 1658 and the Treaty of Roskilde, Denmark had to give up all its territory on the southern Scandinavian peninsula, and Helsingborg became Swedish. King Charles X Gustav of Sweden landed there on 5 March 1658 to take personal possession of the Scanian lands, and a delegation led by Peder Winstrup, bishop of Lund, met him. The town then had barely 1,000 people. Denmark recaptured Scania twice but could not hold it, and the last attempt came in 1710, when 14,000 men landed near Helsingborg. The Battle of Helsingborg was fought just outside the city on 10 March, and the town recovered slowly, with only 1,321 inhabitants in 1770.

From the middle of the 19th century industrialisation made Helsingborg one of the fastest-growing Swedish cities, rising from 4,000 people in 1850 to 20,000 in 1890 and 56,000 in 1930. A train ferry linked it with Helsingør from 1892. In October 1943 it was one of the main landing points for Danish Jews, over 7,200 of whom, with 680 non-Jews, were smuggled across the Øresund to Sweden in three nights.

Helsingborg is the seat of its municipality in Scania, the second-largest city of that province after Malmö, with a population of 151,404 in 2024. Its medieval fortress, Kärnan, about 600 years old, stands in the city centre among old stone churches. Ferries still cross to Helsingør around the clock, and IKEA has its international corporate headquarters in the city.
helsingor: Helsingør stands at the narrowest part of the Øresund strait. Together with Helsingborg in Sweden, about 4 km across the water, it forms the northern reaches of the Øresund Region, which is centred on Copenhagen and Malmö. The first part of the name is believed to come from the word hals, meaning neck or narrow strait, and the ending from the Old Norse aurr or eyrr, a gravel or sandy shore. The town is first mentioned as Hælsingør in the Liber Census Daniæ of King Valdemar the Victorious, dating from 1231.

Around 1200 the first church, Saint Olaf's Church, was built; its oldest parts date from the 13th century and show that the fishing village had grown into a town of importance. The town as it is known today was founded in the 1420s by King Eric of Pomerania, who established the Sound Dues in 1429.

Ships had to stop at Helsingør to have their cargo taxed, and the income paid for a castle called Krogen, which Frederik II rebuilt in the 1570s as Kronborg. From 1479 to 1581 the number of ships passing through the strait grew 6.5 times, and in 1672 Helsingør was the third-largest town in Denmark. The abolition of the dues in 1857, by the Copenhagen Convention, was a heavy loss, and population grew slowly in the following decades.

During the Second World War the town was one of the main transport points in the rescue of Denmark's Jews. After Georg Ferdinand Duckwitz, a German diplomatic attaché, passed on word on 28 September 1943 of an order to deport them, Danes hid Jews in houses, farm lofts and churches in north Zealand and carried them in fishing boats and ferries across the Øresund to Sweden. In three nights over 7,200 Jews and 680 non-Jews were taken to safety in Helsingborg and Malmö.

The Helsingør shipyard, founded in 1882, employed 3,600 people at its height in 1957 and closed in 1983. The Wiibroe brewery, founded in 1840, brewed its last beer there in 1998. The old dockyard now holds a cultural centre, opened in 2010, and the Danish Maritime Museum. Kronborg Castle is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and Shakespeare's Hamlet, set mostly there under the English spelling Elsinore, has been performed in its courtyard every year since 1937. The ferry line to Helsingborg is the busiest car ferry route in the world.
henan: Henan means south of the river, the river being the Yellow River, though changes in its course and in administrative boundaries mean that about a quarter of the province now lies north of it. The province is also abbreviated Yu, after Yuzhou, the name of the region in the ancient system of nine provinces. Most of it forms part of the North China Plain, called the breadbasket of China, with floodplains in the east and mountains in the west. The Yellow River enters from the north-west, and its silt has raised the river bed and caused floods that shaped the region. Mount Song and its Shaolin Temple lie near Zhengzhou.

Prehistoric cultures such as the Yangshao and Longshan were active in what is now northern Henan. The later Erlitou culture has been controversially identified with the Xia dynasty. The Shang dynasty, from about 1600 to about 1046 BCE, had its capitals in the province, and the oracle bone inscriptions found at Yinxu in Anyang give insight into its writing, rituals and social structure. After the Zhou overthrew the Shang at the Battle of Muye, the political centre moved away from Henan for the first time. Under the Han, Luoyang became the political and cultural heart of the empire.

Henan passed repeatedly between rival regimes from 220 to 589, yet remained an agricultural base. Emperor Yang of Sui had the Grand Canal extended to Luoyang. In the Five Dynasties period Kaifeng became the capital of four dynasties, and under the Song, who reunified China in 982, Kaifeng overtook Luoyang and Chang'an as the largest city in China and in the world. In 1127 the Jurchens captured Kaifeng and took the Song emperor prisoner, and in 1194 the Yellow River changed course, displacing millions.

After the rebel Li Zicheng took Luoyang in 1641, his forces besieged Kaifeng three times. During the third, Ming troops breached the Yellow River dikes to flood the rebels. The water submerged the city, and of its 378,000 residents only 30,000 survived. A dike breach at Zhengzhou on 30 September 1887 killed over two million people by one account, with estimates from 930,000 to 7 million. In 1938 the government led by Chiang Kai-shek bombed the Huayuankou dam to halt the Japanese advance, causing floods that killed hundreds of thousands. A famine followed in 1942–43.

Henan is a province of central China with Zhengzhou as its capital. Four historical capitals of China, Luoyang, Anyang, Kaifeng and Zhengzhou, lie within it. It has a population of over 99 million, the third largest of any province and the largest among inland provinces. The capital moved from Kaifeng to Zhengzhou in 1954 because of the city's importance for rail transport.
henri-de-saint-simon: Henri de Saint-Simon was born in Paris on 17 October 1760 into an aristocratic family, a younger relative of the memoirist the Duc de Saint-Simon. Ambitious from youth, he drew up schemes for a canal joining the Atlantic and the Pacific and another from Madrid to the sea. Between 1779 and 1783 he fought alongside the Marquis de Lafayette in the American Revolution and took part in the siege of Yorktown under George Washington. He was captured by British forces near the end of his service, and on his release he studied engineering and hydraulics at the École de Mézières.

In 1789 he endorsed the ideals of the French Revolution and raised funds by land speculation for a large industrial project. With Talleyrand he planned to buy the cathedral of Notre-Dame, strip its roof and sell the metal. He was imprisoned on suspicion of counter-revolutionary activity and released in 1794. Currency depreciation had made him rich, but a business partner then took his fortune, and he lived in poverty for the rest of his life. His first book, Lettres d'un habitant de Genève (1802), called for a religion of science with Isaac Newton as a saint.

In 1817 he published a Declaration of Principles in L'Industrie. The industrial class, which he also called the working class, covered everyone engaged in productive work, from scientists and bankers to manual labourers. He saw its chief enemy in an idling class of able people who lived from the work of others, and he wanted hierarchies of managers and scientists, ranked by merit, to take decisions, with government limited to keeping production unhindered.

On 9 March 1823, in despair at the lack of results from his writing, Saint-Simon shot himself in the head six times and survived, losing the sight of one eye. His last work, Le Nouveau Christianisme (1825), returned to renewing society through Christian brotherly love. He died on 19 May 1825 and was buried in the Père Lachaise Cemetery.

His disciples formed a Saint-Simonian movement that stressed a planned economy, the abolition of inheritance and the emancipation of women. Marx and Engels counted him among the utopian socialists, while criticising his hope of change by persuading elites, and he also influenced John Stuart Mill, Pierre-Joseph Proudhon and Thorstein Veblen.
henri-matisse: Henri Émile Benoît Matisse was born on 31 December 1869 in Le Cateau-Cambrésis in northern France, the oldest son of a wealthy grain merchant. In 1887 he went to Paris to study law and afterwards worked as a court administrator. He began to paint in 1889, when his mother brought him art supplies while he was convalescing from appendicitis, and decided to become an artist, which deeply disappointed his father. In 1891 he returned to Paris to study at the Académie Julian under William-Adolphe Bouguereau and at the École Nationale des Beaux-Arts under Gustave Moreau.

The intensity of colour in the works Matisse painted between 1900 and 1905 brought him notoriety as one of the Fauves, French for wild beasts. The movement lasted only from 1904 to 1908, and he and André Derain were its leaders. In 1904 he painted at St. Tropez with the neo-Impressionists Signac and Henri-Edmond Cross, and in 1905 he worked with Derain at Collioure. Around April 1906 he met Pablo Picasso, eleven years younger, and the two became lifelong friends and rivals. Americans in Paris, among them the Stein family and the Cone sisters of Baltimore, collected his work.

In 1917 Matisse moved to Cimiez, a suburb of Nice. His work of the next decade relaxed and softened, though some critics found his odalisque paintings shallow and decorative, and after 1930 a bolder simplification appeared. He was in Paris when the Germans invaded France in June 1940 but returned to Nice and stayed, though his son Pierre begged him to leave.

Diagnosed with abdominal cancer in 1941, Matisse underwent surgery that left him often bedridden. With assistants he began to make cut paper collages from sheets pre-painted with gouache, and the pieces grew into murals and room-sized works. In 1948 he began designs for the Chapelle du Rosaire at Vence, and after 1951 the paper cut-out was his only medium. He called his last years his second life. He died of a heart attack on 3 November 1954, aged 84, and is buried at Cimiez. The Matisse Museum at Le Cateau was established in 1952 and the Musée Matisse in Nice opened in 1963.
henrik-ibsen: Henrik Johan Ibsen was born on 20 March 1828 into an affluent merchant family in the port town of Skien in Telemark. His father, Knud Plesner Ibsen, was a timber and luxury goods merchant, and his mother, Marichen Cornelia Martine Altenburg, belonged like him to the extended Paus family, which had held wealth and power in Telemark since the mid-1500s. Older biographies pictured a descent from privilege into hardship, with a failed and tyrannical father, but a later reading finds this romanticised. At fifteen Ibsen left school and became an apprentice pharmacist in Grimstad, where he began writing plays. His first play, the tragedy Catilina, was published in 1850 under a pseudonym but not performed.

Ibsen established himself as a theatre director in Norway during the 1850s, though the many plays he wrote in those years were unsuccessful. In 1864 he left Christiania for Sorrento and spent the next 27 years in Italy and Germany, mostly in Rome, Dresden and Munich, before returning to Christiania in 1891. Brand and Peer Gynt, the second with incidental music by Edvard Grieg, brought him critical acclaim and some financial success. After Peer Gynt he abandoned verse for realistic prose, and he came to treat what he called the drama of ideas.

His plays from A Doll's House of 1879 onward, among them Ghosts, An Enemy of the People, The Wild Duck, Rosmersholm and Hedda Gabler, examined the morals and family life of the middle class and caused an uproar not only in Norway but across Europe and in America. Many of them are set in Norwegian bourgeois surroundings resembling Skien, and he took names and characters from his own relatives. Critics often rate The Wild Duck and Rosmersholm his best work, while Ibsen himself regarded Emperor and Galilean as his masterpiece.

Ibsen died at his home in Kristiania on 23 May 1906, after a series of strokes that began in March 1900. When his nurse told a visitor on the previous day that he was a little better, his last word was the reply Tvertimod, meaning On the contrary. He was buried in Vår Frelsers gravlund in Oslo. By 2014 he was the most frequently performed dramatist in the world after Shakespeare, and he influenced writers such as George Bernard Shaw, Oscar Wilde and James Joyce. His son Sigurd Ibsen became prime minister of Norway.
henry-dunant: Henry Dunant was born in Geneva on 8 May 1828, the first son of the businessman Jean-Jacques Dunant and Antoinette Dunant-Colladon. His family was devoutly Calvinist and influential in the city. During the religious awakening known as the Réveil he joined the Geneva Society for Almsgiving at eighteen and helped found the Thursday Association, whose young members studied the Bible and helped the poor. On 30 November 1852 he founded the Geneva chapter of the YMCA. In 1856 he created a business in French-occupied Algeria, a corn-growing and trading company.

Because land and water rights were unclear, Dunant went in 1859 to appeal to Emperor Napoléon III, who was with his army in Lombardy. He arrived at Solferino on the evening of 24 June 1859, the day of a battle nearby. Forty thousand wounded, dying and dead lay on the field with little care. Dunant organised the local population, especially women and girls, to help the wounded of both sides, and the slogan Tutti fratelli, all are brothers, was coined by the women of Castiglione delle Stiviere.

In 1862 he published Un Souvenir de Solferino at his own expense and proposed a neutral organisation to care for the wounded. On 9 February 1863 the Geneva Society for Public Welfare, led by Gustave Moynier, created a five-person committee that included Dunant, Moynier, General Henri Dufour and the doctors Louis Appia and Théodore Maunoir. Their first meeting on 17 February 1863 is regarded as the founding of the International Committee of the Red Cross. On 22 August 1864 twelve states signed the First Geneva Convention.

In April 1867 the bankruptcy of the financial firm Crédit Genevois led to a scandal involving Dunant, who declared bankruptcy. He was removed from the committee in September 1867, left Geneva and never returned. He lived in poverty in Paris and other cities and kept working for disarmament, an international court and a world library. From 1887 he lived in the Swiss village of Heiden. In 1895 a journalist rediscovered him, and in 1901 he shared the first Nobel Peace Prize with the French pacifist Frédéric Passy. He died in Heiden on 30 October 1910.
henry-fielding: Henry Fielding was born on 22 April 1707 at Sharpham Park in Somerset, the seat of his mother's family. His father was Edmund Fielding, a scion of the Earl of Denbigh, and his mother was Sarah Gould. At Eton College he began a lifelong friendship with William Pitt the Elder. His mother died when he was 11. In 1728 he went to Leiden to study classics and law, but lack of money forced him back to London, where he began writing for the theatre and criticised the government of Sir Robert Walpole.

Fielding's plays of 1730, The Author's Farce and Tom Thumb, mark his turn to satirical burlesque. From 1734 to 1739 he wrote anonymously against Walpole in the periodical The Craftsman. The Theatrical Licensing Act 1737 is said to have been a direct response to his dramatic satire, and after it passed, political satire on the stage became all but impossible. He joined the Middle Temple in 1737 and was called to the bar in 1740.

He then turned to prose. Shamela (1741) parodied Samuel Richardson's Pamela, and Joseph Andrews (1742) began as parody and became a novel in its own right, which Fielding called a comic epic poem in prose. The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling (1749) is a comic novel in which a foundling comes into a fortune, and Amelia followed in 1751. Ralph Allen, a wealthy benefactor, helped the family through poverty, and Squire Allworthy in Tom Jones is based on him.

Fielding married Charlotte Craddock in 1734; she died in 1744, and he modelled the heroines of Tom Jones and Amelia on her. His support for the Church of England and his anti-Jacobitism led to his appointment as chief magistrate of Westminster. With his half-brother John Fielding he helped found the Bow Street Runners in 1749, and G. M. Trevelyan counted the brothers among the best magistrates of 18th-century London.

Gout, asthma and cirrhosis of the liver left Fielding on crutches, and in 1754 he went to Portugal seeking a cure. He died two months later in Lisbon, on 8 October 1754, and is buried in the British Cemetery there.
henry-hudson: Almost nothing is known for certain of Hudson's early life. His year of birth is variously estimated between 1560 and 1570, and he may have been born in London. When he first appears in the record in 1607 he was already an experienced mariner.

In 1607 the Muscovy Company hired Hudson to find a northerly route to the Pacific coast of Asia, in the belief that the summer sun would melt the ice. He sailed in the Hopewell, reached Spitsbergen and turned back when ice blocked the north coast. In 1608 he tried the route east around northern Russia but found the ice impenetrable at Novaya Zemlya.

In 1609 merchants of the Dutch East India Company chose him to find an eastern passage. Ice stopped the Halve Maen east of Norway's North Cape, and Hudson, acting outside his instructions, turned west. After landfall in Nova Scotia and a landing in which a dozen of his men attacked a village, he reached Cape Cod and the coast to the north. On 3 September he came to the estuary of the river now named for him. Verrazzano had known it since 1524. Hudson sailed up the river for ten days, buying oysters and beans from Lenape in canoes and trading for furs.

In 1610, backed by the Virginia Company and the East India Company, Hudson sailed the Discovery. He passed Iceland and Greenland, entered Hudson Strait on 25 June and, on 2 August, Hudson Bay. Ice trapped the ship in James Bay in November and the crew wintered ashore.

When the ice cleared in spring 1611 Hudson meant to press on exploring, but most of the crew wished to go home and mutinied in June. Hudson, his teenage son John and seven others were set adrift in an open shallop and were never seen by Europeans again; later searches, among them Thomas Button's in 1612, found nothing. The main source, the account of Abacuk Pricket, blames Henry Greene and Robert Juet, and historians have doubted it, since the survivors faced trial in England and the men blamed were dead. Some survivors were tried, but none was punished.

Hudson's 1609 voyage established Dutch claims to the region and to its fur trade; a trading post stood at Albany in 1614, and New Amsterdam became the capital of New Netherland in 1625. Hudson Bay later gave the Hudson's Bay Company access to a fur trade along its shores for more than two centuries.
henry-ii-holy-roman-emperor: Henry was born in May 973, son of Duke Henry II of Bavaria and Gisela of Burgundy, and was a great-grandson of King Henry I of Germany. Because his father rebelled against two emperors, he spent long periods in exile, where he turned to Christianity at an early age, first finding refuge with Bishop Abraham of Freising and later studying at the cathedral school in Hildesheim. He succeeded his father as Duke of Bavaria in 995.

When Emperor Otto III died childless in January 1002, Henry's right to succeed him was contested by rivals including Count Ezzo of Lotharingia, Margrave Eckard I of Meissen and Duke Herman II of Swabia. Henry was crowned king on 9 July 1002 and spent the following years consolidating his power. In Italy, Margrave Arduin of Ivrea proclaimed himself king, but Henry was anointed King of Italy on 15 May 1004, and he was crowned emperor by Pope Benedict VIII on 14 February 1014, after Benedict had fled to Germany and appealed to him for protection.

Where Otto III had pursued a renewal of the Roman Empire, Henry's seal spoke of a renewal of the Frankish kingdom, and he spent most of his reign on the territories north of the Alps. He made only three journeys south of the Alps. His long conflict with Duke Bolesław I of Poland, who had once been a loyal ally of Otto III, filled over sixteen years, with peace treaties made and broken in 1012 and 1013. Henry also relied on bishops and abbots, whom he made princes of the empire, as a counterweight to the secular nobles, and in 1004 he ordered the diocese of Merseburg re-established, appointing the chronicler Thietmar as its bishop.

In 1007 Henry announced a new diocese at Bamberg, a place he was fond of, where he had given estates to his wife Cunigunde of Luxembourg. He died on 13 July 1024 at Göttingen and was buried at Bamberg Cathedral. As the marriage was childless, the Ottonian line ended with him, and the nobles elected Conrad II, the first of the Salian emperors. Henry was canonised by Pope Eugene III in the twelfth century and Cunigunde in 1200. He is the only medieval German monarch honoured as a saint, and the patron saint of the city of Basel.
henry-ii-of-england: Henry was born at Le Mans on 5 March 1133, the eldest child of the Empress Matilda, daughter of Henry I of England, and Geoffrey Plantagenet, Count of Anjou. By the age of 14 he was involved in his mother's effort to claim the English throne, then held by her cousin Stephen of Blois. In 1150 his father made him Duke of Normandy, and in 1151 Henry inherited Anjou, Maine and Touraine. His marriage to Eleanor of Aquitaine brought him that duchy. After a military expedition to England in 1153, Stephen agreed by the Treaty of Wallingford to leave the kingdom to Henry, who inherited it a year later.

Henry was crowned with Eleanor at Westminster Abbey on 19 December 1154. He inherited a country damaged by civil war, with unauthorised castles and a depleted royal income, and in the early years he restored royal administration. His invasion of Wales in 1157 met defeat at the Battle of Ewloe, where he was nearly killed. His desire to control the English Church brought conflict with Thomas Becket, Archbishop of Canterbury, a controversy that lasted much of the 1160s and ended in Becket's murder in 1170. He also fought Louis VII of France for decades, in a struggle the historian Jean Dunbabin likened to a cold war.

His domains, later called the Angevin Empire, were a loose network of family connections and lands, each with its own customs. Henry travelled constantly, producing what the historian John Edward Austin Jolliffe describes as a government of the roads and roadsides. His court was probably the largest in Europe. He expanded royal justice in England, and the Treatise of Glanvill summarised the system at the end of his reign.

Henry and Eleanor had eight children, three of them kings: Henry the Young King, Richard I and John. Tensions over the inheritance, encouraged by Louis VII and his son Philip II, led in 1173 to a rebellion by Young Henry, joined by Richard, Geoffrey and Eleanor. Young Henry died during a second failed revolt in 1183, and Geoffrey died in 1186. By 1189 Philip had won Richard to his side, and Henry, weakened by a bleeding ulcer, was decisively defeated. He died soon afterwards, on 6 July 1189, and was succeeded by Richard. His empire collapsed quickly under John, but his legal reforms are generally considered to have laid the basis for the English Common Law.
henry-ii-of-france: Henry was born on 31 March 1519 at the Château de Saint-Germain-en-Laye, the second son of Francis I and Claude, Duchess of Brittany. After Francis I was captured at the Battle of Pavia in 1525, Henry and his elder brother were sent to Spain as hostages and stayed there for over four years. On 28 October 1533 he married Catherine de' Medici, both being fourteen.

He formed a close attachment to Diane de Poitiers, more than twenty years older than he, whose colours he wore at a tournament in 1531. He became heir in August 1536 when his brother died after falling ill following a game of tennis; an autopsy report gave no sign of poison. Catherine bore their first son in 1544, and Henry's loyalty to Diane caused a breach with his father until 1545.

Francis I died on 31 March 1547, and Henry was crowned at Reims on 25 July 1547. He intensified the repression of Protestants. An edict of 5 April 1547 reaffirmed punishments for blasphemy, and in October a new chamber of the Parlement of Paris, called the chambre ardente, was set up to hear heresy cases. The Edict of Châteaubriant followed in 1551.

In foreign policy he declared war on Charles V in the Italian War of 1551–1559, allied himself with German Protestant princes at the Treaty of Chambord in 1552 and continued his father's Franco-Ottoman alliance. He occupied the Three Bishoprics of Toul, Verdun and Metz, and secured them at Renty in 1554. After Philip II's victory at St Quentin, French forces took Calais.

Henry raised Mary, Queen of Scots at his court, and she married the Dauphin Francis on 24 April 1558. Under the Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis of April 1559, France gave up its claims in Italy and restored Piedmont and Savoy but kept Saluzzo, Calais and the Three Bishoprics. During his reign Henry also introduced the idea of publishing a description of an invention in exchange for monopoly rights, the beginning of the patent specification.

On 30 June 1559, at a tournament held to celebrate the peace, Henry was wounded in the eye by a splinter of the lance of Gabriel Montgomery, captain of his Scottish Guard. Surgeons including Ambroise Paré and Andreas Vesalius could not save him, and he died ten days later. Modern analysis points to an infection from a retained wooden fragment.

His death played a part in the decline of jousting in France. He left four young sons and a widow, Catherine de' Medici. Three of the sons became king, but their youth and Catherine's regency led to challenges from powerful nobles and helped to spark the French Wars of Religion, and in time the Valois dynasty ended.
henry-iii-of-england: Henry was born at Winchester Castle on 1 October 1207, the eldest son of King John and Isabella of Angoulême. When John died, Henry was at Corfe Castle in Dorset. John's deathbed wishes placed him under the guardianship of William Marshal, who knighted him, and Cardinal Guala Bicchieri, the papal legate, oversaw his coronation at Gloucester Cathedral on 28 October 1216, in the middle of the First Barons' War.

Guala declared the war against the rebels a crusade, and Henry's forces under William Marshal defeated them at Lincoln and Sandwich in 1217. The government reissued a version of Magna Carta, and Henry promised to abide by the Great Charter of 1225.

Hubert de Burgh, made Earl of Kent, dominated the government after William Marshal's death in 1219 until his fall in 1232. A failed invasion of France in 1230 and a revolt led by Richard Marshal in 1232 marked the early years. Henry then ruled in person. He left the post of justiciar vacant, made the chancellor a junior figure and took decisions with a small circle of advisers, which made it harder for outsiders to press grievances.

In 1236 he married Eleanor of Provence, then twelve years old. He was known for piety, attended mass at least once a day and took Edward the Confessor as his patron saint. His expeditions to Poitou in 1242 ended in the Battle of Taillebourg, and he spent large sums in a failed attempt to put his son Edmund Crouchback on the throne of Sicily.

By 1258 his foreign policy, his Poitevin half-brothers and his officials' tax collecting had made him unpopular, and a coalition of barons seized power and imposed the Provisions of Oxford. In 1259, under the Treaty of Paris, Henry gave up his claims in France except Gascony, which Louis IX recognised as his. In 1263 Simon de Montfort seized power, beginning the Second Barons' War. Henry was defeated and captured at Lewes in 1264, and his son Edward beat Simon at Evesham the following year. The Dictum of Kenilworth softened the revenge on the rebels.

Henry also took a heavy toll from the Jews of England, whose position as a source of royal loans he used until it crippled their ability to do business, and he later introduced the Statute of Jewry to separate them from the rest of the population. He died on 16 November 1272, leaving Edward as his successor.

He was buried in Westminster Abbey, which he had rebuilt in the second half of his reign, and his body was moved to its present tomb in 1290. His reign of 56 years was the longest in medieval England and was not exceeded by an English or British monarch until George III.
henry-iv-holy-roman-emperor: Henry was born on 11 November 1050, most likely at his father's palace at Goslar, the son of Emperor Henry III and Agnes of Poitou. He belonged to the Salian dynasty, which governed Germany from 1024 to 1125. His father named him successor at Christmas 1050, and at the age of six he became sole ruler while his mother acted as regent. In April 1062 Archbishop Anno II of Cologne and other nobles removed her in the Coup of Kaiserswerth, luring Henry onto a ship on the Rhine; he leapt into the river and was rescued by Egbert I of Brunswick. Henry was girded with a sword at Worms on 29 March 1065.

Around 1069 Henry set out to recover royal estates lost during his minority, most of them in Saxony. He used Swabian ministeriales as officials and built royal castles garrisoned by Swabian troops, which angered the Saxons, and he put down revolts there in 1069 and 1071. His insistence on appointing bishops and abbots brought conflict with Pope Alexander II, who excommunicated some of his advisers in 1073.

After crushing a new Saxon rebellion in 1075 he turned to Italy and appointed Tedald archbishop of Milan against the wishes of Pope Gregory VII, who threatened excommunication. At Worms on 24 January 1076 two archbishops and twenty-six bishops declared Gregory's election invalid. Gregory excommunicated Henry, and in 1077 Henry sought absolution in his penitential walk to Canossa. German opponents then elected Rudolf of Rheinfelden king on 14 March 1077. Excommunicated again in 1080, Henry was supported by an antipope, Clement III, who crowned him emperor in Rome in 1084.

From 1089 to 1096 he campaigned in Italy against Matilda of Tuscany and Welf I of Bavaria; his son Conrad turned against him in 1093. In 1103 he proclaimed the first imperial peace covering all Germany. His diplomas protected the Jews of Speyer and Worms from violence and forced baptism.

In December 1104 his younger son Henry deserted him, and in 1105 forced his abdication. Henry fled to Cologne in February 1106, where the townspeople received him, and he sought allies to regain the throne. He fell ill and died in 1106 without absolution. His conflicts with the popes, his sons and his subjects produced a rich polemical literature in his lifetime. The Song of the Saxon War praised him as pious, while Lampert of Hersfeld said he had inherited a peaceful realm and rendered it bloodstained and a prey to internal conflicts.
henry-iv-of-england: Henry was born at Bolingbroke Castle in Lincolnshire in about April 1367, the son of John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster, and Blanche of Lancaster, and a grandson of King Edward III. He took the name Bolingbroke from his birthplace. As a youth he rode, hunted and jousted, and was besieged with Richard II in the Tower of London during the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.

He joined the Lords Appellant's rebellion against his cousin in 1387, though Richard later made him Duke of Hereford. He went on crusading expeditions with the Teutonic Order to Lithuania in 1390 and 1392, and in 1392–93 made a pilgrimage to Jerusalem.

In 1398 a remark attributed to Thomas de Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk, led to a planned duel, which Richard halted by exiling Henry, and Mowbray for life. When Gaunt died in February 1399, Richard cancelled the documents allowing Henry to inherit automatically. Henry returned from exile with Thomas Arundel, the former archbishop of Canterbury, while Richard was campaigning in Ireland, and gathered enough support to have himself declared king, imprison Richard and bypass Richard's heir-presumptive, Edmund de Mortimer, Earl of March. Richard died in prison in February 1400, probably of starvation, whether self-imposed or forced being a matter of historical speculation.

He put down the Epiphany Rising in January 1400, and invaded Scotland in August 1400, a campaign that accomplished little. Owain Glyndŵr declared himself Prince of Wales in 1400. The Percy rebellions followed, and in 1403 the royal army defeated them at the Battle of Shrewsbury, where Henry Percy, known as Hotspur, was killed and the king's eldest son, Henry of Monmouth, was wounded by an arrow in the face. In 1401 the statute De heretico comburendo prescribed burning for heretics, to suppress the Lollards.

From 1405 Henry suffered a disfiguring skin disease and acute attacks of a grave illness, whose nature medical historians still debate. His son Henry of Monmouth took over much of the government in 1410. Henry died on 20 March 1413 in the Jerusalem Chamber at Westminster Abbey, during a meeting of Parliament.

He was buried not at Westminster but at Canterbury Cathedral beside the shrine of Thomas Becket, with his second wife, Joan of Navarre. Historians connect the choice with his wish to legitimise his dynasty. His son succeeded as Henry V, and the usurpation later contributed to the dynastic disputes of the Wars of the Roses.
henry-iv-of-france: Henry was born at the Château de Pau, the capital of Navarre and Béarn, the son of Jeanne III of Navarre and Antoine de Bourbon, Duke of Vendôme. He was baptised a Catholic but raised as a Huguenot by his mother. Under the Huguenot leader Gaspard II de Coligny he witnessed the battles of Jarnac, La Roche-l'Abeille and Moncontour, and he saw combat for the first time in 1570 at Arnay-le-Duc.

On 9 June 1572 his mother died and Henry became King of Navarre. He married Margaret of Valois in Paris on 18 August 1572, and within days the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre killed several thousand Protestants who had come for the wedding. Henry survived by promising to convert, lived at court until early 1576, then escaped and returned to the Protestant side. When Henry III of France died in 1589 he nominally became king, but the Catholic League, backed by Spain, refused to accept him and Pope Sixtus V excommunicated him. He won at Arques and Ivry but failed to take Paris in 1590.

On 25 July 1593 he converted to Catholicism, which secured the allegiance of most of his subjects and earned the resentment of the Huguenots and of Elizabeth I of England. He was crowned at Chartres on 27 February 1594, since the League still held Reims, and Pope Clement VIII lifted the excommunication on 17 September 1595. After his victory at Amiens in September 1597 the Peace of Vervins ended the war with Spain in 1598, the year of the Edict of Nantes. Working through his minister Maximilien de Béthune, Duke of Sully, he regularised finance, promoted agriculture and built roads, bridges and canals.

Henry was the target of at least twelve assassination attempts. On 14 May 1610 François Ravaillac, a Catholic zealot, stabbed him in Paris while his coach was halted on the Rue de la Ferronnerie. Ravaillac was seized and executed days later. Henry was buried at the Basilica of Saint Denis, and his widow Marie de' Medici acted as regent for their nine-year-old son Louis XIII until 1617. His statue was set up on the Pont Neuf in 1614, torn down in the Revolution and rebuilt in 1818.
henry-morton-stanley: Henry Morton Stanley was born John Rowlands in Denbigh, Wales, to the unmarried Elizabeth Parry, who was 18. She abandoned him as a baby, and his father died within weeks of his birth. The stigma of illegitimacy weighed on him all his life. He spent ten years of his childhood in the workhouse at St Asaph, and emigrated to the United States in 1859 at the age of 18. By his own account he took the name of a trader he met at New Orleans, Henry Hope Stanley, though discrepancies in the story have led some biographers to doubt it.

Stanley went to Zanzibar in March 1871 on an expedition funded by James Gordon Bennett Jr., publisher of the New York Herald, and found David Livingstone. In 1874 the New York Herald and the Daily Telegraph financed a second expedition to map the Central African Great Lakes and rivers and to locate the source of the Nile.

In 1878 King Leopold II of the Belgians received him, since the Foreign Office and the Prince of Wales would not, and signed a five-year contract with him. Stanley reached Stanley Pool on 3 December 1882 after almost two years of moving 50 tonnes of equipment past rapids, and began Léopoldville, now Kinshasa. In 1886 he led the Emin Pasha Relief Expedition, mapped the Ruwenzori Range and Lake Edward, and came out of the interior at the end of 1890. He then married the artist Dorothy Tennant, took British citizenship and sat as Liberal Unionist member for Lambeth North from 1895 to 1900.

Stanley's books, among them How I Found Livingstone (1872) and Through the Dark Continent, fostered a public reputation as a hard and cruel leader. In 1871 a House of Commons committee investigated missionary reports of his violence, and John Kirk's unpublished report accused him of reckless use of modern weapons against people who had never heard a gun fired. Tim Jeal holds that Stanley, unlike Richard Burton and Samuel Baker, was not a racist, and Stanley praised the Zanzibari Wangwana who formed the backbone of his expeditions. He also wrote that Africans must submit to Europeans.
His reputation suffered further in the 20th century from his part in founding the Congo Free State for Leopold. He was knighted as a Knight Grand Cross of the Order of the Bath in 1899.
henry-purcell: Henry Purcell was born in Westminster in 1659, in St Ann's Lane, and the family lived a few hundred yards from Westminster Abbey. His father, also named Henry, died in 1664, and the child was placed under the guardianship of his uncle Thomas, a gentleman of the Chapel Royal. Thomas arranged for him to become a chorister, and he studied under Captain Henry Cooke and then Pelham Humfrey, a pupil of Lully. The composer Matthew Locke was a family friend.

When his voice broke in 1673 he left the Chapel Royal and became assistant to the organ-builder John Hingston. The earliest work identified as his with certainty is an ode for the King's birthday written in 1670, when he was eleven. After Humfrey's death he studied under John Blow, was a pupil at Westminster School, and in 1676 was appointed copyist at Westminster Abbey.

In 1679 Blow resigned the post of organist of Westminster Abbey in Purcell's favour, and he devoted himself almost entirely to sacred music for six years. Soon after his marriage in 1682 he became organist of the Chapel Royal as well. In 1685 he wrote the anthems I was glad and My heart is inditing for the coronation of King James II, and in 1694 he composed Come Ye Sons of Art, one of his most elaborate works, to a birthday ode by Nahum Tate for Queen Mary.

He returned to the theatre in 1687 with music for John Dryden's Tyrannick Love. His later stage works included Dioclesian in 1690, King Arthur in 1691 and The Fairy-Queen in 1692, an adaptation of Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream whose score was rediscovered in 1901. His chamber opera Dido and Aeneas, to a libretto by Nahum Tate, was written for private performance. In his last six years he wrote music for forty-two plays. His Te Deum and Jubilate Deo of 1694 was the first English Te Deum with orchestral accompaniment.

Purcell died on 21 November 1695 at his home in Marsham Street, at the height of his career, aged about 35 or 36. The cause is unclear: one theory is that he caught a chill, another that he died of tuberculosis. He was buried in the north aisle of Westminster Abbey beside the organ, and the music he had written for the funeral of Queen Mary was performed at his own. His widow Frances published many of his works, including the collection Orpheus Britannicus.

John Blow wrote an ode on his death, and later composers admired him. His setting of Thou knowest Lord has been sung at every British state funeral since William Croft preserved it in 1724. Benjamin Britten arranged many of his vocal works. A Purcell Society, founded in 1876, published new editions of his music.
henry-the-fowler: Henry was born in Memleben, in what is now Saxony-Anhalt, into the Liudolfing line of Saxon dukes, the son of Otto the Illustrious, Duke of Saxony. His mother, Hedwiga, was probably a great-granddaughter of Charlemagne through her mother. In 906 he married Hatheburg of Merseburg, a former nun; the church annulled the marriage in 909. In the same year he married Matilda, daughter of Dietrich of Ringelheim, who was later canonised. He succeeded his father as duke in 912 and rebelled against King Conrad I over lands in Thuringia before they reconciled in 915.

Conrad I died on 23 December 918 after recommending Henry as king, since only he could hold the kingdom together against revolts and Magyar raids. At the Diet of Fritzlar in 919 Franconian and Saxon nobles elected him, the first non-Frank on the throne. Archbishop Heriger of Mainz offered to anoint him, but he refused, the only king of his time to do so, allegedly because he wished to be king by acclamation of the people and not by the church's. He then had to subdue the other dukes. Arnulf of Bavaria, who had crowned himself king of Bavaria in 919, submitted only in 921, keeping substantial autonomy.

Henry did not seek a centralised monarchy and ruled through autonomous stem duchies. In 925, after Duke Gilbert of Lotharingia rebelled, he invaded and besieged Gilbert at Zülpich, then in 928 married his daughter Gerberga to Gilbert, bringing Lotharingia back as the fifth stem duchy. He agreed a ten-year truce with the Magyars in 924 in return for annual tribute, and used it to build fortified towns and train a cavalry force. In 932 he refused the tribute, and in 933 he crushed the Magyars at the Battle of Riade.

During the truce he marched on the Hevelli in the winter of 928 and seized their capital, Brandenburg. In 929 he forced Duke Wenceslaus I of Bohemia to resume tribute, and in 934 he conquered Schleswig.

Henry planned a journey to Rome to be crowned emperor, but died on 2 July 936 and was buried at Quedlinburg Abbey, founded by Matilda. He had prevented a collapse of royal power such as occurred in West Francia and left a stronger kingdom to his son Otto I, the first of the Ottonian rulers who held East Francia and later the Holy Roman Empire from 919 until 1024. Richard Wagner made him a character in his opera Lohengrin in 1850.
henry-vii-of-england: Henry was the only child of Lady Margaret Beaufort, then 13, and Edmund Tudor, 1st Earl of Richmond, who died three months before his birth. Margaret was a great-granddaughter of John of Gaunt, so Henry's claim to the throne descended from Edward III through the Beaufort line. Edmund was the half-brother of the Lancastrian king Henry VI. Henry was raised by his uncle Jasper Tudor, a Lancastrian, and by William Herbert, a Yorkist supporter. After Edward IV retook the throne in 1471, Henry spent 14 years in exile in Brittany.

At Rennes Cathedral on Christmas Day 1483 Henry pledged to marry Elizabeth of York, eldest daughter of Edward IV. A first attempt to land in England failed. He then escaped to France, which supplied troops, and landed at Mill Bay near Dale in Pembrokeshire with a small French and Scottish force. Although outnumbered, he defeated Richard III at the Battle of Bosworth Field on 22 August 1485, after several of Richard's allies, among them the Earl of Northumberland and Lord Stanley, changed sides or left the field. He was crowned at Westminster Abbey on 30 October, married Elizabeth in 1486 and defended the crown at Stoke Field in 1487.

Henry came to the throne with no experience of financial administration, yet restored an effectively bankrupt exchequer. He kept the same advisers throughout and introduced efficient mechanisms of taxation, supported by his chancellor, Archbishop John Morton, whose argument, known as Morton's Fork, held that nobles who spent little must have savings and those who spent much could afford to pay. The Magnus Intercursus of 1496 restored trade with the Burgundian Netherlands after his embargo of 1494. To curb powerful nobles he passed laws against livery and maintenance and used the Court of Star Chamber.

In 1502 his heir Arthur, Prince of Wales, died at Ludlow Castle, very likely of the sweating sickness, and Elizabeth died the following year; the king, normally reserved, grieved intensely. Henry VII died on 21 April 1509, after nearly 24 years on the throne, and was peacefully succeeded by Henry VIII. Historians have compared him with Louis XI of France and Ferdinand II of Aragon, and Francis Bacon published a History of the Reign of King Henry VII in 1622.
henry-viii-of-england: Henry was born on 28 June 1491 at the Palace of Placentia in Greenwich, the second son of King Henry VII and Elizabeth of York. As a small child he was given many offices, including Constable of Dover Castle and Duke of York, which allowed his father to keep lucrative positions in personal control. His elder brother Arthur, Prince of Wales, died in 1502, making Henry the heir. He succeeded at 17 in April 1509 and married his brother's widow, Catherine of Aragon, on 11 June 1509.

Henry joined the Holy League against France in 1511, and his invasion force of 1513 numbered some 30,000 men. In the later 1520s he grew impatient with Catherine's failure to produce a male heir and became enamoured of Anne Boleyn. Historians such as E. L. Woodward see the annulment as the occasion rather than the cause of the English Reformation. On 23 May 1533 Thomas Cranmer declared the marriage to Catherine void, and Anne was crowned on 1 June. Their daughter Elizabeth was born on 7 September 1533.

In 1536 Henry assented to the Laws in Wales Act, which united England and Wales. The day after Anne Boleyn's execution he became engaged to Jane Seymour; his minister Thomas Cromwell later arranged the marriage to Anne of Cleves, and Henry afterwards married Catherine Howard, who was beheaded, and Catherine Parr in July 1543. In 1538 the shrine of Thomas Becket at Canterbury was dismantled, and in 1542 the remaining monasteries were dissolved and their property transferred to the Crown.

Henry's later years were marked by obesity and a leg wound that festered after a jousting accident on 24 January 1536. He died on 28 January 1547 and was succeeded by his only surviving son, Edward VI, aged nine. Henry's will named sixteen executors, and Edward Seymour became Lord Protector. It excluded the Stuart descendants of his sister Margaret, a provision that failed when James VI of Scotland became king of England in 1603. John D. Mackie judged that Henry carried England through a perilous time of change.
henry-wadsworth-longfellow: Longfellow was born on 27 February 1807 in Portland, then a town of the District of Maine in Massachusetts. His father, Stephen Longfellow, was a lawyer, and his maternal grandfather, Peleg Wadsworth, had been a general in the American Revolutionary War and a member of Congress. He was the second of eight children and descended from English colonists of New England, among them Mayflower Pilgrims. A studious child fluent in Latin, he published his first poem at the age of 13, a patriotic piece in the Portland Gazette on 17 November 1820.

After graduating from Bowdoin College in 1825 he was offered a professorship of modern languages there. He toured Europe from May 1826 to August 1829, learned French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese and German mostly without formal instruction, and met Washington Irving in Madrid, who encouraged him to write. At Bowdoin he translated textbooks, and his first published book, in 1833, was a translation of the poems of the medieval Spanish poet Jorge Manrique. He later taught at Harvard College. His collections Voices of the Night (1839) and Ballads and Other Poems (1841) made him instantly popular. He retired from teaching in 1854 to devote himself to writing.

His first wife, Mary Potter, died in 1835 after a miscarriage. In 1843 he married Frances Appleton, daughter of the Boston industrialist Nathan Appleton, after a long courtship. She died on 10 July 1861 after her dress caught fire, and Longfellow, burned while trying to save her, could not attend her funeral. He grew a beard from then on. He turned for a time to translation and, from 1864, met friends every Wednesday in the Dante Club to refine his version of Dante Alighieri's Divine Comedy, published in three volumes in 1867. He was the first American to translate it completely.

Longfellow wrote lyric poems known for their musicality, many telling stories from mythology and legend, and he used many forms, including hexameter, blank verse, ballads and sonnets. His best-known works include Evangeline (1847), The Song of Hiawatha (1855) and Paul Revere's Ride. He supported abolitionism and, after the American Civil War, hoped for reconciliation between North and South. His poem Christmas Bells later became the basis of a carol. He died on 24 March 1882.

He was the most popular American poet of his day and had success overseas. His seventieth birthday in 1877 took on the air of a national holiday. Soon after his death his reputation declined, as academics turned to Walt Whitman, Robert Frost and others, and critics judged his verse sentimental and derivative of European models. In 2020 Nicholas A. Basbanes defended him as the victim of an orchestrated dismissal.
henryk-sienkiewicz: Henryk Sienkiewicz was born on 5 May 1846 at Wola Okrzejska in the Kingdom of Poland, then part of the Russian Empire. His family were impoverished Polish nobles, on his father's side descended from Lipka Tatars who had settled in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. He grew up on family estates and in Warsaw, where he studied at the Imperial University and moved from medicine and law to the Institute of Philology and History. He finished in 1871 without a diploma, having failed the examination in Ancient Greek, and lived in poverty as a part-time tutor.

He debuted as a journalist in 1869 and wrote under the pen name Litwos. In 1876 he went to the United States with the actress Helena Modrzejewska, and Gazeta Polska paid for his journey in exchange for travel essays, which won him a popular following. He stayed in California and returned to Poland in 1879. From 1883 he turned to historical novels. With Fire and Sword was serialised from 1883 to 1884, The Deluge from 1884 to 1886 and Sir Michael from 1887 to 1888. Together these make the Trilogy, which established him as the most popular contemporary Polish writer.

He wrote the first chapters of Quo Vadis in February 1895, and the novel was finished by March 1896 and soon gained international renown. He began serialising Krzyżacy, The Teutonic Knights, in 1897, and it was finished in 1900. In 1900 the Polish people gave him an estate at Oblęgorek near Kielce, where he later opened a school for children.

Poland remained partitioned between Russia, Austria and Prussia, later Germany, and Sienkiewicz used his fame to influence world opinion for the Polish cause. He criticised the policy of Germanization of the Polish minority in Germany, supported the Września schoolchildren in 1901, and in 1907 appealed to the intellectual community amid German attempts to expropriate Polish land. A moderate, he declined to stand for the Russian Duma and gave to struggling writers.

In 1905 he won the Nobel Prize in Literature for his merits as an epic writer. In his acceptance speech he said that Poland had been pronounced dead and that the prize was proof that she lived. He died on 15 November 1916.
hephthalites: The Hephthalites, sometimes called the White Huns, called themselves Ebodalo, a name they wrote in the Bactrian script on some of their coins. Sources for their history are sparse, there is no king-list, and historians disagree about how the group arose and what language it first spoke. The most prominent view at present is that they were of Turkic origin and later adopted Bactrian, an Eastern Iranian language written in the Greek alphabet, as their official language. Chinese chronicles derived them from the Gaoju or the Da Yuezhi. Scholars have reached no consensus on any link with the Huns of Eastern Europe.

The Hephthalites were at first vassals of the Rouran Khaganate and borrowed much of their political organisation from it, including the title khan. They split from their overlords in the early fifth century. Persian sources show them fighting Yazdegerd II from 442. In 458 a Hephthalite king named Akhshunwar helped Peroz I seize the Sasanian throne from his brother, and with Hephthalite aid Peroz reportedly ended Kidarite rule in Transoxiana by 467.

Their stronghold was Tokharistan, on the northern slopes of the Hindu Kush, and their capital was probably Kunduz. They may have conquered Sogdia as early as 479. In the late fifth century they crossed the Pamir Mountains and took the western Tarim Basin, including Kashgar and Khotan, from the weakening Rourans, and by the early sixth century they were sending embassies to the Northern Wei. They did not go beyond the Hindu Kush, which the Alchon Huns held, a people once thought to be part of the Hephthalites and now usually treated as separate.

Their power ended when the First Turkic Khaganate and the Sasanians under Khosrow I allied against them and defeated them after an eight-day battle near Qarshi, the Battle of Gol-Zarriun, perhaps in 557. Afterwards Hephthalite principalities remained in Tokharistan until the Tokhara Yabghus took over in 625.

The Hephthalites were a tribal confederation that included both nomadic and settled urban communities, and many of the people they ruled were probably Iranian speakers. Central control was weak, and local dynasties paid tribute. The Chinese considered them excellent archers, and they probably had a strong cavalry. Chinese sources report that brothers shared one wife, with the number of horns on a married woman's headdress matching the number of her husbands. Murals at Balalyk tepe and at the Buddhas of Bamiyan show figures with round beardless faces and cropped hair. The complex at Bamiyan was developed under Hephthalite rule.
hera: The name Hera is attested in Mycenaean Greek, written e-ra in Linear B on tablets from Pylos and Thebes, and it has no clear etymology. A Pylos tablet mentions offerings to Zeus-Hera-Drimios. Hera was the protecting goddess of Argos and may have Mycenaean origin. Homer's formula boōpis potnia Hērē, cow-eyed mistress Hera, probably relates her to a Mediterranean goddess of nature. Scholars have proposed Near Eastern and Indo-European origins, and some think that in certain cults she was an earth goddess. Others, following Johann Jakob Bachofen, have asked whether she was originally the goddess of a matriarchal people who lived in Greece before the Hellenes.

In historical times most Greeks recognised Hera as the consort of Zeus. She was the goddess of marriage, women and family and the protector of women in childbirth, and queen among the twelve Olympians. In myth she is the daughter of the Titans Cronus and Rhea. Her marriage with her brother Zeus is the main theme of most festivals held for her, in which young married women performed dances and rites. Her epithets include Gamēlios, presiding over marriage, and Anassa, queen.

Myths show her as jealous and vengeful towards Zeus's lovers and their children. She tricked Semele into asking Zeus to appear in his true form, which destroyed her. She delayed the birth of Heracles, whose name means glory of Hera, so that Eurystheus was born first. In art she is a dignified, matronly figure, upright or enthroned, crowned with a polos or diadem and sometimes veiled. Her sacred animals included the cow and the cuckoo, and in Hellenistic times the peacock.

The chief centre of her cult was the north-eastern Peloponnese, around Argos, Tiryns and Corinth. The oldest temple at Olympia belonged to her, and she was worshipped on Samos, Euboea, Rhodes and Crete. One of the earliest Greek temples was her temple of Hera Akraia at Perachora, built in the 9th century BCE. Her Roman counterpart is Juno, and Renaissance art joined Hera and Juno in one iconography.
heracles: Heracles, whose name means glory of Hera, was born Alcaeus or Alcides. He was considered the son of Zeus and Alcmene and the foster son of Amphitryon. Hera's hatred shaped his myths, since she plotted against Zeus's mortal children as revenge for his infidelities. Unlike other Greek heroes, no tomb was identified as his. At some festivals he received sacrifice first as a hero and then as a god upon an altar, so that he is the closest Greek approach to a demigod. His figure drew at first on Near Eastern motifs such as the lion fight.

In one tradition Hera drove Heracles mad and he killed his wife Megara and their children. The Oracle of Delphi told him to serve King Eurystheus for twelve years and perform ten tasks. Eurystheus added two more, which gave the twelve Labours. They included killing the Nemean lion and the Lernaean Hydra, stealing the golden apples of the Hesperides and capturing Cerberus. Other stories have him sailing with the Argonauts, killing the eagle that tormented Prometheus and sacking Troy before the Trojan War. After killing Iphitus in another fit of madness, he served a year as the slave of Omphale, queen of Lydia.

He married four times. His wife Deianira was deceived by the dying centaur Nessus into giving him a tunic smeared with poisoned blood. Unable to remove it, he burned himself on a pyre on Mount Oeta, and he ascended to Olympus as a god and married Hebe. His descendants are the Heracleidae. He is shown with a lion skin and a club, and was patron of young men and gymnasia.

The Greeks held the festival of the Heracleia, which commemorated his death, in late July or early August, and several ancient cities were named Heraclea for him. In the 5th century BCE he was increasingly given an ethical character, as in the parable of the Choice of Heracles, in which he chooses a severe but glorious life over an easy one. In Rome he was honoured as Hercules, and Roman emperors such as Commodus and Maximian identified themselves with him.

Herodotus connected him to the Egyptian god Shu and to the Phoenician god Melqart. Christian writers read the cult in a Euhemerist way, treating him as a historical king of Argos who was deified after death. Through Greco-Buddhist culture, Heraclean symbolism travelled to the Far East, and an example survives in the Nio guardian deities at Japanese Buddhist temples.
heraclitus: Little is known of the life of Heraclitus. He was the son of Blyson and came from the Ionian city of Ephesus, a port on the Cayster River on the western coast of Asia Minor, which was then part of the Persian Empire. Ephesus appears to have kept a close relationship with Persia; when Darius the Great suppressed the Ionian revolt in 494 BCE, Ephesus was spared, while Miletus, home of the earlier philosophers, was sacked.

The main source for his life is the doxographer Diogenes Laërtius, whose information is mostly unreliable. His story that Heraclitus gave up the hereditary title of king to his younger brother may at least suggest an aristocratic family. Heraclitus appears to have had little sympathy for democracy or the masses.

Heraclitus is said to have produced a single work on papyrus, which has not survived; more than 100 fragments are preserved in quotations by other authors. Its title is unknown, though later writers call it On Nature. According to Diogenes Laërtius he deposited it in the Artemision as a dedication. Its oracular, wordplay-filled style earned him the epithets the dark and the obscure, and the weeping philosopher, in contrast to the laughing Democritus.

The hallmarks of his thought are the unity of opposites and constant change. He is quoted as saying that everything flows and that no man steps in the same river twice. Among his sayings on opposites are 'The way up is the way down' and 'The straight and the crooked path of the fuller's comb is one and the same'. He saw harmony and justice in strife, and he stands opposed to Parmenides, who believed in a static being.

Like the Milesians before him, Heraclitus named a fundamental element, the arche: Thales had chosen water, Anaximander the apeiron and Anaximenes air, while Heraclitus chose fire. In one fragment he calls the world-order 'ever-living fire, kindling in measures and being quenched in measures'. He also spoke of the logos, a word meaning speech, discourse or reason, which seems to designate the rational structure of the world and a kind of divine law.

His writings influenced Plato, Aristotle and the Stoics, and later Hegel, Nietzsche and Heidegger. Plato presented Cratylus as a Heraclitean, and according to Aristotle Cratylus went further, saying that one cannot step into the same river even once. Two of his fragments occur in the Derveni papyrus, an Orphic poem. Whether he had students in his lifetime is unknown.
heraclius: Scholars debate the origin of Heraclius, chiefly because they debate that of his father, Heraclius the Elder, who is often considered of Armenian descent. Little is known of his life before he became emperor. In 608 the elder Heraclius, Exarch of Africa, renounced his loyalty to the unpopular emperor Phocas. His nephew Nicetas invaded Egypt, while the younger Heraclius sailed east with a second force. When he reached Constantinople the Excubitors deserted to him, and he entered the city without serious resistance. Phocas was executed, and Heraclius was crowned on 5 October 610.

The war with Sasanian Persia had begun in 602, when Khosrow II used the murder of the emperor Maurice as an occasion to attack. The Persians took Damascus in 613, Jerusalem in 614, where they captured the True Cross, and Egypt by 622. Heraclius himself was defeated near Antioch in 613. He raised money by borrowing Church treasure and cutting other spending, and left Constantinople on 4 April 622 to campaign in Armenia and the Caucasus. In 626 the Avars and Slavs, supported by a Persian army, besieged Constantinople, and the siege failed.

Late in 627 Heraclius launched a winter offensive into Mesopotamia and defeated the Persians at the Battle of Nineveh. Khosrow was overthrown and killed by his son Kavad II, who sued for peace and agreed to withdraw from all occupied territory. In 629 Heraclius restored the True Cross to Jerusalem.
