The recovered lands were soon exposed to the Arabs: after the Battle of Yarmouk in 636 the Levant was lost within three years, and most of Egypt had fallen by 641. He also promoted Monothelitism in his Ecthesis, hoping to reconcile the Miaphysites, but the popes condemned it.

Heraclius died of an illness on 11 February 641, aged sixty-six, and was succeeded by his sons Heraclius Constantine and Heraclonas. Edward Gibbon judged his reign inconsistent, with a brilliant middle between idle first and last years. Warren Treadgold praises his success against the Persians and thinks his performance against the Arabs respectable, since he preserved the empire where the Persian king Yazdegerd III lost his. Greek became the official language of the state during his reign, and in 629 he began to use the title Basileus. Western medieval Christians remembered him as the first crusader, for the recovery of the True Cross.
heraklion: The name Herakleion comes from an ancient port, Heracleium, the harbour of Knossos, named for the hero Heracles. Knossos had a port on the site from the start of the Early Minoan period. After the fall of the Minoans the area developed little, and early in Byzantine times it abounded with pirates and bandits. The Arabic name of the city meant Castle of the Moat and became Chandax in Greek, which gave Candia. That name was used for the whole island as well as the city. After the Byzantine reconquest the city was locally known as Megalo Kastro, meaning Big Castle.

Moors expelled from Al-Andalus under Abu Hafs Umar took Crete from the Eastern Roman Empire and chose the site as capital in 824. They dug a moat round the city, and the Emirate of Crete lasted from about 827 to 961. When Nikephoros Phokas took the city in March 961 after a prolonged siege, the inhabitants were slaughtered and the city was looted and burned. It stayed Byzantine for 243 years. In 1204 the Republic of Venice bought it as part of a political deal arising from the Fourth Crusade. The Venetians built a wall in places up to 40 metres thick with seven bastions, and made Candia the capital of the Regno di Candia.

The meeting of Venetian and Cretan cultures led to the Cretan Renaissance in letters and the arts. In the Cretan War the Ottomans besieged the city for 21 years, from 1648 to 1669, and Köprülüzade Fazıl Ahmed Pasha took it in 1669. Under the Ottomans the harbour silted up and shipping moved to Chania, which became the capital of Crete in 1849. An earthquake on 12 October 1856 destroyed most of the city's over 3,600 homes. The city joined the Kingdom of Greece in 1913, was badly damaged in the German invasion of May 1941, and became capital of Crete again in 1971.

Heraklion is the fourth largest city in Greece, with a municipal population of 179,302 in 2021. Its Venetian walls, the Koules Fortress and the arsenal dominate the port area. The Heraklion Archaeological Museum and the University of Crete are among its institutions. The writer Nikos Kazantzakis and the painter El Greco were born there.
herat: Herat lies in western Afghanistan, south of the Paropamisus Mountains in the fertile valley of the Hari River. It stands on the Silk Road between West Asia, Central Asia, South Asia and East Asia and was traditionally known for its wine. The city and its district take their ancient name from the river: under the Achaemenid Empire (550-330 BCE) the district was called Haraiva, and classical sources call the region Areia.

The date of Herat's foundation is unknown. At the time of the Arab invasion in the middle of the 7th century, Sasanian power in the province was largely nominal, and Hephthalite tribal lords had settled in the region. The Hephthalites and some Turks opposed the invaders at the battle of Qohestān in 651-52 but were defeated. In the Middle Ages Herat was one of the important cities of Khorasan, known as the Pearl of Khorasan. In 994 Alptegin and Mahmud of Ghazni defeated its rebellious governor Faik and annexed Herat, Nishapur and Tous.

After its conquest by Timur the city became an important centre of intellectual and artistic life in the Islamic world. Under Shah Rukh and Husayn Bayqara it was the focal point of the Timurid Renaissance, whose grandeur is thought to have matched that of Florence in the Italian Renaissance. It then remained part of Safavid Iran until the early 18th century. In 1716 the Abdali Afghans in the city revolted and set up the Sadozai Sultanate of Herat, and in 1732 it became part of Afsharid Iran. Ahmad Shah Durrani took it in 1747. In the first half of the 19th century it was an independent city-state and faced several invasions from Qajar Iran. It was incorporated into Afghanistan in 1863.

Herat is the capital of Herat Province and a major industrial and trading centre of Afghanistan. Most of its people speak Dari, a form of Persian, and Pashto is the second major language. Its historic sites include the Great Mosque of Herat, the Herat Citadel and the Musalla Complex.
herbert-spencer: Spencer was born in Derby on 27 April 1820. His father, William George Spencer, a religious dissenter, ran a school based on the teaching methods of Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi and served as secretary of the Derby Philosophical Society, founded in 1783 by Erasmus Darwin. Through its members Spencer met pre-Darwinian ideas of biological evolution, particularly those of Erasmus Darwin and Jean-Baptiste Lamarck. His uncle, the Reverend Thomas Spencer, taught him some mathematics, physics and Latin, and passed on firm free-trade and anti-statist views. Otherwise Spencer was an autodidact.

He worked as a civil engineer during the railway boom of the late 1830s while writing for radical provincial journals. While sub-editor of The Economist from 1848 to 1853 he published Social Statics, in which he predicted that humanity would become adapted to life in society and that the state would wither away. Through the publisher John Chapman's salon he knew John Stuart Mill, Harriet Martineau, George Henry Lewes and Mary Ann Evans, and he introduced Thomas Henry Huxley, who became a lifelong friend. Lewes and Evans acquainted him with Auguste Comte's positivism, from which he strongly dissented.

Spencer set out his evolutionary view in the essay Progress: Its Law and Cause in 1857. He held that all structures in the universe develop from a simple, undifferentiated sameness to a complex, differentiated variety, a law he applied to stars, organisms, societies and the human mind. His agnosticism won him notoriety, though he said he wanted to reconcile science and religion.

In his last decades Spencer was lonely and disillusioned. He never married and after 1855 was a lifelong hypochondriac. He was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1902, which went to Theodor Mommsen, and he died on 8 December 1903 at the age of 83. By the 1870s and 1880s he may have been the only philosopher to sell over a million copies in his own lifetime, yet his influence declined sharply after 1900. His name is often linked with Social Darwinism, although such themes are absent from his sociological works, and libertarians have claimed him as a precursor.
herceg-novi: Herceg Novi lies at the western entrance to the Bay of Kotor in the Coastal region of Montenegro, at the foot of Mount Orjen. Its municipality stretches from Prevlaka to the Verige strait, with an almost unbroken string of towns along the coast. The climate is humid subtropical, with much more rain in winter than summer, and the town has about 200 sunny days a year. The name appears in several languages: Castelnuovo in Italian, Neókastron in Greek and Kala-i Novi in Ottoman Turkish, all meaning new castle.

Finds from the Luštica peninsula and the Vranjaj cavern show that the area was settled in the Neolithic and early Bronze Age. Rome ruled it from the 3rd century BCE, after its victory over the Illyrians, and the Eastern Roman Empire afterwards. Slavic tribes settled in the 7th century, and the district of Dračevica later passed through the Principality of Travunija, the Kingdom of Serbia and the Balšić family.

In 1382 King Tvrtko I of Bosnia built a fortress on the site of a small fishing village. Bosnia's coast from the Neretva to the Bay of Kotor lacked a significant port, and Tvrtko, pressed by the War of Chioggia and a Ragusan embargo, wanted a new salt-trading centre. The fortress was named for Saint Stephen, but it was soon known as Novi. It passed to Duke Sandalj Hranić of the Kosača family, and then to his nephew Stjepan Vukčić Kosača, who made it his winter seat; his title herceg gave the town its present name.

The Ottomans held the town until 1687, apart from 1538–1539, when the Spaniards held it before they were defeated in the Siege of Castelnuovo. The Ottomans built the Kanli Tower, and an earthquake devastated the town in 1608. In 1687 the Republic of Venice took it under Girolamo Corner and placed it in Albania Veneta. Habsburg Austria annexed it in 1798, Russia occupied it in 1806–1807, and France took over in 1807, joining it to the Illyrian Provinces in 1809. Austria held the Bay of Kotor until 1918.

The municipality had 30,864 residents at the 2011 census. The Old Town keeps the Forte Mare fortress and the Kanli Tower, a clock tower built by the Austrians in the 19th century, and several Serbian Orthodox churches and monasteries, among them the Savina Monastery. The town was once a Catholic bishopric and remains a titular see, Novi. It is known as a spa and holiday destination.
herculaneum: Dionysius of Halicarnassus states that the Greek hero Heracles founded the town, while Strabo says the Oscans founded the first settlement. The town sided with the Allies against Rome in the Social War of 91–88 BCE and was defeated by Titus Didius, a legate of Sulla, and in 89 BCE it became a Roman municipium.

Smaller than Pompeii, with about 5,000 people, Herculaneum was wealthier. It flourished as a seaside retreat for the Roman elite, with a dense cluster of luxurious houses. The Villa of the Papyri, built on four terraces on the shore, is thought to have belonged to the consul Lucius Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus, Julius Caesar's father-in-law.

The course of the eruption is reconstructed from excavation and from two letters of Pliny the Younger to Tacitus. Vesuvius began to throw out material at about one in the afternoon of the first day. The winds blew towards the south-east, so Pompeii received most of the fall, while only a few centimetres of ash fell on Herculaneum, which lies west of the mountain. The ash led most inhabitants to flee. At one in the morning the eruptive column collapsed, and the first pyroclastic surge swept through the town at about 160 km/h.

Six flows and surges buried the town to about 20 metres. In some areas they left buildings and objects almost intact; elsewhere they knocked down walls. Intense heat, of at least 250 °C, rather than suffocation, is now thought to have killed people within ten kilometres.

According to the usual account the town was found by chance in 1709, when a well was being dug; the Prince d'Elbeuf tunnelled from its bottom and reached a theatre. Regular excavation began in 1738 under Charles III of Spain, and the publication of Le Antichità di Ercolano influenced early Neoclassicism. Work stopped in 1762 after Winckelmann criticised its treasure-hunting methods, and Pompeii, covered by only four metres of material against twenty, drew attention away.

Between 1752 and 1754 workmen recovered blackened papyrus scrolls from the Villa of the Papyri. In 1980–1981 hundreds of skeletons were found in the boat houses by the ancient shore, showing that many people had not escaped. More than three quarters of the town remains buried, and the modern towns of Ercolano and Portici lie above it.
herge: Georges Prosper Remi was born on 22 May 1907 in Etterbeek, a suburb of Brussels, to a lower-middle-class family: his father Alexis Remi was a Walloon who worked in a confectionery factory, and his mother Elisabeth Dufour was Flemish. His first language was French, but he also learned Dutch. His pen name, Hergé, is the French pronunciation of his reversed initials, RG. He began his career contributing illustrations to Scouting magazines, and in 1926 started his first comic series, The Adventures of Totor, for Le Boy-Scout Belge.

Working for the conservative Catholic newspaper Le Vingtième Siècle, Hergé created The Adventures of Tintin in 1929 on the advice of its editor, Norbert Wallez. The early albums, Tintin in the Land of the Soviets, Tintin in the Congo and Tintin in America, were designed as conservative propaganda for children. From 1934, influenced by his friend Zhang Chongren, he put far more emphasis on background research. Casterman began publishing the albums in book form from the volume of Cigars of the Pharaoh, and Hergé also produced Quick and Flupke and The Adventures of Jo, Zette and Jocko. All were drawn in his distinctive ligne claire style.

After the Allied liberation of Belgium in 1944, the newspaper Le Soir, in which Tintin had appeared during the German occupation, was shut down, and its staff, including Hergé, were accused of collaboration. He was arrested on 3 September 1944 and was arrested on three further occasions, spending one night in jail. No charges were brought, but he faced accusations of being a traitor and collaborator for years afterwards. In 1946 he founded Tintin magazine with Raymond Leblanc, and in 1950 he established Studios Hergé, whose staff included Bob de Moor and Jacques Martin.

Hergé died on 3 March 1983. His work has been widely praised for its clarity of draughtsmanship and its meticulously researched plots, and he remains a strong influence on comics, particularly in Europe. He has also faced repeated accusations of racism, notably over the portrayal of the Congolese in Tintin in the Congo, which was not seen as controversial when it appeared and came to be seen as racist in the later twentieth century. The Hergé Museum, in Louvain-la-Neuve, opened in 2009.
herisau: Herisau lies in the former District of Hinterland, at the crossing point of two major routes through the region, the road from St. Gallen to the Toggenburg and the road from Gossau to Appenzell. It consists of the village of Herisau and scattered hamlets, together with residential and industrial districts. About one third of the population of the whole half-canton lives there. Before 1648 the municipality controlled about twice as much land as it does now, since Schwellbrunn was then part of it.

Herisau was first mentioned in 837 as Herinisauva, and its church is mentioned in 907. The place suffered repeatedly in the struggles with the monastery of St. Gallen. It was destroyed in 1084 during battles around the monastery, and again in 1248 and 1249 when the monastery destroyed it to establish loyalty. In 1401 Herisau joined an alliance with other places in Appenzell during the Appenzell Wars, and between 1517 and 1518 it managed to buy itself free from the monastery.

Herisau was already an important centre of trade and commerce by 1537. Its town hall was built in 1601, and in 1606 the town was largely destroyed by fire. In 1648 Schwellbrunn separated and became an independent village. Between 1798 and 1803 Herisau was the capital of the canton of Säntis.

Herisau is the capital of the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden and the seat of its government and parliament, while the judicial authorities are in Trogen. Several buildings are listed as heritage sites of national significance: the central hamlet and the houses around the central square, the Protestant church of 1580, the houses Wetter and zur Rose, both of 1737, the hamlet of Schwänberg, and the government building with the state archive.

The majority of residents speak German. In 2003 Herisau was named Alpine Town of the Year, and with other Alpine towns it takes part in the association of that name, which works to put the Alpine Convention into effect and to achieve sustainable development in the Alpine region.
hermann-goring: Hermann Wilhelm Göring was born on 12 January 1893 in Rosenheim, Bavaria. His father, Heinrich Ernst Göring, had been the first governor-general of German South West Africa. His godfather, Hermann Epenstein, a wealthy Jewish physician and businessman, provided the family with a home in Berlin and then with a small castle. In the First World War Göring served in an infantry regiment, then transferred to the air service. He became a fighter pilot, received the Pour le Mérite and was the last commander of Jagdgeschwader 1, the wing once led by Manfred von Richthofen. After the war he worked as a pilot in Denmark and Sweden and married Carin von Kantzow on 3 February 1922.

Göring joined the Nazi Party in 1922 after hearing a speech by Adolf Hitler and took command of the Sturmabteilung in March 1923. He was wounded in the Beer Hall Putsch that year and became addicted to morphine. When Hitler became chancellor on 30 January 1933, Göring was made minister without portfolio and, on 11 April, Minister-President of Prussia and chief of the Prussian police. He oversaw the creation of the Gestapo, which he ceded to Heinrich Himmler in 1934. After the Reichstag fire of 27 February 1933 he called for a crackdown on Communists, and some 4,000 party members were arrested. In 1936 he became Plenipotentiary of the Four Year Plan.

On 1 September 1939 Hitler designated him his successor. After the Fall of France in 1940 he received the specially created rank of Reichsmarschall. His standing declined as the Luftwaffe failed to stop Allied bombing and to supply the forces encircled at Stalingrad, and he devoted his attention to collecting property and art, much of it stolen from Jewish victims of the Holocaust. When he asked on 22 April 1945 to take over leadership of the Reich, Hitler regarded this as treason and ordered his arrest.

Göring supported the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 and required the registration of all Jewish property. After Kristallnacht he proposed that Jews be fined one billion marks, and minutes read out at his trial showed his knowledge of and complicity in their persecution. He was convicted at the Nuremberg trials in 1946 of conspiracy, crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity. His request to be shot was refused and he was sentenced to hang. On the night of 15 October 1946, before the execution, he died by suicide by taking cyanide.
hermann-hesse: Hermann Karl Hesse was born on 2 July 1877 in the Black Forest town of Calw, in Württemberg. His grandparents served at a Basel Mission in India, and his mother, Marie Gundert, was born at a mission in South India. The family lived in Basel from 1881 for six years before returning to Calw. In 1891 Hesse entered the Evangelical Theological Seminary at Maulbronn Abbey, where a serious personal crisis began. In March 1892 he fled the seminary and was found in a field a day later. After an attempt at suicide in May he spent time in institutions, and in 1893 he passed the examination that ended his schooling.

On 17 October 1895 Hesse began work in a bookshop in Tübingen, and after twelve-hour days he read theology, Goethe, Lessing and Schiller, and from 1895 Nietzsche. In 1904 he married Maria Bernoulli and settled in Gaienhofen on Lake Constance, where he wrote Beneath the Wheel, published in 1906.

When the First World War broke out in 1914 he registered as a volunteer and was assigned to the care of prisoners of war. On 3 November he published an essay, "O Friends, Not These Tones", urging intellectuals not to fall for nationalistic hatred. The German press attacked him, though Theodor Heuss and Romain Rolland supported him. By 1919 his marriage had fallen apart, and he resettled alone in Ticino, moving to Montagnola on 11 May. Siddhartha appeared in 1922. He married Ruth Wenger in 1924, divorced in 1927 and married Ninon in 1931.

Hesse's best-known novels are Demian, Steppenwolf, Siddhartha, Narcissus and Goldmund and The Glass Bead Game, each exploring an individual's search for authenticity, self-knowledge and spirituality. His interest in Eastern religious and philosophical traditions, and in Jungian analysis, shaped his work. He wrote that for different people there are different ways to God. He was widely read in the German-speaking world in his lifetime and received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1946. His works were little read in the United States when he died in 1962, but in the mid-1960s they became bestsellers there in paperback, a revival credited to their association with themes of the counterculture.
hermes: The earliest written record of Hermes comes from Linear B tablets of the Mycenaean Bronze Age found at Pylos, Thebes and Knossos, where his name appears as e-ma-a, always beside those of goddesses. Later worship of Hermes also took place mostly within sanctuaries dedicated chiefly to goddesses such as Hera and Demeter. The name has long been derived from the Greek herma, a heap of stones, but this is disputed. Hermes began as a god with strong underworld associations, a psychopomp who led souls along the road between the upper and lower worlds. This role widened to roads in general and then to boundaries, travellers, sailors and commerce. He is described as the youngest Olympian and may have joined the Olympian pantheon late.

In myth Hermes is the herald and messenger of the gods, often presented as the son of Zeus and Maia. The Homeric Hymn to Hermes gives the best-known account of him as a divine trickster. He killed the hundred-eyed giant Argus, which earned him the epithet Argeïphontes. He wore winged sandals, and in Roman art a winged cap, and carried the caduceus, a winged staff entwined with snakes. He was also the patron of flocks and shepherds.

His name was given to the herma, first a roadside pile of stones to which each traveller added one. In the 6th century BCE Hipparchus, son of Pisistratus, replaced the cairns that marked the midway points between Athenian demes with pillars topped by a bust of Hermes. Such herms stood at crossroads and doorways, served as boundary and grave markers, and were thought to protect a household. Only three temples dedicated to him in Classical Greece are known, all in Arcadia, where Mount Cyllene was among the oldest places of his worship.

In Ptolemaic Egypt Greeks identified the god Thoth with Hermes, and their city Khemenu became Hermopolis. Hermes thereby gained the character of a god of learning and secret wisdom. The Romans adopted him as early as the 4th century BCE under the name Mercury, combining his attributes with those of the Etruscan Turms. After the Christian suppression of pagan worship in the 4th century CE, Christian scholars still treated Hermes Trismegistus as a mortal prophet who had foretold Christianity, and Renaissance philosophers used the Hermetic writings to support a belief in a single true theology shared by all religions.
hernan-cortes: Hernán Cortés was born around 1485 in Medellín, in Extremadura, to Martín Cortés, an hidalgo of distinguished ancestry but slender means, and Catalina Pizarro; through his mother he was a distant relation of Francisco Pizarro. At fourteen he was sent to study Latin with an uncle in Salamanca. He sailed for Hispaniola in 1504, registered as a citizen of Santo Domingo, received an encomienda and became a notary at Azua de Compostela. In 1511 he accompanied Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar in the conquest of Cuba, where he served as clerk to the treasurer and became a magistrate of the second Spanish town.

In 1518 Velázquez put Cortés in command of an expedition to the mainland, then revoked his charter at the last minute. Cortés ignored the order and sailed in February 1519 with about 11 ships, 500 men, 13 horses and a few cannon. On the Yucatán coast he found Geronimo de Aguilar, a Spanish priest who had learned Chontal Maya, and he also used Doña Marina as his interpreter. He allied with some native peoples against others. In mid-August 1519 he marched on Tenochtitlán with 600 soldiers, 15 horsemen, 15 cannons and hundreds of indigenous carriers and warriors, after Moctezuma II had repeatedly refused to meet him.

Cortés's force reached Tlaxcala after the battle of Otumba, having lost 870 men. With their allies and reinforcements from Cuba, they prevailed. Cortés cut off supplies, subdued the cities allied to the Aztecs and built brigantines on the lake. He destroyed the city block by block, and the siege ended in Spanish victory and the destruction of Tenochtitlán. He wrote to Charles V asking to be rewarded rather than punished for mutiny, and received the title of Marquis of the Valley of Oaxaca, while the viceroyalty went to Antonio de Mendoza in 1535. From 1524 to 1526 he led an expedition to Honduras, during which Cuauhtémoc was executed.

Cortés returned to Spain in 1541, hoping to answer lawsuits brought by his opponents, and joined the emperor's expedition against Algiers, in which he nearly drowned in a storm. Heavily in debt after financing his own expeditions, he made a claim on the royal treasury in February 1544 and was ignored for three years. He set out for Mexico in 1547 but was taken ill at Seville and died at Castilleja de la Cuesta on 2 December 1547, aged 62. His letters to Charles V, the cartas de relación, are his only surviving writings. Mexico City was built on the ruins of Tenochtitlán, and the Paso de Cortés, the pass between the volcanoes Iztaccíhuatl and Popocatépetl through which he led his soldiers, bears his name.
hernando-de-soto: Hernando de Soto was born in Extremadura, in what is now the province of Badajoz, to parents who were both hidalgos, nobles of modest means. Badajoz, Barcarrota and Jerez de los Caballeros each claim to be his birthplace; Ursula Lamb considers Jerez most likely, and his will asked that his body be buried there. The region was poor, and young men sought fortune overseas. He sailed to the New World with Pedro Arias Dávila, the first governor of Panama, landing as a teenager in 1514.

De Soto took part in an expedition to Veragua in 1520 and in the conquest of Nicaragua from 1524, where he received an encomienda and an office in León. He became known as a horseman and tactician, and for extorting native villages by seizing their chiefs. He then joined Francisco Pizarro and became one of his captains. At Cajamarca he led one of three mounted groups in the attack on the Inca Atahualpa. During the king's captivity in 1533 he grew friendly with him and taught him chess. He returned to Spain in 1536 with plunder from Peru, entered the Order of Santiago and married Isabel de Bobadilla.

The crown granted him the governorship of Cuba and the right to conquer Florida. With about 620 Spanish and Portuguese men, among them Atlantic Creoles who were enslaved, and with horses and pigs, he landed on the Florida coast in May 1539. He found Juan Ortiz, a Spaniard living among the Mocoso, who served as interpreter in Timucuan-speaking areas. The expedition wintered at the Apalachee village of Anhaica, then went north-east through Georgia and was received by the female chief of Cofitachequi in South Carolina, where it found no gold.

The army crossed the Appalachian Mountains into eastern Tennessee, and reached the Mississippi on 8 May 1541, building flatboats and crossing at night. It then travelled west through Arkansas, Oklahoma and Texas. De Soto died of a fever on 21 May 1542 in the native village of Guachoya. He had persuaded local people that he was an immortal Son of the Sun, so his men hid his death, and by one account sank his body in the Mississippi. Luis de Moscoso Alvarado took command, and the survivors built boats and descended the river. The expedition had lost nearly half its men and found neither treasure nor a site for a colony.

The Spanish counted it a failure. Its pigs escaped and became ancestors of feral razorbacks, and clashes it provoked set many peoples against Europeans. Whether it brought epidemics is disputed, since the first documented smallpox epidemic in the south-east dates from 1696. The route is debated beyond Mabila in Alabama, where John R. Swanton and Charles M. Hudson differ.
hero-of-alexandria: Almost nothing is known of the life of Hero of Alexandria, including his birthplace and background. The first surviving mention of him is in the Collection of Pappus in the 4th century, and scholarly estimates of his dates range widely. Alexandria had been founded by Alexander the Great and was by his time a cosmopolitan city of the Roman Empire, its intellectual life centred on the Mouseion, whose members spoke and wrote in Greek. Because some of his writings read like lecture notes or textbooks in mathematics, mechanics, physics and pneumatics, it has been inferred that he taught there.

Many devices are ascribed to Hero, some of them developed from the work of Ctesibius. The best known is the aeolipile, a steam-driven reaction engine; another engine used air heated in a closed chamber by an altar fire to push water from a sealed vessel, and the weight of the water collected pulled a rope that opened temple doors.

He described a coin-operated machine that released a fixed measure of water for ablutions, a force pump used in a fire engine, a fountain driven by its own water pressure, a self-filling wine bowl with a float valve and a wind-wheel that drove an organ. His mechanical theatre ran an entire play of almost ten minutes from ropes, knots and a rotating cogwheel.

In mathematics he wrote a commentary on Euclid's Elements and the Metrica, a work on applied geometry. The Metrica contains an iterative method for square roots, now called Heron's method, and the formula for the area of a triangle from the lengths of its sides, with which his name is chiefly linked.

He also treated a problem of the shortest path between two points by way of a line, from which he drew the principle that light travelling between two points in one medium takes the shortest path. In the Middle Ages Ibn al-Haytham extended the principle, and Pierre de Fermat stated it in a more general form in 1662.

Much of Hero's original writing has been lost. Some works survive in manuscripts from the Byzantine Empire and, to a lesser extent, in Latin or Arabic translations. Historians have sometimes run the aeolipile together with the temple-door engine and claimed that it did useful work, which the sources do not show.
herod-antipas: Antipas was a son of Herod the Great and Malthace, a woman from Samaria. His date of birth is unknown, but he, his full brother Archelaus and his half-brother Philip were educated in Rome. He was not Herod's first choice of heir. That place went to Aristobulus and Alexander, sons of the Hasmonean princess Mariamne, until they were executed, and to Antipater, who was convicted of trying to poison his father. In Herod's final will Archelaus was to be king, while Antipas would rule Galilee and Perea as tetrarch. The three heirs travelled to Rome, where Augustus largely confirmed the division of territory.

Galilee and Perea were separated by the Decapolis, and both were unsettled. While Antipas was in Rome, dissidents had attacked the palace of Sepphoris, and Quinctilius Varus, the Roman governor of Syria, burned the town and sold its inhabitants as slaves. Antipas rebuilt and fortified Sepphoris and added a wall to Betharamphtha in Perea, later called Livias and then Julias. His main construction was his capital Tiberias on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, named for the emperor Tiberius. Pious Jews at first refused to live there because it was built over a graveyard, so Antipas settled it with foreigners, forced migrants, poor people and freed slaves. His coins carried no images, out of respect for Jewish prescriptions against idolatry.

He divorced his first wife Phasa'el, daughter of King Aretas IV of Nabatea, in order to marry Herodias, who had been married to his half-brother Herod II. According to the Gospels, John the Baptist condemned the marriage, and Antipas had him imprisoned at Machaerus and beheaded. Josephus says instead that John's influence made Antipas fear rebellion. In Luke's account Pilate, learning that Jesus was a Galilean, sent him to Antipas, who questioned and mocked him and sent him back. Some scholars doubt that this trial took place.

The divorce added to disputes with Aretas over the border, and in a war around 36 Antipas's army was defeated. Tiberius ordered a counter-offensive under Lucius Vitellius, but it was abandoned when Tiberius died in March 37.

Antipas's nephew Agrippa, brother of Herodias, became a friend of Caligula and received Philip's former tetrarchy with the title of king in 37. According to Josephus, Herodias urged Antipas to ask for the title of king too, but Agrippa accused him before Caligula of conspiring with Sejanus and with King Artabanus. In the summer of 39 Antipas was exiled and his territory passed to Agrippa. Josephus names Lugdunum in Gaul and, elsewhere, Hispania as the place. He died in exile at an unknown date.
herod-the-great: Herod was born in Idumea, south of Judea, the second son of Antipater the Idumaean, a high-ranking official under the ethnarch Hyrcanus II, and Cypros, a Nabatean princess from Petra. His father was by descent an Edomite, and his ancestors had been forcibly converted to Judaism. Herod was raised as a Jew. Historians dispute his ethnic background: Strabo held that the Idumaeans were of Nabataean origin, while others argue that the Edomites were not Arab. Josephus, whose works record many details of his life, made him a descendant of the Hasmoneans.

Judea had been ruled by Hasmonean kings from 140 until 63 BCE, when Pompey's conquest made them clients of Rome. Herod's war against the Hasmonean Antigonus began in 39 BCE, and after the conquest of Jerusalem Mark Antony executed Antigonus. Herod ruled under Roman overlordship until his death and established the Herodian dynasty. In 30 BCE Octavian confirmed him as King of Judea at Rhodes.

His most ambitious project was the expansion of the Second Temple in Jerusalem, begun in 20-19 BCE, for which he employed 1,000 priests as masons and carpenters to comply with religious law. It was destroyed in 70 CE, and only the retaining walls remain, including the Western Wall. He also built the fortresses of Masada and Herodium and founded Caesarea Maritima. Late in his reign he had his sons Alexander and Aristobulus tried before a Roman court at Beirut, and they were executed. The Gospel of Matthew describes him ordering the killing of all boys of two and under in Bethlehem, the Massacre of the Innocents.

Herod died in Jericho after a painful illness. Josephus says the pain led him to attempt suicide by stabbing, and that his cousin stopped him. Most 20th-century scholarship followed Emil Schürer's chronology of 1896 in dating his death to 4 BCE. Josephus says he was buried at Herodium, and in 2007 a team led by Ehud Netzer announced the discovery of a tomb there, with a broken sarcophagus but no remains.

Augustus respected Herod's will and divided the kingdom among three sons. Herod Archelaus became ethnarch of Judea, Samaria and Idumea, Herod Antipas tetrarch of Galilee and Peraea, and Philip tetrarch of the lands north and east of the Jordan.
herodotus: Herodotus was, by his own statement at the beginning of his work, a native of Halicarnassus in Anatolia, and it is generally accepted that he was born there in the early fifth century BCE. The Suda, a Byzantine encyclopaedia of the 10th century, says that his family was influential, that he was the son of Lyxes and Dryo and that he was related to the epic poet Panyassis. Since Lyxes and Panyassis are Carian names, he was probably at least partly a Hellenised Carian. Halicarnassus was within the Persian Empire, which made him a Persian subject.

The evidence for his life is slight and late. According to the Suda he learned the Ionian dialect on Samos, to which his family fled from the tyrant Lygdamis, and later returned to lead the revolt that overthrew him. Inscriptions show that Ionic Greek was used in official documents at Halicarnassus, and since the Suda is the only source for the liberation, its account is doubtful.

Herodotus's eyewitness accounts indicate that he travelled in Egypt in association with Athenians, probably after 454 BCE. He probably went to Tyre next and then down the Euphrates to Babylon. For some reason he became unpopular in Halicarnassus and around 447 BCE migrated to Athens, whose people and democratic institutions he openly admired. In 443 BCE or shortly afterwards he moved to Thurii, in modern Calabria, as part of an Athenian-sponsored colony.

He made his researches known through oral recitations. According to Lucian he read the whole of the Histories at the Olympic Games in one sitting. The work deals chiefly with the lives of prominent kings and with battles such as Marathon, Thermopylae, Artemisium, Salamis, Plataea and Mycale, and digresses into cultural, ethnographic and geographical background. Nothing in it can be dated with certainty to later than 430 BCE.

The place of his death is unknown. He may have returned to Athens and died there in the plague, or died in Macedonia or at Thurii. His is the earliest Greek prose work to survive intact. Cicero called him the Father of History, but his many strange stories and folk-tales led critics to brand him the Father of Lies. Thucydides dismissed him as a story-teller. Herodotus answered that he reported what he could see and what he was told.
hertfordshire: Hertfordshire is a ceremonial county in the East of England. It borders Bedfordshire to the north-west, Cambridgeshire to the north-east, Essex to the east, Greater London to the south and Buckinghamshire to the west, and covers about 1,640 square kilometres. It centres on the headwaters and upper valleys of the rivers Lea and Colne, both of which flow south. The higher ground lies in the north and west, where the chalk of the Chiltern Hills rises to 244 metres near Tring.

Human life is attested in the county from the Mesolithic period. After the Roman conquest of Britain in 43 CE the Catuvellauni accepted peace and adapted to Roman life, and new towns developed, among them Verulamium, beside modern St Albans. There, around 293, the first recorded British martyrdom is traditionally believed to have taken place, when Saint Alban, a Romano-British soldier, took the place of a Christian priest and was beheaded. After the Roman legions left in the early 5th century the area was colonised by Anglo-Saxons, and by the 6th century most of it belonged to the Kingdom of Essex, which later lost its western areas to Mercia.

In 913 Edward the Elder built a fortress at Hertford to check Norse activity, and the area was assigned to it. His father, Alfred the Great, had fixed the River Lea as a boundary with the Norse lord Guthrum, which put the north and east of the county within the Danelaw. The name Hertfordshire is first recorded in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle in 1011. St Albans Abbey was an early drafting place of Magna Carta, and the town saw two battles of the Wars of the Roses. The New River, opened in 1613, brought fresh water to London from Ware. In 1903 Letchworth became the first garden city, and Stevenage was the first town redeveloped under the New Towns Act 1946.

Hertfordshire has ten districts, with Hertford as county town and Watford as its largest settlement, and about 1.2 million people in 2021. Much of its undeveloped land is farmland and part of the Metropolitan green belt. Among its surviving landmarks are the Roman remains of Verulamium, St Albans Cathedral, Berkhamsted Castle and the Jacobean Hatfield House.
hesiod: What is known of Hesiod's life comes from his own poems, where he lets his audience in on a few details. He describes his family's patrimony, a small piece of ground at the foot of Mount Helicon, which led to lawsuits with his brother Perses. Perses at first seems to have cheated him of his share through corrupt authorities, whom Hesiod calls kings, but later became poor and had to rely on the thrifty poet.

Unlike his father, Hesiod disliked sea travel, yet he once crossed the strait to Euboea to take part in the funeral games of Amphidamas of Chalcis, where he won a tripod in a singing contest. He also tells of meeting the Muses on Mount Helicon while pasturing sheep. They gave him a laurel staff, and scholars have inferred from this that he was not a trained rhapsode, who would have received a lyre. He probably wrote his poems down or dictated them.

Two works are generally accepted as his. The Theogony, commonly considered the earlier, treats the origin of the world and of the gods, beginning with Chaos, Gaia, Tartarus and Eros, and is the earliest known source for the myths of Pandora and Prometheus. According to Herodotus, Hesiod's retelling became the accepted version that linked all Hellenes. The Works and Days, of over 800 lines, rests on two truths: labour is the lot of humankind, and he who is willing to work will get by. It sets out the five Ages of Man, from a golden age through silver, bronze and iron, with a heroic age inserted before the last, and it attacks idleness, usury and unjust judges.
The Shield of Heracles, attributed to him in antiquity, is now known to be spurious. His creation myth has long been held to show Eastern influences, such as the Babylonian Enuma Elis.

Two early traditions place Hesiod's grave. In one, the Delphic oracle warned him that he would die at Nemea, so he fled to Locris, where he was killed at the temple of Nemean Zeus and buried. In the other, first mentioned in an epigram by Chersias of Orchomenus, the people of Ascra took his ashes to Orchomenus and placed them in the agora. Ancient authors credited Hesiod and Homer with establishing Greek religious customs. Later writers began to put Homer earlier, and most scholars today agree, though there are good arguments on both sides.
hesse: Hesse is a landlocked state in Germany and the only one that straddles the western and central parts of the country. It borders Lower Saxony, Thuringia, Bavaria, Baden-Württemberg, Rhineland-Palatinate and North Rhine-Westphalia. Its most populous towns lie in the south-west, in the Frankfurt Rhine-Main region, among them Frankfurt am Main, Wiesbaden, Darmstadt, Offenbach and Hanau. The name Hessen derives from the Hessians, who ultimately continue the tribal name of the Chatti; the ancient name appears by the 7th century as Chassi and from the 8th century as Hassi or Hessi.

Central Hesse was inhabited in the Upper Paleolithic, and the Züschen tomb near Fritzlar, a gallery grave of about 3000 BCE belonging to the Late Neolithic Wartberg culture, is one of the most important megalithic monuments in Central Europe. From 962 the land that would become Hesse was part of the Holy Roman Empire. The French Republic occupied the left bank of the Rhine in 1794, and the reorganisation of the Empire in 1803 gave Hesse-Kassel and Hesse-Darmstadt further territories and made the Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel a Prince-Elector, so that his state became the Electorate of Hesse.

In the 19th century, before German unification, the territory comprised the Grand Duchy of Hesse, or Hesse-Darmstadt, the Duchy of Nassau, the free city of Frankfurt, the Electorate of Hesse, the Principality of Waldeck and the Landgraviate of Hesse-Homburg. The modern territory was delineated only in 1945, as Greater Hesse under American occupation, and corresponds loosely to the medieval Landgraviate of Hesse. Hesse has been a parliamentary republic since 1918, except under Nazi rule from 1933 to 1945.

Hesse has a population of over six million, nearly four million of them in the Rhine-Main region. Wiesbaden is the capital and Frankfurt the largest urban area, and Darmstadt and Kassel are other major historic cities. Rhenish Hesse, the part of the former Grand Duchy west of the Rhine, has belonged to Rhineland-Palatinate since 1946. Hesse has several UNESCO World Heritage Sites, among them the Bergpark Wilhelmshöhe in Kassel, Lorsch Abbey, the Messel Fossil Pit and the Saalburg, part of the Roman Limes.
heydar-aliyev: According to his official biography, Heydar Aliyev was born in Nakhchivan on 10 May 1923, though some sources claim he was born two years earlier in a village now in Armenia. He studied architecture at the Azerbaijan Industrial Institute from 1939 to 1941. During the Second World War he commanded a Smersh battalion, which conducted intelligence operations on Soviet forces and executed soldiers who deserted or fought insufficiently hard. He joined the Azerbaijan SSR's state security organs in 1944, served 28 years in them to 1969, and became head of the Azerbaijani KGB in 1960, eventually with the rank of major general.

The Azerbaijan Communist Party elected him first secretary on 12 July 1969, reportedly on the advocacy of Semyon Tsvigun, Leonid Brezhnev's brother-in-law. He dominated Soviet-era Azerbaijan, building a patronage network and promoting people from his native Nakhchivan, as well as Azerbaijani culture and language. He became a candidate member of the Politburo in 1976, and on 22 November 1982 Yuri Andropov made him a full member and first deputy chairman of the Council of Ministers, the highest position an Azerbaijani had reached in the Soviet Union. Mikhail Gorbachev dismissed him in 1987, officially on health grounds, after the two fell out.

He returned to Nakhchivan in 1990 and was elected chairman of its Supreme Soviet in 1991. In 1993 a military coup led by Surat Huseynov ousted President Abulfaz Elchibey; historians say Aliyev did not appear to have a direct role. Aliyev was installed as president and won an election on 3 October 1993 with 98.8 per cent of the vote against two little-known candidates. He was re-elected in 1998. A new constitution, confirmed by referendum on 12 November 1995, divided power among a parliament, a president and the courts. On 20 September 1994 an agreement to develop the Azeri and Chirag oil fields in the Caspian was signed with a consortium of 11 companies from six countries.

His health failed from 1999, when he had a major heart bypass operation at the Cleveland Clinic. Less than two weeks before the election of 2003 he withdrew and named his son Ilham as his party's candidate. He died at the Cleveland Clinic on 12 December 2003 and was buried in the Alley of Honor cemetery in Baku. Critics describe his rule as authoritarian, and a cult of personality has developed around him.
hezbollah: Hezbollah was conceived in 1982 by Lebanese clerics and funded by Iran, primarily to fight the Israeli invasion of Lebanon. The Israeli invasions of 1978 and 1982 had created a humanitarian crisis: many villages in the south were destroyed and large numbers of Shia were displaced. The Shia had also long been underrepresented in Lebanese politics, and both factors bred resentment among them. The movement was set up by local Shia committees under the leadership of Iran's first supreme leader, Ruhollah Khomeini, and its forces were trained and organised by about 1,500 Iranian Revolutionary Guards, who reached a base in the Beqaa Valley with the permission of the Syrian government.

In the 1980s Hezbollah emerged in South Lebanon during a consolidation of Shia militias, as a rival to the older Amal Movement. It opposed US forces in 1982–83 and fought Amal and Syria in the War of the Camps of 1985–88. Its manifesto of 16 February 1985, issued by Sheikh Ibrahim al-Amin, named the struggle against what it called US and Israeli imperialism as its first aim, called for the destruction of Israel, and looked to Iran's revolution. Several attacks of 1983 in Beirut, among them the US Embassy bombing and the barracks bombing, were attributed to it by some Western intelligence agencies; Hezbollah denied responsibility, and some scholars doubt it existed in that form yet.

Through the 1980s and 1990s Hezbollah waged a guerrilla campaign against Israeli forces and the South Lebanon Army, and Israel withdrew from southern Lebanon in 2000. In the 1990s it turned from a revolutionary group into a political one, a process called its Lebanonisation. It fought in the 2006 Lebanon War and later alongside the government of Bashar al-Assad in the Syrian civil war. A new manifesto of 30 November 2009 opposed political sectarianism and favoured a national unity government. From October 2023 it fought a war with Israel, which brought a ceasefire in November 2024.

Hezbollah follows the doctrine of the guardianship of the Islamic jurists developed by Khomeini, and its formal structure concentrates authority in its religious leaders. Its military branch is the Jihad Council, which includes the Islamic Resistance, and its parliamentary bloc is the Loyalty to the Resistance Bloc. It runs an extensive social programme of schools, hospitals and reconstruction projects, and since 1991 it has run the satellite station Al-Manar. Its support is concentrated among the Shia in the south, in Beirut and its surroundings, and in the northern Beqaa Valley and Hermel region. Whether to call it a resistance movement or a terrorist group is contested, and many states list it as the latter.
hidalgo-state: Hidalgo is bordered by San Luis Potosí and Veracruz on the north, Puebla on the east, Tlaxcala and the State of Mexico on the south and Querétaro on the west. It covers roughly 20,813 square kilometres and is divided into 84 municipalities. Its terrain is very rugged, running from a few metres above sea level to more than 3,300 metres. It has three geographical regions: the Atlantic Coastal Plain, the Sierra Madre Oriental and the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt, which holds the highest peaks. The wet Huasteca area lies near the Gulf Coast, and the very northern part of the Valley of Mexico lies within the state.

Prehistoric artifacts have been found at Tepeapulco, Tulancingo, Actopan and Huichapan, dating from about 14,000 to 2,500 BCE, and the oldest evidence of occupation is at Huapalcalco in Tulancingo. Obsidian was worked in the Sierra de las Navajas during the Preclassic period, and the first evidence of social stratification in the region comes from La Loma. The area lay within Mesoamerica, and many peoples passed through it from the north, often settling in the Valley of Mexico. The Toltecs first settled at Xochicoatlán, now Molango, at the beginning of the 7th century, and later had their capital Tollan, today Tula.

Benito Juárez created the State of Hidalgo in 1869 and made Pachuca its capital. The suffix de Soto was added later to honour Manuel Fernando Soto, regarded as the chief driving force behind the state's creation. Its name honours Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla, who began the Mexican War of Independence. Mining has shaped its population: when mining activity fell in the mid-20th century the population fell as well, and recovery began in the 1980s. Cornish miners arrived in the 19th century in the Pachuca and Real del Monte areas, and their descendants keep the Protestant faith in many cases and the Cornish pasty, called pastes, as a signature dish.

The state's population is 2.858 million. The Nahua, Otomi and Tepehua each still speak their own language; the Otomi are the largest group, with over 250,000 speakers in the state. The Mezquital Valley preserves much of the Otomi culinary heritage, including edible insects such as escamoles, and the state dish is barbacoa. Its attractions include the ruins of Tula, thermal springs, old mining haciendas and mountain ranges. Pachuca is nicknamed the Beautiful Windy City because of its strong winds.
hiiumaa: Hiiumaa covers 989 square kilometres and lies 22 km from the Estonian mainland, in the West Estonian archipelago of the Baltic Sea. Its relief is low, reaching 68 m above sea level, and it is formed mostly of limestone, exposed in cliffs along parts of the coast. The Soela Strait separates it from Saaremaa to the south and the Muhu Strait from the mainland. Its names include Dagö in Swedish, Dagden in German and Hiidenmaa in Finnish. The island rose from the sea about 8,500 years ago through isostatic uplift after the ice cap retreated, and the land is still rising.

Mesolithic settlements on the Kõpu Peninsula date from about 5500 BCE and seem to have been tied to seal hunting. Because the land has risen, they now lie far from the coast. Stone-cist graves on the island span the Late Bronze Age to the Late Iron Age.

The island is first recorded as Dageida in 1228, when it and the rest of Estonia were conquered by Germanic crusaders. In 1254 it was divided between the Bishopric of Ösel-Wiek and the Livonian branch of the Teutonic Order, acting partly for the Hanseatic League.

The oldest surviving church, at Pühalepa, was built in 1259, although it was rebuilt in the 18th century, and the Hanseatic League built a lighthouse at Kõpu in the 16th century. As Dagö the island belonged to Swedish Estonia and later passed to the Russian Empire, whose rule left the Swedish population most of its privileges. Most of the numerous Swedish speakers later emigrated or were Estonianised, though a minority remained into the 20th century.

German forces occupied Hiiumaa in the First World War, and in 1918 it became part of independent Estonia. The Soviet Union occupied it in 1940, Germany in 1941 and the Soviet Union again in 1944. Until Estonia regained independence in August 1991 the island was closed to foreigners and to most of mainland Estonia.

Hiiumaa is the main island of Hiiu County, and its largest town is Kärdla. Tourism, livestock, farming and fishing support its economy. The natural environment is protected in the Tahkuna Nature Reserve and the West Estonian Archipelago Biosphere Reserve. A ferry links the island to the mainland, and in winter an ice road can cross the frozen sea.
hilary-of-poitiers: Hilary was born at Poitiers, either at the end of the 3rd century or the beginning of the 4th. His parents were pagans of distinction, and he received a good education that included a high level of Greek. Through study of the Old and New Testament writings he abandoned Neoplatonism for Nicene Christianity, and he, his wife and his daughter, traditionally known as Abra of Poitiers, were baptised. Arianism was becoming popular among Christians in this period, though the bishops at the Council of Nicaea, sponsored by Constantine the Great, had rejected it.

Around 355 Hilary wrote to Emperor Constantius II a remonstrance against the persecutions by which the Arians had sought to crush their opponents. At the synod of Béziers in 356 an imperial rescript banished him, with Rhodanus of Toulouse, to Phrygia. The traditional explanation is that he refused to subscribe to the condemnation of Athanasius and the Nicene faith. More recently several scholars have suggested that political opposition to Constantius and support for the usurper Claudius Silvanus may have led to his exile.

In Phrygia he continued to govern his diocese and attended several synods, including the council at Seleucia in 359, which saw the triumph of the homoion party. In 360 he failed to gain an audience with Constantius, and when the council at Constantinople ratified the decisions of Ariminum and Seleucia he answered with the bitter In Constantium, which attacked the emperor as Antichrist. His repeated requests for public debates with Ursacius and Valens proved so inconvenient that he was sent back to his diocese, which he reached about 361.

At home he spent two or three years persuading local clergy that the homoion confession was a cover for Arian subordinationism, and synods in Gaul condemned the creed of Ariminum. In 364 he accused Auxentius, bishop of Milan, of heterodoxy, and Valentinian I summoned him to Milan, but Auxentius gave satisfactory answers. Hilary described the failure in a work published in 365.

His early Commentarius in Evangelium Matthaei, written before his exile, is the first Latin commentary on Matthew to survive entire. De synodis, written in 358 and early 359, reviews the creeds of the Eastern bishops and argues that the difference from orthodox belief was sometimes in words rather than ideas, which led him to counsel the western bishops to be more reserved in condemnation. De trinitate, in twelve books, composed in 359 and 360, was the first successful expression in Latin of the theology worked out in Greek. Some regard him as the first Latin Christian hymn writer. Pope Pius IX recognised him as a Doctor of the Church in 1851, and his feast day is 13 January.
hildegard-of-bingen: Hildegard was born around 1098 to Mechtild of Merxheim-Nahet and Hildebert of Bermersheim, a family of the free lower nobility in the service of Count Meginhard of Sponheim. Sickly from birth, she is traditionally considered their youngest and tenth child, although there are records of only seven older siblings. She said that she first saw what she called the Shade of the Living Light at the age of three, and understood by five that she was having visions.

Her parents offered her as an oblate to the Benedictine monastery of Disibodenberg. The date of her enclosure is debated: her Vita says she was eight when she was professed with Jutta, daughter of Count Stephan II of Sponheim, but Jutta's enclosure is known to have been in 1112, when Hildegard would have been 14, and some scholars think the two were enclosed together then.

Her three volumes of visionary theology are Scivias, composed 1142 to 1151, the Liber Vitae Meritorum, composed 1158 to 1163, and the Liber Divinorum Operum, begun around 1163 or 1164. In each she first describes a vision and then interprets it in the words of the voice of the Living Light. For Scivias, a contraction of Sci vias Domini, she perceived a command to write what she saw and heard, and the work records 26 visions. She also wrote two volumes on natural medicine, which spring from her work in the monastery's herbal garden and infirmary and from her reading in its library.

Sixty-nine musical compositions, each with its own poem, survive, among the largest repertoires of any medieval composer, together with the Ordo Virtutum, a Latin morality play with 82 songs, which is thought to date as early as 1151 and is not attached to any liturgy. She also invented the Lingua ignota, about 1,000 invented nouns with German and Latin glosses, and an alphabet, the Litterae ignotae; scholars differ on whether the language was meant to bind her nuns together or to serve the abbey more widely.

Hildegard died on 17 September 1179. Her hagiography, the Vita Sanctae Hildegardis, was compiled after her death by the monk Theoderic of Echternach from the Libellus begun by Godfrey of Disibodenberg and the sources Guibert of Gembloux left. Her name appears in the Roman Martyrology from the end of the 16th century, with her feast on 17 September. On 10 May 2012 Pope Benedict XVI extended her veneration to the whole Catholic Church by equivalent canonization, and on 7 October 2012 he named her a Doctor of the Church. Her relics are in the pilgrimage church at Eibingen.
hildesheim: Hildesheim lies on the Innerste river, a tributary of the Leine. According to tradition the city was named after its founder Hildwin. It may have been founded when the bishop moved from Elze to the ford across the Innerste, an important market on the Hellweg trade route. The settlement around the cathedral grew quickly into a town, and King Otto III granted it market rights in 983. The present market place was laid out at the beginning of the 13th century, when the city had about 5,000 inhabitants.

Hildesheim obtained city status in 1249 and was then one of the biggest cities in northern Germany. The clergy ruled it for four centuries, until a town hall was built, work on the present one beginning in 1268. It joined the Hanseatic League in 1367. Most of its inhabitants became Lutherans in 1542, and during the Thirty Years' War it was besieged and occupied several times. The Kingdom of Hanover, to which it belonged, was annexed by Prussia after the Austro-Prussian War of 1866.

On 22 March 1945 British air raids bombed the historic centre, which had kept its medieval character, and almost levelled it. Some 29 per cent of the houses were destroyed and 45 per cent damaged, and around 200 of 800 half-timbered houses survived. Most of the major churches were soon rebuilt in their original style, and reconstruction of the historic centre began in the 1980s.

The Romanesque cathedral, with its ancient bronze doors made around 1015, and St. Michael's Church, an early Romanesque church of Ottonian architecture built from 1010 to 1022, are both on the UNESCO World Heritage list. A rose bush on the wall of the cathedral apse, reputed to be 1,000 years old, still flowers. The market place was reconstructed in 1984–90, and the University of Hildesheim was founded in 1978.
himachal-pradesh: Himachal Pradesh lies in the western Himalayas and is India's northernmost state. It borders Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh to the north, Punjab to the west, Haryana to the south-west and Uttarakhand to the south-east, and it shares an international border with the Tibet Autonomous Region of China to the east. It covers 55,673 square kilometres. The Zanskar range runs in the north-east, the Dhauladhar and Pir Panjal ranges form much of the core, and the Shiwalik range forms the south and west. Reo Purgyil, at 6,816 metres, is the highest peak. The name means snowy slopes, from the Sanskrit hima, snow, and acala, slopes or abode.

Tribes such as the Koli, Hali, Dagi, Dhaugri, Dasa, Khasa, Kanaura and Kirata inhabited the region from prehistoric times, and the foothills were inhabited by people of the Indus Valley Civilisation. For most of its history the region was ruled by local kingdoms, some of which accepted the suzerainty of larger empires. Before independence it comprised the hilly regions of the Punjab Province of British India.

After independence the Chief Commissioner's Province of Himachal Pradesh was organised on 15 April 1948 by the integration of 30 small princely states of the western Himalayas with four southern hill states of the Punjab. The State of Bilaspur was merged into it on 1 July 1954. It later became a union territory, hilly areas of neighbouring Punjab were merged into it in 1966, and it was granted full statehood in 1971.

Shimla is the summer capital and Dharamshala the winter capital. The state is divided into 12 districts. Agriculture, horticulture, hydropower and tourism are the main parts of its economy, and its perennial rivers supply hydroelectric plants. Hill stations such as Shimla, Manali, Dharamshala and Dalhousie attract visitors.
himalayas: The Himalayas run west-northwest to east-southeast in an arc 2,400 km long, between the Indo-Gangetic Plain in the south and the Tibetan Plateau in the north. Nanga Parbat anchors the western end, near the northernmost bend of the Indus, and Namcha Barwa the eastern end, near the great bend of the Yarlung Tsangpo. The range is 350 km wide in the west and 151 km in the east. It consists of four parallel ranges from south to north: the Sivalik Hills, the Lower Himalayan Range, the Great Himalayas, which is the highest and central range, and the Tibetan Himalayas. More than 100 peaks exceed 7,200 metres, and the Mahalangur Himal holds four of the world's six highest mountains, including Everest.

The mountains were uplifted after the Indian tectonic plate collided with the Eurasian plate. India had begun to split away from Gondwana about 70 million years ago and moved north. Its thick, buoyant continental plate could not subduct, and the upper crust piled up in sheets called nappes. The geophysicist Peter Molnar noted that most of the Himalayas are slices of rock that once were the top part of India's crust.

The Himalayas span Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan, and the sovereignty of the range in Kashmir is disputed. The Indus, the Ganges and the Tsangpo–Brahmaputra rise in the range, and their drainage basin is home to some 600 million people, while 53 million live in the Himalayas themselves. The range holds about 15,000 glaciers and is sometimes called the Third Pole. Kathmandu, the capital of Nepal, is the largest city in the Himalayas. The snow leopard is the main predator at high altitudes, and the red panda lives in the bamboo forests of the eastern Himalayas.

The name comes from the Sanskrit Himālaya, abode of snow. The range has profoundly shaped the cultures of South Asia and Tibet. For Hindus the Himalayas are personified as Himavat, king of the mountains and father of the goddess Parvati, and the temples at Pashupatinath and Muktinath are major pilgrimage places. Muktinath is also a pilgrimage place for Tibetan Buddhists, and Paro Taktsang is where Padmasambhava is said to have founded Buddhism in Bhutan. In Jainism, Mount Ashtapada is where the first tirthankara, Rishabhanatha, attained moksha. The summits of several peaks, including Nanda Devi and Gangkhar Puensum, are off limits to climbers.
himnusz: The title in Kölcsey's manuscript, Hymnus, is the Latin word for a hymn, which came into Latin from the Ancient Greek hýmnos, meaning song, hymn or ode. As the poem gained acceptance as the de facto national anthem of Hungary, the Hungarian form himnusz took on the meaning of a national anthem. The lyrics are a prayer that begins with the words "God bless the Hungarians" (Isten, áldd meg a magyart). Its full meaning is evident only to those well acquainted with Hungarian history.

Although Kölcsey finished the poem in 1823, it was first published only in 1829, in Károly Kisfaludy's Aurora, without the subtitle that had been part of the manuscript. It appeared in a collection of his works in 1832 with the subtitle restored. A competition for composers to make the poem suitable for singing by the public was held in 1844 and won by Ferenc Erkel, who conducted at the National Theatre. His setting was first performed there in July 1844, then before a larger audience on 10 August 1844. By the end of the 1850s it was customary to sing it on special occasions. The first stanza is sung at official ceremonies.

In the early 1900s members of the Hungarian parliament proposed making it the official anthem within Austria-Hungary, but the proposals never gained enough support. In the 1950s the communist leader Mátyás Rákosi planned to replace it, but the poet Gyula Illyés and the composer Zoltán Kodály, whom he had in mind for the task, both refused. Erkel's setting was officially recognised as the national anthem only in 1989, when the Constitution of Hungary named it. Vörösmarty's Szózat enjoys a nearly equal standing as a de facto second anthem; tradition has Himnusz sung at the beginning of ceremonies and Szózat at the end.
hindu-kush: The range is about 800 kilometres long and lies west of the Himalayas, running from central and eastern Afghanistan into north-western Pakistan and far south-eastern Tajikistan. It divides the valley of the Amu Darya, the ancient Oxus, in the north from the Indus valley in the south. Its highest point is Tirich Mir, at 7,708 metres in Pakistan. Numerous high passes, known as kotal, make a network for caravans, and the Salang Pass north of Kabul is the most important in Afghanistan.

The name Hindu Kush is first mentioned by Ibn Battuta in the 14th century, who explained it as Hindu-slayer, because slaves taken from India to Turkestan died in the harsh climate. Other scholars take it as a corruption of Hindu Koh, mountains of India. In the time of Alexander the Great it was the Caucasus Indicus. Its significance was recorded from the time of Darius I of the Achaemenid Empire, and Alexander's army crossed it in the spring of 329 BCE.

After Alexander's death in 323 BCE the region passed to the Seleucid Empire, then around 305 BCE to the Maurya Empire, and around the start of the common era to the Kushan Empire. Buddhism flourished there, with monasteries, trade networks and the rock-carved Bamiyan Buddhas. Kabul fell to the army of the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun in 808. The Hindu Shahi dynasty of Kabul later held the range until Sabuktigin conquered its lands west of Peshawar. The people of Kafiristan kept polytheistic traditions until 1896, when Afghans under Amir Abdur Rahman Khan converted them, and the region was renamed Nuristan.

The mountains have long supplied lapis lazuli, mined in the Kowkcheh Valley, and emeralds from the Panjsher valley. Mountain areas are mostly barren or sparsely wooded, with coniferous forests at higher levels. Meltwater from the range feeds the Amu Darya, the Helmand River and the Kabul River, a major tributary of the Indus.
hindustan: Hindustan is the Persian name for India, used at different times for the northern part of the Indian subcontinent and for the whole of it. It comes from the Persian word Hindū, related to the Sanskrit Sindhu, meaning the Indus River. According to Asko Parpola, the Proto-Iranian change of s to h took place between 850 and 600 BCE, so that the Rigvedic sapta sindhava, the land of seven rivers, became hapta hindu in the Avesta. In 515 BCE Darius I annexed the Indus Valley, including Sindh, which Persian called Hindu.

The suffix -stān, meaning a country or region, was added in Middle Persian, probably from the first century CE. The inscription of Shapur I at Naqsh-e-Rustam, from about 262 CE, refers to Sindh as Hindūstān. The Arabic equivalent is al-Hind, which Arab traders used for a much wider region, from the Makran coast to the Indonesian archipelago.

The tenth-century Hudud al-Alam defined Hindustan as roughly the subcontinent, with the Indus as its western limit and Kamarupa, present-day Assam, as its eastern. With the Turko-Persian conquests from the eleventh century the name took a narrower sense. In the early eleventh century a satellite state of the Ghaznavids in the Punjab, with its capital at Lahore, was called Hindustan. Once the Delhi Sultanate (1206-1526) was established, north India, especially the Gangetic plains and the Punjab, came to be called Hindustan, while the wider meaning continued beside it.

The Mughals (1526-1857) called their lands Hindustan, and the word grew as the empire expanded. Their sources also used it for the whole subcontinent, as the Baburnama and the Ain-i-Akbari do. In Mughal sources Hindustani commonly meant the Muslims of Hindustan, and non-Muslim Indians were called Hindus. Prithvi Narayan Shah, who unified Nepal, called his kingdom Asal Hindustan, the real Hindustan, because north India was ruled by the Mughals.

Europeans carried over the double meaning. James Rennel's atlas of 1792, Memoir of a Map of Hindoostan or the Mogul Empire, in fact showed the whole subcontinent. An Anglo-Indian dictionary of 1886 states that in native usage the word had come to mean the region north of the Narmada River, excluding Bihar and Bengal. In the independence movement Indians called their land India, Hindustan and Bharat, and Muhammad Iqbal's song Tarānah-e-Hindī was a popular patriotic anthem. After the Lahore Resolution of 1940 the Dominion of India came to be called Hindustan in popular speech.
hippocrates: Historians agree that Hippocrates was born around 460 BCE on the island of Kos; other biographical information is likely to be untrue. Soranus of Ephesus, a 2nd-century Greek physician, was his first biographer and is the source of most personal information. Hippocrates is mentioned in passing by two contemporaries, in Plato's dialogues Protagoras and Phaedrus and in Aristotle's Politics.

According to Soranus his father Heraclides was a physician and his mother was Praxitela. He learned medicine from his father and grandfather, and studied other subjects with Democritus and Gorgias. He was probably trained at the asklepieion of Kos, and took lessons from the Thracian physician Herodicus of Selymbria. He taught and practised medicine throughout his life, travelling at least as far as Thessaly, Thrace and the Sea of Marmara.

Hippocrates is credited as the first person to hold that diseases had natural causes rather than being sent by gods. In On the Sacred Disease, on epilepsy, the writer argues that the disease is no more divine than others and that people regard it as divine from ignorance and wonder. Hippocratic medicine held that disease came from environmental factors, diet and living habits, though it also held convictions based on incorrect anatomy and physiology, such as humorism. Its therapy was gentle and passive, resting on the healing power of nature, and it gave weight to prognosis and to careful case histories.

The Hippocratic Corpus is a collection of around seventy early medical works, written in Ionic Greek and gathered in Alexandrian Greece. Whether Hippocrates himself wrote any of them has not been conclusively answered, and given the variety of subjects and styles the corpus could not have been written by one person. It includes the Hippocratic Oath, Aphorisms and On Airs, Waters and Places, and its works sometimes contradict one another. Very little is known concretely about what Hippocrates himself thought, wrote and did.

Several accounts of his death exist. He died probably in Larissa, at the age of 83, 85 or 90, though some say he lived well over 100. Although he neither founded the school of medicine named after him nor wrote most of the treatises attributed to him, he is traditionally regarded as the Father of Medicine. His teachings were so revered that for a long time they were taken as too great to be improved upon. The Islamic world adopted its methods in the Middle Ages, and after the Renaissance they were revived in western Europe. Clubbing of the fingers is still called Hippocratic fingers, and the Hippocratic Oath is the foundation of later oaths taken by medical graduates.
hiri-motu: Hiri Motu is also called Police Motu, Pidgin Motu or simply Hiri. It is a simplified version of Motu, a language of the Austronesian family, and is spoken around Port Moresby, the capital of Papua New Guinea. It is strictly neither a pidgin nor a creole, though it has features of both. Differences in sound and grammar make it not mutually intelligible with Motu, although the two languages are very similar in vocabulary and share a simplified Austronesian structure.

The word hiri names the traditional trade voyages that shaped the way of life of the Motu people, who live along the southern coast of their country. The voyages carried prized goods to the peoples of the Gulf of Papua. The language developed among those taking part in the hiri trade, chiefly in sago and clay pots, between the Motu and their neighbours on the south-east coast of New Guinea, and it is older than European contact.

In early colonial times the use of Hiri Motu spread because the Royal Papuan Constabulary adopted it, which is why it was called Police Motu. By the early 1960s it was the lingua franca of a large part of the country, and it was the first language of many children of policemen and other public servants whose parents came from different language groups.

The name Hiri Motu was proposed in the early 1970s at a conference held by the Department of Information and Extension Services. The committee argued that the New Guinea Police Force had taken up Pidgin when the forces were united in 1946, and that the name should reflect the language's legacy and everyday use rather than the police. Since the early 1970s or earlier its use has declined in favour of English and Tok Pisin. Today its speakers tend to be elderly and concentrated in Central and Gulf provinces, and younger speakers of Motu proper often understand it poorly. It has some statutory recognition.

Hiri Motu has two dialects, called Austronesian (or central) and Papuan (non-central), named for the first languages of the people who used it as a lingua franca. The Papuan dialect was more widely spoken and has been the standard of official publications since about 1964, while the Austronesian dialect, closer to Motu in grammar and sound, was the prestige form. It uses postpositions, such as ai for in, on or at. Sentences end with a verb, and either subject–object–verb or object–subject–verb order is used; a subject marker, ese, is used when meaning would otherwise be unclear. Its pronouns distinguish an inclusive we from an exclusive we.
hirohito: Hirohito was born on 29 April 1901 at Tōgū Palace in Aoyama, Tokyo, the first son of Crown Prince Yoshihito, the future Emperor Taishō, during the reign of his grandfather Emperor Meiji. Ten weeks after his birth he was placed in the care of Count Kawamura Sumiyoshi, and he returned to court at the age of three when Kawamura died. He was proclaimed crown prince on 2 November 1916.

From March to September 1921 he visited the United Kingdom, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, Vatican City and Malta, the first European visit by a Japanese crown prince, achieved despite strong opposition in Japan. On his return he became regent on 25 November 1921 in place of his ailing father. He married Princess Nagako Kuni on 26 January 1924.

Hirohito became emperor on 25 December 1926, and the Shōwa era began. The early reign unfolded against financial crisis and growing military power in government. The killing of Prime Minister Inukai Tsuyoshi in 1932 marked the end of civilian control of the military. In 1931 Japan staged the Mukden incident as a pretext to invade Manchuria, and Hirohito did not voice objection. On 27 September 1940 Japan joined Germany and Italy in the Tripartite Pact.

Hirohito formally sanctioned the decision to go to war against the United States and its allies on 1 December 1941. After the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the Soviet invasion of Manchuria and Korea, he called on the armed forces to surrender in a radio broadcast on 15 August 1945. Historians agree that he was involved to some extent in strategy and war crimes, but the degree remains disputed.

He was not tried by the International Military Tribunal for the Far East. General Douglas MacArthur believed a cooperative emperor would help a peaceful occupation, and evidence that could have incriminated him was excluded. In 1946 he renounced his divinity, and the constitution of 1947 defined him as the symbol of the State and of the unity of the People.

Hirohito died on 7 January 1989 at the age of 87 and was succeeded by his son Akihito, beginning the Heisei era. His reign of more than sixty years was the longest of any historically attested emperor of Japan.
hiroshima: The site was originally a small fishing village on the shores of Hiroshima Bay, which from the 12th century prospered through its ties to a Zen Buddhist temple, Mitaki-dera, and through growing trade with the rest of Japan under the Taira clan. The warlord Mōri Terumoto founded Hiroshima in 1589 on the delta coast of the Seto Inland Sea, and the name means wide island. His castle was quickly built, and he moved in in 1593. After Terumoto sided with the losers at the Battle of Sekigahara, Tokugawa Ieyasu took most of his fiefs, including Hiroshima, and gave Aki Province to the daimyō Masanori Fukushima. From 1619 until 1871 the Asano clan ruled the city.

After the han was abolished in 1871 the city became the capital of Hiroshima Prefecture and, with the building of Ujina Harbor in the 1880s, an important port. The San'yō Railway reached it in 1894. During the First Sino-Japanese War the government moved there temporarily, and Emperor Meiji kept his headquarters at Hiroshima Castle from 15 September 1894 to 27 April 1895.
