In the Second World War the Second General Army and the Chūgoku Regional Army were headquartered there, and the port was a key centre for shipping and supply depots.

At 8:15 a.m. on Monday, 6 August 1945, the American B-29 Enola Gay, flown by Paul Tibbets, dropped the bomb Little Boy on the city. It directly killed at least 70,000 people, among them thousands of Korean forced labourers, and fewer than 10 per cent of the casualties were military. The population before the bombing was about 345,000. About 70 per cent of the buildings were destroyed and another 7 per cent badly damaged.

Hiroshima is the capital of Hiroshima Prefecture and the largest city of the Chūgoku region of western Honshu. In 1949 the national parliament proclaimed it a City of Peace and passed the Hiroshima Peace Memorial City Construction Law to help rebuild it. The Peace Memorial Park was designed that year, and the Peace Memorial Museum opened in 1955. The Genbaku Dome, formerly the Prefectural Industrial Promotion Hall and the building closest to the explosion that survived, is part of the Hiroshima Peace Memorial, a World Heritage Site since 1996. The castle was rebuilt in 1958. The population, which had dropped to 137,197 after the bombing, had returned to its prewar level by 1955.
hiroshima-prefecture: The prefecture covers 8,479 square kilometres and borders Okayama Prefecture to the east, Tottori to the north-east, Shimane to the north and Yamaguchi to the south-west. It also touches Ehime Prefecture for 74 metres on the island of Hyōtanjima. Most of it is mountainous, with the Chūgoku Mountains in the north leading towards Shimane, and rivers have made rich plains near the coast. It faces Shikoku across the Seto Inland Sea, where Hiroshima Bay opens, and it includes many small islands. The sheltered Inland Sea makes the climate very mild.

The area was formerly divided into Bingo Province and Aki Province. It has been a centre of trade and culture since the beginning of Japan's recorded history. Hiroshima is a traditional centre of the Chūgoku region and was the seat of the Mōri clan until the Battle of Sekigahara. The prefecture is known worldwide for the atomic bombing of 1945, after which the city was rebuilt as a major regional centre of industry, education and culture. The Atomic Dome, one of the few remnants of prewar Hiroshima, stands as a reminder of that event.

Hiroshima is the capital and the largest city of the Chūgoku region, and other major cities are Fukuyama, Kure and Higashihiroshima. The population is 2,811,410 in 2019. With Nara and Tokyo it is one of three prefectures with more than one UNESCO World Heritage Site: the Atomic Dome and the Itsukushima Shrine on Miyajima, famed for appearing to float when the tide fills round it. Mazda has its headquarters in the prefecture, and automobile manufacturing and tourism are among its main industries. Fukuyama and Hiroshima are international container ports, and ferries link Hiroshima Port with Miyajima, Matsuyama and Beppu.
hispaniola: Hispaniola lies in the Greater Antilles between Cuba and Puerto Rico, about 80 kilometres east of Cuba across the Windward Passage and 130 kilometres west of Puerto Rico across the Mona Passage. It covers 76,192 square kilometres, of which 27,750 belong to Haiti and the rest to the Dominican Republic. The northeast trade winds drop their rain on the northern slopes and leave a dry southern coast. The Hispaniolan hutia and the Hispaniolan solenodon are its two endemic land mammals.

People of the Archaic Age reached the island from Central or South America about 6,000 years ago. The Taíno, descended from Arawakan speakers who migrated into the Caribbean in the 1st millennium BCE, were the dominant group at European contact. Each society was a small kingdom under a cacique, and in 1492 five kingdoms ruled the island. Early chroniclers recorded its native names as Bohío, Haiti and Quisqueya, though doubts have been raised about Quisqueya.

Christopher Columbus landed in December 1492 and named it Española, or little Spain. His flagship Santa Maria ran aground on 24 December, and he left 21 men in the fort of La Navidad. Hispaniola became the site of the first European fort, the first settlement, La Isabela, and the first permanent settlement, Santo Domingo, founded in 1498. Gold mining with forced Indigenous labour began early. In 1606 Philip III ordered the island's inhabitants to move close to Santo Domingo to fight piracy, but French, English and Dutch pirates then set up bases on the north and west coasts.

The French occupied the west and built a plantation colony on the enslavement of Africans that became the most prosperous of the French empire in the Americas. A slave revolt broke out in Saint-Domingue in 1791, and by the Treaty of Basel in 1795 Spain ceded the eastern two thirds to France. After the Haitian Revolution, Jean-Jacques Dessalines proclaimed the Empire of Haiti, and in 1809 Spain regained the east. The United States occupied Haiti from 1915 to 1934 and the Dominican Republic from 1916 to 1924.

The island is divided between the Spanish-speaking Dominican Republic in the east, with Santo Domingo as its capital, and Haiti in the west, where Haitian Creole is spoken by nearly the whole population. The name Hispaniola became widely used after 1918, when American leaders recommended it to the National Geographic Society.
hitler-youth: In 1922 the Munich-based Nazi Party established its official youth wing, the Jugendbund der NSDAP, announced on 8 March and holding its inaugural meeting on 13 May. After the failed Beer Hall Putsch of November 1923 the party's youth wings were ostensibly disbanded, though many continued underground. In April 1924 the Jugendbund was renamed the Grossdeutsche Jugendbewegung. After a short power struggle with a rival organisation, Gerhard Roßbach's Schilljugend, Kurt Gruber prevailed, and in July 1926 the movement was renamed Hitler-Jugend, Bund deutscher Arbeiterjugend. By 1930 it had enlisted over 25,000 boys aged 14 and upward, with a junior branch, the Deutsches Jungvolk, for boys aged 10 to 14, and a parallel League of German Girls.

Membership rose from about 1,200 in 1923 to 107,956 by the end of 1932. Chancellor Heinrich Brüning banned the movement in April 1932, and his successor Franz von Papen lifted the ban in June. After the Nazis came to power in 1933, with Baldur von Schirach as Reichsjugendführer, membership reached 2,300,000 by the end of that year, partly through the forcible takeover of other youth organisations. A law of December 1936 declared it the only legally permitted youth organisation in Germany. In March 1939 the Youth Service Duty conscripted all German youths into it, even over their parents' objections, and by 1940 it had eight million members. Non-members could be refused a diploma.

Its activities included camping, hiking and sport, but over time many resembled military training, and its members were indoctrinated with Nazi racism. In the war, under Artur Axmann, who succeeded Schirach in August 1940, it became an auxiliary force. In 1944 the 12th SS-Panzer-Division Hitlerjugend fought in the Battle of Normandy. By 1945 boys as young as twelve were being drafted into the Volkssturm, and in the Battle of Berlin Hitler Youth formations were part of the last line of defence.

The Hitler Youth was outlawed by the Allied Control Council on 10 October 1945. Schirach was sentenced to 20 years in prison, for crimes against humanity as Gauleiter of Vienna rather than for his youth leadership. Axmann received a 39-month sentence in May 1949. Because membership had been compulsory, many senior leaders of both West and East Germany had belonged to it. In the Federal Republic of Germany, its symbols may not be used publicly except for educational or research purposes.
hiv-aids: HIV is a retrovirus of the genus Lentivirus, in the family Retroviridae. It infects components of the human immune system, chiefly CD4+ T cells, macrophages and dendritic cells, and destroys CD4+ T cells directly and indirectly. Infection passes through three main stages: an acute stage, often an influenza-like illness two to four weeks after exposure; a long period of clinical latency; and AIDS, when the risk of tuberculosis, other opportunistic infections and rare tumours rises. Without treatment, average survival after infection is estimated at nine to eleven years.

The virus is spread by sexual contact, by significant exposure to infected body fluids or tissues, such as contaminated needles or blood transfusions, and from mother to child during pregnancy, delivery or breastfeeding. Saliva, sweat, tears and urine carry no risk unless they are contaminated with blood. Most infected people develop antibodies within three to twelve weeks of infection.

HIV made the jump from other primates to humans in west-central Africa in the early to mid-20th century. The first news story on the disease appeared on 18 May 1981 in the gay newspaper New York Native, and on 5 June 1981 AIDS was first clinically reported, with five cases in the United States. The patients were injecting drug users and gay men who showed symptoms of Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia, a rare infection of people with badly impaired immunity. Many cases of the skin cancer Kaposi's sarcoma followed, and the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention formed a task force to monitor the outbreak. The cause, HIV infection, was identified in the early part of the decade.

The disease had a large impact on society, both as an illness and as a source of discrimination. Stigma took the forms of ostracism, rejection, compulsory testing without consent, violence and quarantine, and the fear of it kept many people from seeking testing or treatment. The disease was also drawn into controversies involving religion, among them the Catholic Church's position not to support condom use as prevention.

Antiretroviral therapy changed the prognosis. It reduces the death rate by 80% and raises the life expectancy of a newly diagnosed young adult to between 20 and 50 years. A person with an undetectable viral load as a result of long-term treatment has effectively no risk of transmitting HIV sexually, a finding publicised in the Swiss Statement of 2008 and since accepted as medically sound. Annual deaths from the disease peaked at 2 million in 2005.
ho-chi-minh: Ho Chi Minh was born Nguyễn Sinh Cung in 1890 in Kim Liên, in Nghệ An province in northern Central Vietnam. Details of his early life are uncertain: at least four official biographies differ on names, dates and places, and he is known to have used between 50 and 200 pseudonyms. His father, Nguyễn Sinh Sắc, was a scholar and teacher, and the boy studied with him and then with the scholar Vương Thúc Quý, mastering Chinese characters, the basis of Confucian study. At ten he received the name Nguyễn Tất Thành. On 5 June 1911 he left Saigon as a kitchen helper on a French steamer, reaching Marseille on 5 July, and worked on ships until 1917.

In Paris from 1919 he joined the Groupe des Patriotes Annamites, whose members published articles for Vietnamese independence under the name Nguyễn Ái Quốc. Their petition to the powers at the Versailles peace talks was ignored. In 1923 he went to Moscow, where he worked for the Comintern, and in 1924 or 1925 he was sent to Canton to assist the Comintern envoy Mikhail Borodin. There he organised the Vietnamese Revolutionary Youth League and trained young Vietnamese revolutionaries.

He returned to Vietnam in 1941 to lead the Việt Minh. Jailed by Chiang Kai-shek's local authorities in China, he was released in 1943 and from then regularly used the name Hồ Chí Minh. He read the Declaration of Independence on 2 September 1945. An agreement with France of 6 March 1946 soon broke down, and the First Indochina War followed. His government carried out a land reform campaign between 1953 and 1956 that included the execution of landowners. After the 1954 Geneva Conference he remained president of North Vietnam and, from 1959, urged aid to the Việt Cộng in the south, supplied along the trail that bears his name.

Ho Chi Minh died of heart failure at his home in Hanoi on 2 September 1969, aged 79. The government delayed announcing it until the next day because 2 September was Independence Day. About 250,000 people attended the funeral. His will asked for cremation and the scattering of his ashes across a united Vietnam, but his embalmed body lies in a mausoleum in Ba Đình Square. Saigon was later renamed Ho Chi Minh City in his honour.

He was also a poet and journalist who wrote in Chinese, Vietnamese and French. His Poems from the Prison Diary, written while imprisoned in China, has been recognised as a Vietnamese national treasure since 2012. In 1987 UNESCO recommended that its member states commemorate the centenary of his birth.
ho-chi-minh-city: Ho Chi Minh City lies in south-east Vietnam on the Mekong Delta, and its geography is defined by rivers and canals, the largest being the Saigon River. The centre stands about 5 metres above sea level, and the city is fringed by tidal flats that have been altered for agriculture. It has a coast 89 kilometres long on the South China Sea. In the rainy season, tides, rain, river flow and land subsidence together flood parts of the city.

The first known settlement was a Cham one called Baigaur. The Khmer renamed it Prey Nokôr, a fishing village, and Vietnamese settlers in the early 17th century took over the Khmer name as Sài Gòn. It was officially renamed Gia Định in 1698. The name Ho Chi Minh City was given in 1976, after reunification, to honour Ho Chi Minh. Sài Gòn remains in everyday speech and refers to the city centre.

An early Funan temple, said to be the site of the later Phụng Sơn Buddhist temple, was founded in the 4th century CE, and a Champa settlement dates to the 11th century. The Khmer Empire took Baigaur around 1145. In 1620 Princess Nguyễn Phúc Ngọc Vạn, daughter of Lord Nguyễn Phúc Nguyên, married King Chey Chettha II of Cambodia, which eased relations and let people of the two countries move freely. Chey Chettha II in exchange gave Prei Nokor to the Nguyễn lords.

After the fall of the Citadel of Saigon in the Cochinchina campaign in 1859, the city was the capital of French Cochinchina from 1862 to 1949. It was capital of French Indochina from 1887 to 1902 and again from 1945 to 1954, and of the State of Vietnam from 1949 to 1955. After the 1954 partition it was the capital of South Vietnam until its capture by North Vietnam, which led to a unified state in 1976.

Ho Chi Minh City is the most populous city of Vietnam, with more than 14 million people after the merger of Bình Dương and Bà Rịa-Vũng Tàu into it in 2025. French colonial buildings such as the City Hall, the Saigon Central Post Office and the Notre-Dame Cathedral Basilica stand in the centre. The Thien Hau Temple, first built around 1760, is in the Chinese quarter of Chợ Lớn, and the Independence Palace dates from the era of the Republic of Vietnam.
hobart: Hobart lies in the south-east of Tasmania, on the estuary of the River Derwent, and is the southernmost capital city in Australia. Its skyline is dominated by kunanyi / Mount Wellington, which rises to 1,271 metres, and its harbour is the second-deepest natural port in the world, with much of the waterfront built on reclaimed land. The city is built chiefly on Jurassic dolerite around the foothills. It has a cool to mild oceanic climate.

The land was known to the Muwinina people as nipaluna, a name that includes features such as kunanyi / Mount Wellington and the River Derwent. Before British colonisation it had been occupied, possibly for as long as 35,000 years, by Aboriginal Tasmanians, who generally call themselves Palawa or Pakana.

The first European settlement began in 1803 as a military camp at Risdon Cove on the eastern shore of the Derwent, amid British concern over French explorers. The camp was the site of the 1804 Risdon Cove massacre. Later in 1804 Captain David Collins moved the camp, together with soldiers, settlers and convicts from the abandoned Port Phillip settlement, to a better site at Sullivans Cove, the present site of Hobart. He named it Hobart Town, or Hobarton, after Lord Hobart, then British Secretary of State for war and the colonies. The city took the singular name Hobart in 1881.

Whaling soon became a major local industry, and for a time Hobart was the main whaling port of the Southern Ocean. Penal transportation ended in the 1850s, and the city then went through periods of growth and decline. A railway opened in 1876 and Australia's first fully electric tram network in 1893, which allowed the urban area to spread. The early 20th century brought a boom based on mining, agriculture and other primary industries. The first general work of Australian literature to be published appeared in Hobart, and in 1824 Andrew Bent, proprietor of the Hobart Town Gazette, established the first free press in Australia.

Hobart is the capital and most populous city of Tasmania and the seat of the Parliament of Tasmania. Greater Hobart had 247,068 people at the 2021 census, nearly half of the state's population. The city is the home port for Australian and French Antarctic operations.

Hobart is known for its well-preserved Georgian and Victorian buildings. The Theatre Royal, established in 1837 and designed by the colonial architect John Lee Archer, is Australia's oldest continually operating theatre. The Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery was founded by the Royal Society of Tasmania. Salamanca Market and the Museum of Old and New Art, which opened in 2011, are well-known attractions.
hodeidah: Hodeidah lies on a flat plain that slopes gently towards the Red Sea, part of the Tihama coastal plain, which stretches about 300 kilometres from al-Luhayyah in the north to al-Khawkhah in the south and is 60 to 150 kilometres wide. Valleys such as Wadi Mour, Wadi Siham and Wadi Zabid carry flood and rainwater from the highlands to the sea. More than 40 Yemeni islands lie off the coast, among them Kamaran and the Hanish Islands. The climate is hot desert.

Islamic chronicles first mention Hodeidah in 1454/55, and the city grew in importance in the 1520s, when the Ottomans took over the Tihama. In the 1830s Ibrahim Pasha's troops controlled it and handed its administration to Sherif Husayn ibn Ali Haydar, and in 1849 it became part of the Yemen Eyalet. The Malay writer Abdullah bin Abdul Kadir, who visited on his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1854, noted that chewing khat was common. In the 19th century the city had a large slave market, supplied from the Oromia region of modern Ethiopia.

In 1914 German troops under Major Othmar von Stotzingen set up a wireless station at Hodeidah, which relayed messages from Constantinople to German East Africa and broadcast propaganda to Sudan, Somaliland and Abyssinia. Britain occupied the city in January 1919 after the collapse of Ottoman Yemen and left on 29 January 1921, letting the Emirate of Asir take it. The Kingdom of Yemen captured it in April 1925. Saudi forces occupied it briefly during the Saudi-Yemeni war of 1934. A fire in January 1961 destroyed much of the city, which was rebuilt with Soviet aid, and a highway to Sanaa was completed that year.

Hodeidah is the principal port of Yemen on the Red Sea and the capital of Hodeidah Governorate. The Ottomans developed it as a seaport in the mid-19th century. Its harbour was poor: in 1920 the British noted that large ships had to anchor more than two miles out, and a new harbour 10 miles to the north-west was linked to the town by a small railway. The city exported coffee, hides, cotton and dates, and was a centre of dhow building, tanning and sandal making. Hand-woven striped cotton cloth was made by artisans moved there from Zabid and Beit el-Faki. The port of Ras Isa lies just to the north.
hoelun: Most of what is known of Hö'elün comes from the Secret History of the Mongols, a mid-13th-century epic that is very favourable to her; its anonymous author probably had links to her. According to it she was born into the Olkhonud clan of the Onggirat tribe and was married at around fifteen, in about 1160 or 1161, to Chiledu, brother of the Merkit chief. On the journey to his lands the couple were ambushed by Mongols out hawking, led by Yesügei of the Borjigin clan. The kidnapping, omitted from most official chronicles, left a grudge among the Merkit that later became a blood feud.

Yesügei already had a wife, usually named Sochigel by historians, and a son, Behter, but Hö'elün became his primary wife. She bore him four sons, Temüjin, Qasar, Hachiun and Temüge, and a daughter, Temülen. The year of Temüjin's birth is disputed, with 1155, 1162 and 1167 each favoured by different historians.

Yesügei was poisoned by Tatars when Temüjin was about eight. The Tayichiud faction excluded Hö'elün from the ancestor ceremonies and abandoned her camp. The Secret History says the whole Borjigin clan followed, though other sources, such as the Persian historian Rashid al-Din, imply that Yesügei's brothers stood by her. When Temüjin and Qasar ambushed and killed Behter, the Secret History has her angrily reprimand them.

After Temüjin married Börte, the two women managed the economy of his camp, and he turned to them first for counsel when he split from Jamuqa. After his defeat at Dalan Balzhut in 1187, Hö'elün married Münglig, an old retainer of Yesügei, in her third and final marriage. In the following years she probably arranged marriages for her youngest children and maintained alliances while Temüjin was away. The Secret History says she raised numerous foundlings, but problems of chronology indicate that the best known, Shigi Qutuqu, was in fact raised by Börte.

At the assembly of 1206 Hö'elün was reportedly granted 10,000 followers jointly with Temüge, and felt that this undervalued her work; Münglig, by contrast, received the seat at the khan's right hand. When Münglig's son, the shaman Kokechu, divided Genghis Khan from his brothers, she defended Qasar and Temüge vigorously, and with Börte persuaded Genghis that Kokechu must be eliminated. The Secret History claims that she died soon after, worn out by her efforts, an account that some historians, such as Igor de Rachewiltz, have called poetical melodrama. By the time of the Yuan dynasty she had received the posthumous name Empress Xuanyi.
hohhot: Hohhot is the capital and largest city of Inner Mongolia, in the south-central part of the region. It is encircled by the Daqing Shan, the Great Blue Mountains, to the north and the Hetao Plateau to the south. The Mongolian name means Blue City, and in Chinese it can be rendered Qīng Chéng. The climate is cold and semi-arid, with long, dry winters and hot, somewhat humid summers.

In antiquity the area belonged to Yunzhong Commandery, created in the reign of King Wuling of Zhao. Under Qin and Han it was the frontier with the Xiongnu, and from the reign of Emperor Wu it became a base for operations against them. In 127 BCE General Wei Qing led a cavalry force of 40,000 from Yunzhong and conquered the Hetao and Ordos regions. In 386 the Tuoba chieftain Tuoba Gui refounded the Dai state and later renamed it Wei.

In 1557 the Tümed Mongol leader Altan Khan began building the Da Zhao Temple to persuade the Ming government of his leadership of the southern Mongol tribes. The town that grew around it was called Kokegota, the Blue Town. In 1570 Altan Khan negotiated an end to the Ming blockade of Mongol access to iron, cotton and seeds by establishing a vassal-tributary relationship, and in 1575 the Ming renamed the town Guihua. In 1631 Ligdan Khan razed the city. Under the Qing, the garrison town of Suiyuan was built 2 kilometres to the north-east, and in 1913 the Republic of China united the two towns as Guisui.

In the 1930s the Japanese, who created the puppet state of Mengjiang, renamed it Hohhot, and after 1945 it became Guisui again. After 1949 it was renamed Hohhot, and in 1952 the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region chose it as its administrative centre, replacing Zhangjiakou.

Hohhot had 3,446,100 inhabitants at the 2020 census, most of them Han Chinese; many of the Mongols in the city speak Chinese. By regulation, street signs and public transport announcements are in both Chinese and Mongolian. It is known for its historical sites and temples, among them the Da Zhao, and is home to Inner Mongolia University.
hokkaido: Hokkaido is separated from Honshu by the Tsugaru Strait, and the two islands are connected by railway through the Seikan Tunnel. It has coastlines on the Sea of Japan, the Sea of Okhotsk and the Pacific Ocean, and lies about 43 kilometres south of Sakhalin. The centre of the island is mountainous, with volcanic plateaux, and its plains include the Ishikari, Tokachi and Kushiro plains. It has a colder climate than the rest of Japan and heavy winter snowfall, yet it is an agricultural region for many crops.

During the Jōmon period a hunter-gatherer culture flourished in Hokkaido, beginning over 15,000 years ago, and Jōmon beliefs in natural spirits are theorized to have given rise to Ainu spirituality. About 2,000 years ago Yayoi people colonized the island, and much of its population shifted from hunting and gathering to agriculture. In the Muromachi period (1336 to 1573) the Japanese established a settlement at the south of the Oshima Peninsula. Disputes with the Ainu developed into a war, and in 1457 Takeda Nobuhiro killed the Ainu leader Koshamain and defeated the opposition.

His descendants ruled the Matsumae domain, which held exclusive trading rights with the Ainu in the Azuchi-Momoyama and Edo periods and relied on that trade for its economy. The Matsumae held authority over the south of the island, then called Ezochi, until the end of the Edo period.

Shortly after the Boshin War in 1868, Tokugawa loyalists led by Enomoto Takeaki occupied the island temporarily. Their rebellion, commonly but mistakenly called the Republic of Ezo, was defeated in May 1869. Ezochi was then annexed into Japanese territory through colonial practices, and the Meiji government, setting up the Development Commission, renamed it Hokkaido, written 北海道 and translated as "northern sea route". Japanese settlers dispossessed the Ainu of their land and forced them to assimilate. In July 1945 ports, cities and military facilities in Hokkaido were attacked by the United States Navy's Task Force 38, and the Soviet Union prepared an invasion before the Japanese surrender.

Hokkaido is the second-largest of Japan's four main islands, and with its surrounding islands it forms the largest and northernmost prefecture. Its capital and largest city is Sapporo. It became equal with the other prefectures in 1947, when the revised Local Autonomy Act came into effect. The Hokkaido Development Agency was founded in 1949 and absorbed into the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport in 2001. The island has more brown bears than anywhere else in Asia except Russia.
holocaust: Jews have lived in Europe for more than two thousand years. Throughout the Middle Ages they were subjected to antisemitism based on Christian theology, which blamed them for killing Jesus. In the 19th century many European countries granted Jews full citizenship, and political antisemitism, positing an international Jewish conspiracy, emerged with the rise of nationalism and industrialization. After the First World War the German military promoted the untrue idea that Germany had been stabbed in the back by socialists and Jews.

Adolf Hitler was appointed chancellor in January 1933. Within months all other parties were banned and tens of thousands of political opponents arrested. The regime passed anti-Jewish laws, encouraged violence and orchestrated the nationwide pogrom known as Kristallnacht in November 1938, meaning to force all German Jews to emigrate.

After Germany invaded Poland in September 1939, the occupation authorities began to establish ghettos to segregate Jews. Following the invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941, German forces and local collaborators murdered 1.5 to 2 million Jews. Most historians agree that Hitler issued an explicit order to kill all Jews in Europe, but disagree about when. Reinhard Heydrich convened the Wannsee Conference on 20 January 1942, and the Final Solution was implemented to murder all Jews in Europe.

Victims were deported to extermination camps, chiefly Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, Belzec, Sobibor, Chełmno and Majdanek in occupied Poland, where those who survived the journey were gassed. Others were sent to forced labour camps, where many died of starvation, abuse and exhaustion. The murder rate was highest during Operation Reinhard, from March 1942 to November 1943. In 1944 about 437,000 Hungarian Jews were deported in eight weeks, mostly to Auschwitz. The killings continued until 1945.

Around six million Jews were killed, about two-thirds of Europe's Jewish population. Half of the victims came from Poland. Many survivors emigrated from Europe after the war, and the Kielce pogrom convinced many that they could not stay in eastern Europe. Relatively few perpetrators faced criminal trials, and billions of dollars in reparations have been paid, though they fall short of the losses suffered. The Holocaust is considered the largest genocide in human history and has become central to Western historical consciousness.
holodomor: The Holodomor was part of the wider Soviet famine of 1930 to 1933, which affected the major grain-producing areas of the Soviet Union. Ukraine was one of the largest grain-producing states in the USSR and was subject to unreasonably high grain quotas compared with the rest of the country in 1930. Several repressive policies came before and during the famine, among them the persecution of the Orthodox Church, the Law of Spikelets, the blacklisting of villages, the internal passport system and harsh grain requisitions. Between 1926 and 1939 the Ukrainian population grew by only 6.6 per cent, while Russia's grew by 16.9 per cent.

The famine struck the Ukrainian SSR in spring 1932 and again from February to July 1933, with most victims recorded in spring 1933. The authorities continued the grain requisitions and left the population without means of subsistence. The oblasts of Kyiv and Kharkiv had the highest losses although they produced far less grain than other areas, and their quotas had been doubled in 1931 against a national average increase of 9 per cent. Cannibalism was documented, and at least 2,505 people were sentenced for it in 1932 and 1933, though the real number was certainly much higher.

The exact number of victims is unknown. A joint statement to the United Nations signed by 25 countries in November 2003 declared that 7 to 10 million people died, and more recent scholarship has estimated between 3.5 and 5 million. Soviet authorities tried to hide the scale of the disaster, but it became known abroad through journalists such as Gareth Jones and Malcolm Muggeridge.

The Soviet Union long denied that the famine had occurred, and public discussion of it was banned until the glasnost reforms of Mikhail Gorbachev in the 1980s. Scholars agree that it was primarily man-made, but they dispute whether it was intentional, whether it targeted Ukrainians and whether it was a genocide, because no document explicitly orders the starvation of any area. Some historians conclude that Stalin deliberately engineered it to eliminate a Ukrainian independence movement, while others hold that it was chiefly a result of collectivisation and industrialisation.

Ukraine has recognised the Holodomor as a genocide since 2006, and so have the European Parliament and a number of other states. In 2008 the Russian State Duma condemned the Soviet regime for neglecting the lives of people in pursuit of economic and political goals.
holon: Holon lies in the Tel Aviv District, south of Tel Aviv, and is part of the Gush Dan metropolitan area. Its name comes from the Hebrew word holon, meaning a little sand, and refers to the sand dunes on which the city was built. The name also appears in the Book of Joshua (21:15), in the words Holon with its suburbs and Debir with its suburbs. The city has the second-largest industrial zone in Israel, after Haifa.

Holon was founded in 1935 on sand dunes about six kilometres from Tel Aviv. The Łódzia textile factory was established there by Jewish immigrants from Łódź in Poland, along with many other industrial enterprises. In February 1936 the cornerstone was laid for Kiryat Avoda, a Modernist building complex designed by the architect Joseph Neufeld to ease the shortage of housing for municipal workers.

In the early months of the 1948 Arab-Israeli War Holon was on the front line, with constant shooting along the border with the village of Tel al-Rish, a suburb of Arab Jaffa to its north-west, and clashes towards the town of Yazur to the east. An attack on Tel al-Rish by Haganah militia units based in Holon was repulsed with considerable losses. After the establishment of the state, Holon grew to take in Tel al-Rish, renamed Tel Giborim, and the orange groves of Yazur.

Holon is home to more than half of the world's Samaritan population. In 1954 the president of Israel, Yitzhak Ben-Zvi, helped to establish a Samaritan quarter on the outskirts of the city. It was named Neve Pinchas after Pinhas Ben-Abraham, the high priest of the Samaritan community, and has its own synagogues and street signs in Samaritan Hebrew. Holon is one of only two places with a Samaritan community, the other being the village of Kiryat Luza on Mount Gerizim above Nablus.

The city once had the image of a working-class dormitory community, and has presented itself as a children's city. It has the Holon Children's Museum, the Israeli Museum of Caricature and Comics, the Design Museum Holon, the first Israeli museum of design, and an annual street carnival for the festival of Purim, the Adloyada. Landmarks slated for preservation include Derech Habitachon, paved during the 1948 war, and several water towers.
holy-alliance: The Holy Alliance, also called the Grand Alliance, linked the absolute monarchies of Austria, Prussia and Russia. It was created after the final defeat of Napoleon at the behest of Emperor Alexander I of Russia and signed in Paris on 26 September 1815. Alexander wanted to instil the divine right of kings and Christian values in European political life, under the influence of his spiritual adviser Baroness Barbara von Krüdener. The text was written by Alexander and edited by Ioannis Kapodistrias and Alexandru Sturdza.

Under the treaty European rulers would govern as "branches" of the Christian community and offer one another mutual service. The first draft appealed to mysticism through a proposed unified Christian empire, which the other monarchies found disconcerting, and a more pragmatic version was adopted. About three months after the Final Act of the Congress of Vienna, the monarchs of Catholic Austria, Protestant Prussia and Orthodox Russia promised to act on the basis of "justice, love, and peace". The French diplomat Dominique-Georges-Frédéric Dufour de Pradt called the document "an apocalypse of diplomacy".

The agreement was at first secret and was mistrusted by liberals. The United Kingdom rejected it, though George IV consented as King of Hanover, as did the Papal States and the Ottoman Empire. Lord Castlereagh, the British Foreign Secretary, called it "a piece of sublime mysticism and nonsense". Britain nevertheless took part in the Concert of Europe.

In practice the Austrian chancellor, Prince Klemens von Metternich, made it a bastion against democracy and nationalism. It also coordinated the suppression of Polish efforts to restore an independent state, by Austria in Galicia and Lodomeria, by Russia in Congress Poland and by Prussia in Posen and West Prussia. At the Congress of Aix-la-Chapelle in 1818 the monarchs demanded stern measures against university demagogues, carried out in the Carlsbad Decrees of 1819. At Troppau in 1820 and Laibach in 1821 Metternich sought to align his allies against the Carbonari revolt against Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies, and in 1822 the Congress of Verona advised against the Greek Revolution and resolved on the French invasion of Spain.

The alliance is conventionally taken to have become defunct with Alexander's death in 1825, and France went its own way after the July Revolution of 1830. The three eastern powers agreed the Münchengrätz Convention in September 1833 and met again to suppress the revolutions of 1848. The Austro-Russian alliance broke up in the Crimean War, when Austria declared itself neutral and occupied the Danubian Principalities in 1854. Chancellor Otto von Bismarck reunited the three powers as the League of the Three Emperors after German unification in 1871, but it faltered in the 1880s over the decline of the Ottoman Empire.
holy-grail: The word graal comes from Old French graal or greal, related to Old Occitan grazal and Old Catalan gresal, meaning a cup or bowl of earth, wood or metal. The most widely accepted derivation is from Latin gradalis, via cratalis, from the Greek krater, a large wine-mixing vessel. In the 15th century John Hardyng invented a derivation from sang réal, royal blood, which Thomas Malory used and which later fed the theory of a bloodline of Jesus.

Scholars disagree about where the idea came from. Roger Sherman Loomis, Alfred Nutt and Jessie Weston looked to Celtic myth, such as the magical cauldrons of Welsh tradition and Bran the Blessed in the Mabinogion. Others argue for a Christian origin; Joseph Goering points to 12th-century wall paintings from churches in the Catalan Pyrenees showing the Virgin Mary holding a bowl radiating tongues of fire.

The first grail appears in Chrétien de Troyes's unfinished Perceval, the Story of the Grail, dated between 1180 and 1191. Perceval, a guest in the castle of the Fisher King, sees a procession in which a girl carries a decorated graal, a serving dish, and a bleeding lance is borne before him. He stays silent, and later a hermit tells him that the grail holds a host that keeps the crippled king alive; had he asked the right questions he would have healed the king and restored the Wasteland.

Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival makes the Grail a gemstone, lapis exillis, the sanctuary of the neutral angels in Lucifer's rebellion. In Robert de Boron's Joseph d'Arimathie, composed between 1191 and 1202, the Grail becomes the Last Supper chalice in which Joseph of Arimathea caught Christ's blood; Joseph then carries it to Britain. The Lancelot-Grail cycle introduced Galahad as its hero, who achieves the Grail in the Queste del Saint Graal. In the German Diu Crône it is Gawain who does so.

Relics later came to be identified with the Grail, though traditions of a Last Supper relic stayed rare beside those of the True Cross and Holy Lance. The pilgrim Arculf reported a Last Supper chalice near Jerusalem in the 7th century, before the romances. Glastonbury became tied to the legend, and from the 15th century the Grail was prominent in its stories.

In 1818 Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall linked the Grail with the Knights Templar, though no historical evidence connects the order with a search for it, and in 1906 Joséphin Péladan identified the Cathar castle of Montségur with the Grail castle. Richard Wagner's Parsifal premiered in 1882, and Tennyson's Idylls of the King and T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land of 1922 drew on the legend.
holy-land: The term Holy Land denotes areas of the Southern Levant that hold great significance in the Abrahamic religions, chiefly because of their association with people and events in the Hebrew Bible. It is traditionally synonymous with the Land of Israel or the Promised Land in a religious context and with Canaan or Palestine in a secular or geographic one, a region mostly between the Mediterranean Sea and the Jordan River. Christian books often carry maps of it, taken to include Galilee, Samaria and Judea.

In Judaism the land is called Eretz HaKodesh, and researchers hold that the idea of a land made holy as the earthly dwelling of the God of Israel was present by the time of Zechariah in the 6th century BCE. The Tanakh treats it as given to the Israelites by God, and many commandments can be kept only there. Jerusalem was the site of the Temple, the central place of worship for Israelites and Jews.

For Christians the land is holy through the birth, ministry, crucifixion and resurrection of Jesus. In the Middle Ages Christian pilgrimage contributed to the beginning of the Crusades, launched under the banner of restoring Christian sovereignty after the region was lost to the early Muslim conquests. Muslims hold that Muhammad made a night journey from Mecca to Jerusalem's Al-Aqsa Mosque and ascended to heaven from there, and Jerusalem was the first direction of prayer for Muslims before it was changed to the Kaaba. In the 19th century the land became a matter of international diplomacy as part of the Eastern Question about the Ottoman Empire, which led to the Crimean War of the 1850s.

Pilgrims from across the Abrahamic world visit the Holy Land to see and touch physical expressions of their faith. Jerusalem is regarded as the holiest city in Judaism and Christianity and the third-holiest in Islam, after Mecca and Medina. Some sites are contested between religious groups and subject to the Status Quo in Jerusalem and Bethlehem, which bars even minor change without the agreement of all parties concerned. For the Baháʼí Faith, the shrines of Bahá'u'lláh at Acre and of the Báb at Haifa are the holiest places of pilgrimage.
holy-roman-emperor: The title was originally and officially Emperor of the Romans. In the West the imperial title lapsed after the death of Julius Nepos in 480. In 800 Pope Leo III, who owed a great debt to Charlemagne, King of the Franks, declared the throne vacant, on the pretext that a woman could not rule, since the Eastern Emperor Constantine VI had been deposed in 797 and replaced by his mother Irene. He crowned Charlemagne Emperor of the Romans on Christmas Day, using the concept of translatio imperii. The Eastern Empire eventually recognised Charlemagne's successors, but only as Frankish or German emperors.

Carolingian descendants and others held the title until the death of Berengar I of Italy in 924. Traditional historiography assumes continuity between the Carolingian Empire and the Holy Roman Empire, while a modern convention takes the coronation of Otto I in 962 as the starting point. The word sacrum, "holy", was first used in connection with the empire in 1157 under Frederick I Barbarossa. The English term "Holy Roman Emperor" is a modern shorthand that gained currency in the 1920s and 1930s.

Since 911 the German princes had elected the King of the Germans from among their peers, and that king was then crowned emperor by the pope. From a Carolingian autocracy the title evolved by the 13th century into an elective monarchy. The seven prince-electors are named in the Golden Bull of 1356: the archbishops of Mainz, Trier and Cologne, the king of Bohemia, the count palatine of the Rhine, the duke of Saxony and the margrave of Brandenburg. Candidates made concessions to the electors, known as electoral capitulations. The Ottonians, the Salians and the Hohenstaufen each held the title for long periods.

The interregnum of the 13th century left Rudolf I, Adolf and Albert I as kings who were never crowned emperor, until Henry VII was crowned on 29 June 1312. From 1452 to 1806 the Habsburgs held the title with only one interruption, Charles VII, a Wittelsbach, and the last emperors were from the House of Habsburg-Lorraine from 1765. The emperor was widely perceived to rule by divine right, though he often rivalled the pope, most notably in the Investiture Controversy.

The emperor-elect had to be crowned by the pope until 1508, when Pope Julius II allowed Maximilian I to use the title of elected Roman emperor without a coronation in Rome. Charles V was the last emperor crowned by a pope, at Bologna in 1530. The Empire never had an empress regnant, though women such as Theophanu and Maria Theresa exerted strong influence. After the Reformation the elected emperor was always a Catholic. Francis II dissolved the Empire after Napoleon's victory at Austerlitz, and the final emperor-elect abdicated in 1806.
holy-roman-empire: The Holy Roman Empire developed in the Early Middle Ages, and its beginning is dated either to 800 or to 962. On 25 December 800 Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne, king of the Franks, as Roman Emperor, reviving the title more than three centuries after the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476. The title lapsed again by 924 and was revived in 962 when Pope John XII crowned Otto of Saxony, known as Otto the Great, as emperor. At first the empire consisted of three kingdoms, Germany, Italy and, from 1032, Burgundy, held together by the emperor's overlordship. The term holy was first used under Frederick Barbarossa in 1157, and the form Holy Roman Empire is attested from 1254.

From 962 until the 13th century the empire was one of the most powerful monarchies in Europe. The Investiture Controversy set Pope Gregory VII against Henry IV, who made the Walk to Canossa in 1077 to have his excommunication lifted. The empire reached its apex in the mid-13th century under the House of Hohenstaufen, but this was an overextension and led to a partial collapse. Difficulties in electing the king led to a fixed college of prince-electors, whose procedures the Golden Bull of 1356 set down. By the 15th century governance was concentrated on the Kingdom of Germany.

Martin Luther launched the Reformation in 1517 and it divided the empire along religious lines, the north, the east and cities such as Strasbourg, Frankfurt and Nuremberg becoming Protestant while the south and west largely stayed Catholic. Lutheranism was recognised in the Peace of Augsburg of 1555 and Calvinism in the Peace of Westphalia of 1648. Rivalry between Austria and Prussia dominated the empire's history after 1740. On 6 August 1806 Emperor Francis II abdicated and formally dissolved the empire, after Napoleon created the Confederation of the Rhine from client states loyal to France.

The empire was neither a centralised state nor a nation-state. It was divided into dozens, and eventually hundreds, of entities governed by kings, dukes, counts, bishops, abbots and other rulers, collectively known as princes. Emperors could gain little control over the lands they formally owned and had to grant more and more autonomy to local rulers, a process that began with the Investiture Controversy and was more or less concluded by the Peace of Westphalia. The Imperial Diet was more a forum for negotiation than a legislature. The imperial office was traditionally elected, mostly by a handful of prince-electors and archbishops, and until 1555 Catholicism was the single official religion.
homer: The identity of Homer is a mystery, and scholars generally regard the ancient picture of a single author behind the Iliad and the Odyssey as a fictional narrative. Their composition is thought to date to the late eighth or early seventh century BCE. Many accounts of his life circulated in antiquity. The most widespread made him a blind bard from Ionia, a region including the central west coast of Anatolia and the islands of Chios and Samos, but modern scholars regard these accounts as apocryphal. The earliest implicit references to Homer, in the 7th century BCE, are in works by Archilochus, Alcman, Tyrtaeus and Callinus.

Pindar is credited with saying that Homer came from Chios and Smyrna. The historian Ephorus held that he studied poetry with the bard Phemius and was born in Cyme, Philochorus thought Argos was his birthplace, and later writers believed it was Pylos or Athens. The Byzantine Suda described him as descended from a Muse, Apollo, Orpheus or others. No account of his origin became mainstream, but most place his death on the island of Ios, where two epigrams by Alcaeus of Messene commemorate his burial.

The Iliad centres on a quarrel between King Agamemnon and the warrior Achilles in the last year of the Trojan War. The Odyssey chronicles the ten-year journey home of Odysseus, king of Ithaca, after the fall of Troy. Both are in Homeric Greek, a literary language mixing Ionic and Aeolic features, and are composed in unrhymed dactylic hexameters. Most researchers believe they were first transmitted orally, and set phrases such as crafty Odysseus and rosy-fingered Dawn aided the bard. Both begin with an invocation to the Muse.

The poems were put into written form between the eighth and sixth centuries BCE. Ancient tradition held that Pisistratus collected them in Athens in the late sixth century BCE. After the 24 books were fixed, scholars at Alexandria such as Aristarchus of Samothrace helped establish a canonical text.

The Homeric poems were widely used as school texts in Greek and Hellenistic cultures, the first literary works taught to all students. Plato said that Homer had educated Greece. Interpreters, especially the Stoics, read the poems as allegories containing hidden wisdom. The first printed edition was produced in Florence in 1488 by Demetrios Chalkokondyles. In 1873 Heinrich Schliemann announced the discovery of Homer's Troy at Hisarlik in modern Turkey.

Ancient chronology dated the sack of Troy to 1184 BCE, and some scholars think the destruction of Troy VIIa around 1220 BCE gave rise to the myth. The poems depict customs from different periods: their heroes use bronze weapons but are cremated, an Iron Age practice. Virgil's Aeneid was heavily influenced by Homer, and later works from Tennyson's Ulysses to James Joyce's Ulysses retell his stories.
homs: Homs lies on the Orontes River in western Syria, 162 km north of Damascus, and is the central link between the interior cities and the Mediterranean coast. For about 2,000 years it has been a key agricultural market and trade centre for the villages of northern Syria. Excavations at the Citadel of Homs show settlement from around 2300 BCE. In 1274 BCE Ramesses II of Egypt and Muwatalli II of the Hittite Empire fought at Kadesh on the Orontes, near Homs, in what may have been the largest chariot battle ever fought.

The Emesene dynasty, an Arab line, gave the city its Latin name Emesa. After Pompey's submission of the Seleucid state of Syria to the Roman Republic in 64 BCE, the dynasty was confirmed as client kings of Rome, and its kingdom reached from the Bekaa Valley to the border with Palmyra. Emesa was a centre of worship of El-Gabal, a sun god, and gained importance in Christianity under the Byzantines. In 637 CE the Rashidun army under Khalid ibn al-Walid captured the city peacefully, since its inhabitants agreed to pay a large ransom. Caliph Umar made Homs the capital of Jund Hims, a district of Bilad al-Sham.

In 1098 the Crusaders besieged Homs but failed to take it. It came under Duqaq, the Saljuqid ruler of Damascus, who made it a fortified camp from which Muslim forces raided the Crusader coast. In 1149 the Zangids under Nur al-Din captured it. In 1516 Homs became part of the Ottoman Empire. It lost political importance but remained an economic centre, known for silk and wool weaving, and by the end of the 16th century it had about 24,000 people. Its cotton industry boomed in the 19th century. The French moved their military academy there in 1932, and many of its graduates became officers in the Syrian army.

Homs is the capital of the Homs Governorate. Its population includes Sunni and Alawite Muslims and Christians, and the city has a number of historic mosques and churches. It lies close to the Krak des Chevaliers castle, a World Heritage Site. Large parts of the city were devastated in the Syrian civil war.
hong-kong: Hong Kong is situated on China's southern coast, 60 kilometres east of Macau and on the eastern side of the Pearl River estuary. It is surrounded by the South China Sea on all sides except the north, where it neighbours the city of Shenzhen along the Sham Chun River. The territory consists of Hong Kong Island, the Kowloon Peninsula, the New Territories, Lantau Island and over 200 other islands. Its highest point is Tai Mo Shan, at 957 metres, and about 70 square kilometres of its land has been reclaimed from the sea.

The name was first romanised as He-Ong-Kong in 1780 and originally referred to a small inlet between Aberdeen Island and the southern coast of Hong Kong Island. It is generally believed to be an early phonetic rendering of a Cantonese phrase meaning 'fragrant harbour' or 'incense harbour'. The second colonial governor, Sir John Davis, offered an alternative origin, 'red torrent'. The name was often written as one word, Hongkong, until 1926, when the government officially adopted two words.

The earliest known human traces date to 35,000 to 39,000 years ago, based on knapped stone tools found at Wong Tei Tung in the Sai Kung Peninsula. About 6,000 years ago the region was widely occupied, and rice cultivation had been introduced by the Late Neolithic. The Qin dynasty incorporated the area into China for the first time in 214 BCE, after conquering the indigenous Baiyue. After the Qin collapsed it was consolidated under the Nanyue kingdom, and China recaptured it after the Han conquest. During the Mongol conquest in the 13th century the southern Song court was briefly located at the Sung Wong Toi site in Kowloon City, before its defeat at the Battle of Yamen in 1279.

The Qing dynasty ceded Hong Kong Island to the British Empire in 1841 to 1842 after losing the First Opium War. The colony expanded to the Kowloon Peninsula in 1860, and in 1898 the United Kingdom obtained a 99-year lease of the New Territories. Japan occupied Hong Kong from 1941 to 1945 during the Second World War. The territory was handed over from the United Kingdom to China in 1997.

Hong Kong is a special administrative region of China. Under the principle of one country, two systems and the Sino-British Joint Declaration, its Basic Law serves as the regional constitution, and it keeps separate governing and economic systems from those of mainland China. Its population was estimated at 7,413,070 in 2021, the great majority of them Chinese. Its culture is described as a hybrid of Eastern and Western influences.
hong-kong-island: Hong Kong Island is the second largest island in Hong Kong, after Lantau, with a land area of about 78.59 square kilometres. It was known originally, and on road signs, simply as Hong Kong. Its northern coast forms the southern shore of Victoria Harbour, whose deep waters, favoured by large trading ships, were largely responsible for the development of Hong Kong. The island is one of the three areas of Hong Kong, with Kowloon and the New Territories, and is often called the Hong Kong side or Island side.

Human settlement in the area dates back some 6,000 years, as shown by Neolithic artefacts found at Stanley. In 214 BCE the Qin dynasty defeated the Baiyue and absorbed their lands, including the island, which came under Panyu County in the Nanhai Commandery. Copper coins of the Sui, Tang and Song dynasties unearthed near the site of the Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club suggest commercial activity in those periods. In 1573 the island belonged to Xin'an County.

In 1661 the Shunzhi Emperor ordered the great clearance, which forced people in coastal areas to move inland to keep Ming loyalists in Formosa from reaching the shores. The ban was lifted in 1669, though few of the original residents returned, and piracy was rampant until the cession of 1842.

After the Qing defeat in the First Opium War the island was ceded to the United Kingdom in perpetuity under the Treaty of Nanking in 1842, and British forces established the City of Victoria, named for Queen Victoria. The Battle of Hong Kong began on 8 December 1941, eight hours after the attack on Pearl Harbor. Defenders from British, Canadian and Indian forces and the Hong Kong Volunteer Defence Forces held the Wong Nai Chung Gap for a time, but the British surrendered on 25 December 1941, and the Governor, Mark Young, gave himself up at the Peninsula Hotel. The population of Hong Kong fell from 1.6 million in 1941 to 600,000 in 1945.

After the Second World War the population of the island grew rapidly, and areas such as North Point, Shau Kei Wan and Aberdeen were developed. Sovereignty over the island passed to the People's Republic of China on 1 July 1997, together with Kowloon and the New Territories. The Central area in the north-east remains the historical, political and economic centre of Hong Kong, with the Government House, the Legislative Council Complex and the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. The Peak is among its best-known sights, and the island's mountains are popular for hiking.
hongwu-emperor: Zhu Yuanzhang was born on 21 October 1328 at Zhongli village, in Haozhou, present-day Fengyang in Anhui, then under the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty. He was the youngest of four sons of a peasant family and was named Zhu Chongba at birth. His maternal grandfather had served the Song in its last struggle against the Mongols, and his mother told him stories of Song loyalism. When he was sixteen, an epidemic killed his parents and brother. The orphan briefly lived as a novice monk, begging for alms, and learned of the hardships of ordinary people; he also developed a dislike of book-dependent scholars.

Taxation, famine and catastrophic Yellow River floods led to widespread opposition to the Yuan, and in 1351 the Red Turban Rebellion broke out. In 1352 Zhu joined the rebels at Haozhou and quickly rose to command his own army. In 1355 he crossed the Yangtze into the south and captured Nanjing in 1356. He nominally acknowledged the Red Turban figurehead Han Lin'er, but ran his own administration on Yuan lines. After defeating the rival rebels Chen Youliang and Zhang Shicheng, he declared himself King of Wu on 4 February 1364.

In 1368 he renamed his realm Da Ming, meaning Great Radiance, and took Hongwu, Vastly Martial, as his era name. In four years of war he drove out the Mongol forces loyal to the Yuan and unified the country, but he failed to conquer Mongolia. His capital was Nanjing, whose walls, almost 26 km long, were built by a workforce of 200,000. He restricted the consumption of the wealthy, abolished slavery, exempted newly cultivated land from tax for three years, and banned private foreign trade and enforced a strict sea ban. By the winter of 1395 some 40,987 dams and drainage canals had been built.

Fearing conspiracies, he made his sons princes with military commands on the border. After Chancellor Hu Weiyong was executed for treason in 1380 he abolished the office of grand chancellor and the Central Secretariat, placing six ministries directly under himself; the Embroidered Uniform Guard served as secret police. He also carried out purges of generals, notably after 1393.

His heir Zhu Biao died in 1392, and the emperor named his grandson Zhu Yunwen as successor. He died on 24 June 1398 and was succeeded by that grandson, the Jianwen Emperor, who was overthrown in 1402 by the emperor's fourth son Zhu Di, who became the Yongle Emperor. Traditional historiography revered him as a typical founder of a dynasty, credited with ending civil war and foreign rule. His ministers gave him the temple name Taizu, Grand Progenitor.
honiara: Honiara lies on the north-western coast of Guadalcanal and includes the seaport of Point Cruz. The Matanikau River flows through the town, past Chinatown, and the town centres on the Kukum Highway, which connects it with Honiara International Airport, about 11 kilometres to the east across the Lunga River. The airport was formerly Henderson Field. The climate is tropical, with an average daytime temperature of about 28 °C and a wetter season between November and April. The name comes from nagho ni ara, which roughly means place of the east wind, in one of the Guadalcanal languages. Little detailed material exists on the town's early history.

The airport area to the east of the town was the site of the Battle of Henderson Field in 1942, the last of the three major land offensives of the Japanese in the Guadalcanal Campaign. The American forces left well developed infrastructure, which led the British government to shift the capital of the Solomon Islands Protectorate to Honiara; government buildings opened in early January 1952.

In the 1960s and 1970s the town received two-thirds of the funds allocated to the country's economic development, although only about 5 per cent of Solomon Islanders lived there. In the 1960s Pijin became its principal language and the mother tongue of a generation of young urban residents, and through Honiara it spread to become the main language of the islands. In 1979 the town still had only 18,346 people. In July 1978 it became the capital of the independent Solomon Islands.

From the late 1990s Honiara was the centre of ethnic violence and political unrest, set off by tension between Malaitans and the people of Guadalcanal. A coup attempt in June 2000 led to fighting between the Malaita Eagle Force and the Isatabu Freedom Movement. In July 2003 the Regional Assistance Mission to Solomon Islands, a Pacific initiative led by Australia, was invited in to restore order. Riots in 2006 destroyed part of Chinatown and left more than 1,000 Chinese residents homeless.

Honiara is the capital and largest city of Solomon Islands, with a population of 129,569 at the 2019 census. A capital territory of 22 square kilometres was proclaimed in 1983. The National Parliament, a conical building inaugurated in 1993, and the national museum stand there, along with the Guadalcanal American Memorial, dedicated in 1992, and the Solomons Peace Memorial Park built by Japanese veterans. The city is predominantly Christian and is the headquarters of the Anglican Church of Melanesia and of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Honiara.
honolulu: Honolulu lies along the southeast coast of the island of Oʻahu in the Pacific Ocean. The name is Hawaiian for sheltered harbour or calm port, and the old name of the area, Kou, roughly covers the heart of the present downtown district. It is the most remote major city in the United States and one of the most isolated in the world: the nearest point on the mainland, Point Arena Lighthouse in northern California, is 2,045 nautical miles away, and the nearest major city is San Francisco. The volcanic field of the Honolulu Volcanics lies partly within the city.

Oral histories and artifacts indicate that there was a settlement where Honolulu now stands in the 11th century, founded by the original Polynesian migrants to the archipelago. After Kamehameha I conquered Oʻahu in the Battle of Nuʻuanu at Nuʻuanu Pali, he moved his royal court from the island of Hawaiʻi to Waikiki in 1804, and in 1809 to what is now downtown Honolulu. The capital moved back to Kailua-Kona in 1812.

The geography of the area and Honolulu Harbor made it desirable as a port, which accounts for the city's growth and importance in the Hawaiian archipelago and the broader Pacific. Honolulu has been the capital of Hawaii since 1845, first as seat of the independent Hawaiian Kingdom until its overthrow in 1893, then of the United States territory established after annexation in 1898, and since 1959 of the state of Hawaii. The city gained worldwide recognition after the Empire of Japan attacked nearby Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941, which brought the United States into the Second World War.

Honolulu is the capital and most populous city of Hawaii and the seat of the consolidated City and County of Honolulu. Pearl Harbor remains a major United States Navy base and hosts the United States Pacific Fleet. The Bishop Museum has the world's largest collection of Hawaiiana and Pacific culture artifacts, and ʻIolani Palace and the USS Arizona Memorial are among the city's sights.
honorius: Honorius was born in Constantinople on 9 September 384, the younger son of Theodosius I and his first wife Aelia Flaccilla. He held the consulate at the age of two. After Theodosius died in January 395, he took the western half of the empire at the age of ten, under the guidance of the general Stilicho, who married his daughter Maria to him and, after her death in 407, his second daughter Thermantia.

The poet Claudian wrote a wedding poem for the first marriage, and it survives. At first Honorius held court at Milan, but when the Visigoths under Alaric I entered Italy in 401 he moved to Ravenna, protected by marshes and strong fortifications. Emperors resided there until the overthrow of Romulus Augustulus in 476.

His reign was beset by invasions of Gaul, Italy and Hispania and by a series of usurpers. Stilicho put down the revolt of Gildo in Africa in 397–398 and defeated Alaric at Pollentia on 6 April 402. In 406 he overcame the invader Radagaisus, but Vandals, Alans and Suebi crossed the Rhine into Gaul on 31 December 406. The soldiers in Britain backed the revolts of Marcus, Gratian and Constantine III, who crossed into Gaul in 407. In 410 Honorius answered a plea for help with the Rescript of Honorius, which some modern scholars think concerns Bruttium in Italy rather than Britain.

In 408 Honorius, persuaded by the minister Olympius that Stilicho was plotting with the barbarians, had him arrested and executed. The purge killed Stilicho's son Eucherius and the families of his allied troops, who then deserted to Alaric. Alaric besieged Rome, had Priscus Attalus proclaimed emperor, and in 410 the Visigoths entered the city, which had not been held by a foreign force for about eight centuries.

The sack was relatively mild, though the shock was great and it prompted Augustine to write The City of God. The general Constantius defeated the usurpers Maximus, Gerontius and Constantine III by 411, and in 418 a treaty gave the Visigoths south-western Gaul. In 417 Constantius married Honorius's sister Galla Placidia against her will, and in 421 Honorius recognised him as co-emperor, though Theodosius II refused to.

Honorius died of edema on 15 August 423, leaving no heir. Joannes was nominated emperor, but in the following year Theodosius II installed Valentinian III, the son of Galla Placidia and Constantius III. By then Britain, Spain and Gaul had been ravaged by invaders. Honorius was judged harshly by some historians of the 19th and 20th centuries, including J. B. Bury. Procopius records a story, probably untrue, that on hearing that Rome had perished the emperor thought of his pet fowl of that name. He banned gladiatorial games in 399 and again in 404.
honshu: Honshu lies between the Pacific Ocean to the east and the Sea of Japan to the west. Its Japanese name, Honshū, means main province or homeland; it was historically also called Akitsushima, the dragonfly island. The island is roughly 1,300 km long and from 50 to 230 km wide, with a total area of 227,960 km2, slightly larger than Britain. It is mountainous and volcanic, with frequent earthquakes; the Japanese Alps span its width, and it holds Japan's highest mountain, Mount Fuji, and its largest lake, Lake Biwa. The Shinano River, Japan's longest, flows through it.

Humans first arrived in Honshu at least about 37,000 years ago, Stone Age hunter-gatherers from Northeast Asia who probably followed ice age megafauna. The island then saw the Jōmon period, from about 14,000 to 300 BCE, one of the earliest known prehistoric cultures of Japan. The Jōmon people are known for cord-marked pottery and dogū clay figurines, many excavated at sites across Honshu, which reflect a complex spiritual life and early sedentary communities along the coasts and river valleys.

Honshu was the historical centre of Japanese cultural and political power, and its past capitals include Kyoto, Nara and Kamakura. The Meiji Restoration of 1868 ended the Tokugawa shogunate and the Edo period (1603-1867) and at least nominally returned control of the country to direct imperial rule under the Emperor Meiji. Its leaders were mostly young samurai, among them men from Chōshū in far western Honshu.

Honshu is the largest of Japan's four main islands and the seventh-largest island in the world. It has about 100 million inhabitants, 81.9 per cent of Japan's population, concentrated in the coastal areas and plains, and about 30 per cent of Japan's people live in the Greater Tokyo Area on the Kantō Plain. Tokyo, the capital, is its largest city. Most of Japan's industry lies in a belt along its southern coast from Tokyo to Nagoya, Kyoto, Osaka, Kobe and Hiroshima, and bridges and tunnels link the island to Hokkaido, Kyushu and Shikoku.
hoplite: Hoplites were citizen-soldiers of the Greek city-states, primarily armed with spears and shields. They were mostly free, propertied farmers and artisans who could afford armour and weapons, estimated at a third to a half of the able-bodied adult male population. Each provided his own equipment, which might be passed down in families. Bronze armour, weighing nearly 32 kilograms, was worn by those who could afford it, but linen armour was more common, and the average farmer-hoplite often carried only a shield, a spear and perhaps a helmet.

The large round shield, the aspis, measured between 80 and 100 centimetres across and weighed between 6.5 and 8 kilograms. Its Argive grip, with the handle at the edge and a leather fastening for the forearm at the centre, kept it from swaying when struck. The main weapon was a spear, the doru, 2.5 to 4.5 metres long, and a short sword, the xiphos, served as a secondary weapon.

The word comes from hoplon, referring to the soldier's equipment. Greek armies began to adopt the phalanx in the eighth century BCE, though historians disagree on how fast the change came. Anthony Snodgrass argues that it took about a hundred years, from 750 to 650 BCE, as armour spread among citizens. Paul Cartledge and Victor Hanson propose a faster transition, from 725 to 675 BCE, and Hans van Wees a longer one. The earliest monumental communal burial of warriors, on the island of Paros, points to a hoplite military organisation in the last quarter of the eighth century.

The competing city-states could rarely field large armies for long, so campaigns were short, often limited to a single summer, and battles were set pieces on level ground intended to be decisive. The phalanx was formed eight to ten rows deep. The front ranks stabbed with their spears, while those behind pushed with their shields to keep the line steady. A soldier carried his shield on his left arm, protecting his neighbour, so the right side was the most exposed and the most experienced men stood there. A man who threw away his shield in flight disgraced himself.

Hoplites proved far superior to Persian infantry at the Battle of Marathon in 490 BCE, at Thermopylae in 480 BCE and at Plataea in 479 BCE. In the Peloponnesian War they were less central, as navies, skirmishers and mercenaries grew in importance, and the Macedonian phalanx later replaced the hoplite. The last major hoplite army was defeated at the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BCE.
horace: Horace was born on 8 December 65 BCE at Venusia, a town on a trade route in Lucania on the border with Apulia. Various Italic dialects were spoken in the area, which perhaps enriched his feeling for language. He may have thought of himself as a Samnite by birth, and references to his childhood setting run through his poems.

He left Rome, possibly after his father's death, and continued his education in Athens, arriving at nineteen. The city was then dominated by Epicureans and Stoics, whose theories made a deep impression on him. There he probably acquired a deep familiarity with Greek lyric poetry. He served as an officer in the republican army defeated at the Battle of Philippi in 42 BCE.

His career coincided with Rome's change from republic to empire. He was befriended by Octavian's right-hand man in civil affairs, Maecenas, and became a spokesman for the new regime. Some commentators see a delicate balance in which he kept a strong measure of independence, while John Dryden called him "a well-mannered court slave". The dating of his works is only approximate: the Satires belong to about 35 to 30 BCE, the Epodes to 30 BCE and Odes 1 to 3 to about 23 BCE, followed by the Epistles, the Carmen Saeculare of 17 BCE, Odes 4 and the Ars Poetica.

He composed in metres borrowed from archaic Greece, hexameters for the Satires and Epistles, iambs for the Epodes and alcaics and sapphics for the Odes. His themes include politics, love, philosophy, ethics, his own social role and poetry itself. In the Odes Epicureanism is the dominant influence, and in Odes 3.30 he claimed to have built a monument more durable than bronze.

Horace died on 27 November 8 BCE. Odes 1 to 3 were at first not well received, but Augustus commissioned a ceremonial ode for the Centennial Games in 17 BCE and encouraged the publication of Odes 4, after which his standing as Rome's premier lyricist was assured. Quintilian regarded the Odes as the only Latin lyrics worth reading, and Ovid and Propertius were among those influenced by him.

His poems probably survived the early Middle Ages in just two or three books, ancestors of six manuscripts of the ninth century. In the 17th and 18th centuries new editions appeared almost yearly and ode-writing became fashionable in England. He remained central to the education of English-speaking elites until the 1960s. For Wilfred Owen, marked by the First World War, his line dulce et decorum est stood for discredited values.
horatio-nelson: Horatio Nelson was born on 29 September 1758 at the rectory of Burnham Thorpe, Norfolk, the sixth of eleven children of the Reverend Edmund Nelson and Catherine Suckling. He was named after his godfather Horatio Walpole, 1st Earl of Orford. His maternal uncle Maurice Suckling, a high-ranking naval officer, is believed to have had a major influence on his life, and through him Nelson joined the Royal Navy in 1771. He kept a strong Christian faith throughout his life.

Nelson received his first command in 1778 but suffered from bouts of illness, and after the American War of Independence ended in 1783 he was put on half-pay. Britain's entry into the French Revolutionary Wars in 1793 brought him back to active service. He took part in the siege of Toulon and the invasion of Corsica, in which he partly lost the sight of his right eye.

At the Battle of Cape St Vincent on 14 February 1797 he disobeyed orders by leaving the British line to engage the Spanish van. He led a boarding party onto the San Nicolas, and then onto the San Josef, and took both. It was the first time in 300 years that a British flag officer had led a boarding party. Soon after, in a failed attack on Santa Cruz de Tenerife, he lost his right arm. In 1798 he won a decisive victory at the Battle of the Nile, but his involvement in Neapolitan politics and his affair with Emma Hamilton damaged his reputation in the navy.

In 1801 he defeated a Danish fleet at the Battle of Copenhagen and helped break up the Second League of Armed Neutrality. After the Napoleonic Wars began in 1803 he resumed active service, blockaded Toulon and pursued the Franco-Spanish fleet to the West Indies and back. In 1805 he took over the blockade of Cádiz.

On 21 October 1805 the Franco-Spanish fleet came out of Cádiz and Nelson engaged it at the Battle of Trafalgar. The battle was a decisive British victory, but Nelson, aboard HMS Victory, was fatally wounded by a French marksman. His body was brought back to England and given a state funeral. His signal before the battle, England expects that every man will do his duty, has been widely quoted. Nelson's Column in Trafalgar Square in London and the Nelson Monument in Edinburgh honour him.
horn-of-africa: The Horn of Africa, also called the Somali Peninsula, lies in the easternmost part of mainland Africa. It runs along the southern edge of the Red Sea and extends into the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. It consists chiefly of mountains raised by the formation of the Great Rift Valley. The Romans called it Regio Aromatica, after its aromatic plants, or Regio Incognita, since classical maps covered it poorly. It is made up of Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Somalia and the partially recognised state of Somaliland. Its main peoples are Cushitic speakers, mostly in the lowlands, and Ethio-Semitic speakers of the highlands, who speak Oromo, Somali, Amharic and Tigrinya among other languages.

Some of the earliest Homo sapiens fossils, the Omo remains of about 233,000 years ago and the Herto skull of about 160,000 years ago, were found in Ethiopia. The ancient Egyptians knew a land called Punt, first mentioned in the 25th century BCE, probably on the coast of Somalia, Djibouti, Eritrea and Sudan. The kingdom of Dʿmt existed in the 8th and 7th centuries BCE, and the Aksumite Kingdom reunited the plateau from the 1st century CE. Aksum traded between the Roman Empire and India and minted its own coins. Under Ezana (fl. 320-360) it became the first major empire to adopt Christianity.

In the Middle Ages the Adal Sultanate, the Ajuran Sultanate, the Ethiopian Empire and the Zagwe dynasty dominated regional trade. The Sultanate of Showa, set up in 896, was one of the oldest local Islamic states, and the Sultanate of Ifat succeeded it around 1285. Adal controlled large parts of Somalia, Ethiopia, Djibouti and Eritrea, and its cities, among them Zeila, Berbera and Harar, flourished. Its armies fought the Solomonic dynasty in the campaign known as the Conquest of Abyssinia.

After the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869, Italy occupied Eritrea, which became an Italian colony on 1 January 1890. Ethiopian forces halted further Italian advances in 1896. By 1936 Eritrea, Ethiopia and Italian Somaliland formed Italian East Africa. Commonwealth forces and the Ethiopian resistance expelled the Italians in 1941.
horseshoe: A horseshoe is attached to the ground side of a horse's hoof, usually nailed through the insensitive hoof wall, which is anatomically akin to the human toenail. Steel and aluminium are the commonest materials, with rubber, plastic, magnesium, titanium or copper in specialised shoes. Some have caulks, protrusions at the toe or heels that give traction. Fitting the shoes is the work of a farrier, who also prepares the feet and assesses lameness. Domestication made shoes necessary: horses kept in colder and wetter places than the dry steppe they came from, and worked with riders, loads or carts, have softer hooves that split and wear.

Historians differ on where the horseshoe began. Because iron was valuable and worn items were usually reforged, clear archaeological evidence is hard to find. Earlier hoof protection included rawhide or leather wrappings in ancient Asia and the strap-on hipposandal, a solid-bottomed boot that the Romans appear to have used in Britain.

In 1897 four bronze shoes with what seem to be nail holes were found in an Etruscan tomb dated around 400 BCE, and a complete shoe with its nails lay in the tomb of the Frankish king Childeric I at Tournai, dated to the fifth century. Catullus mentions mule shoes, which some read as Roman horseshoes, though they may refer to hipposandals.

Written references to the nailed shoe appear around 900 CE, and the earliest clear record of iron horseshoes is a mention of crescent-shaped irons and their nails in 910.
