Around 1000 cast bronze shoes with nail holes became common in Europe. By the Crusades, horseshoes were widespread and, because of the value of iron, were even accepted in place of coin to pay taxes. By the 13th century shoes were forged in large numbers and sold ready made; hot shoeing became common in the 16th century.

In China, rattan and leather shoes were used before iron became common under the Yuan dynasty. Remnants of iron horseshoes from tombs of the Goguryeo period in north-east China are dated to 414 CE. The earliest Chinese reference to iron horseshoes is from 938, when a monk named Gao Juhui wrote that the people of Ganzhou taught him to make a shoe with four holes.

They did not become common for about three more centuries; after the Yuan dynasty was established in 1271 they spread in northern China. Blacksmithing grew into a staple craft of medieval and modern times through the demand for shoes, and in 1835 Henry Burden received the first United States patent for a horseshoe-making machine.
horus: Horus was worshipped from at least late prehistoric Egypt until the Ptolemaic Kingdom and Roman Egypt. His name was written in hieroglyphs as ḥr.w, meaning 'falcon'. The earliest recorded form is the tutelary deity of Nekhen in Upper Egypt, the first known national god, bound to the ruling pharaoh. Egyptian tradition and archaeological evidence indicate that an Upper Egyptian kingdom conquered Lower Egypt at the beginning of Egyptian history. Its rulers called themselves followers of Horus, and Horus became the tutelary deity of the united state and its kings.

The pharaoh was identified directly with Horus, who represented kingship itself. The Pyramid Texts, of about 2400 to 2300 BCE, describe the king as both Horus and Osiris: Horus in life and Osiris in death. In the most common version of the myth Horus is the son of Isis and Osiris. After Set killed Osiris, Isis fled to the marshes of the Nile Delta and bore Horus there. He fought many battles with Set to avenge his father and decide the rightful ruler of Egypt. In The Contendings of Horus and Seth the gods eventually sided with Horus, and Set gave up the throne.

Horus was held to be the sky, with the sun as his right eye and the moon as his left. The Eye of Horus, the wedjat, was a symbol of protection and royal power, and funerary amulets were often made in its shape. Horus appeared as a falcon or as a man with a falcon's head.

Horus had many forms. Heru-ur, Horus the Elder, was worshipped at Letopolis and later at Kom Ombo and Qus, and the Greeks identified him with Apollo. Heru-pa-khered, Horus the child, whom the Greeks called Harpocrates, is shown as a youth with a lock of hair, sucking his finger. Horus of Behdet was the winged sun, depicted above the pylons of temples throughout Egypt. At the temple of Edfu an annual Festival of Victory commemorated the victory of Horus over Set: the king played Horus and struck a hippopotamus, standing for Set, with a harpoon, an act that also legitimised the king.
hosni-mubarak: Hosni Mubarak was born on 4 May 1928 in Kafr El-Meselha, in the Monufia Governorate of Egypt. On 2 February 1949 he left the Military Academy for the Air Force Academy and was commissioned as a pilot officer on 13 March 1950. He served in various units, including two years in a Spitfire fighter squadron, and returned to the Air Force Academy as an instructor until early 1959. From February 1959 to June 1961 he trained in the Soviet Union, at a pilot school in Moscow and at Kant Air Base near Bishkek. He commanded the Egyptian Air Force from 1972 to 1975 and became air chief marshal in 1973.

In April 1975 President Anwar Sadat appointed Mubarak vice president. In September of that year he travelled to Riyadh and Damascus to win Saudi and Syrian acceptance of the Sinai II disengagement agreement with Israel; Syria's president Hafez al-Assad refused to meet him, but in Saudi Arabia he formed a friendship with Crown Prince Fahd. Mubarak was injured when soldiers led by Lieutenant Khalid Islambouli assassinated Sadat in October 1981, and he became the fourth president of Egypt in a single-candidate referendum. He renewed his term by single-candidate referendums in 1987, 1993 and 1999.

Mubarak upheld the Camp David Accords with Israel, though Israeli journalists wrote of a cold peace. Egypt had been suspended from the Arab League because of the treaty; Mubarak met King Fahd of Saudi Arabia in 1982, and in 1989 Egypt's membership was restored and the League's headquarters returned to Cairo. Egypt joined the coalition in the 1991 Gulf War, and afterwards the United States, the Gulf states and Europe forgave about 20 billion dollars of its debt. In 2005, under United States pressure, he held the country's first multi-party election and won it; observers said it was marred by rigging.

The state of emergency in force since the 1967 war was never lifted. Human rights organisations reported arbitrary detention and the systematic use of torture by the security services, and corruption was widespread.

Protests began in Cairo and other cities on 25 January 2011. On 1 February Mubarak announced he would not contest the election due in September, but the demonstrations continued, and on 11 February Vice President Omar Suleiman announced his resignation and the transfer of power to the military. Mubarak was tried on charges of killing protesters, sentenced to life imprisonment in 2012, retried after an appeal, and acquitted by the Court of Cassation on 2 March 2017. He died on 25 February 2020 and was given a military funeral.
house-of-bourbon: The Bourbons began as a branch of the Capetian dynasty, the royal House of France. They date from 1272, when Robert, the youngest son of King Saint Louis IX of France, married the heiress of the lordship of Bourbon. The house then served for three centuries as a cadet branch under the Capetian and Valois kings. The senior line died out in the male line in 1527 with Duke Charles III of Bourbon, who died in the Sack of Rome. When Henry III of France died in 1589 the House of Valois became extinct in the male line, and under Salic law the head of the House of Bourbon became King of France as Henry IV.

Henry IV was raised a Calvinist and became nominal leader of the Huguenots in 1569. On 13 April 1598 he granted the Edict of Nantes, which made Catholicism the official religion but gave the Huguenots a measure of tolerance, ending the religious wars. Bourbon monarchs ruled France and Navarre until the monarchy was overthrown in 1792. Louis XIV succeeded his father at four, and Cardinal Mazarin ended the Thirty Years' War in 1648 and defeated the nobility in the Frondes. Louis XVI convened the Estates-General on 5 May 1789 and was executed in 1793.

Napoleon's abdication on 11 April 1814 restored the dynasty in the person of Louis XVIII, who was restored again after Waterloo. His brother Charles X reigned from 1824 until the July Revolution of 1830, and the cadet House of Orléans then ruled from 1830 to 1848.

In 1700 the Spanish Habsburgs died out in the male line, and Charles II of Spain willed the throne to Louis XIV's second grandson, the Duke of Anjou, who became Philip V. The Treaty of Utrecht of 1713 ratified his renunciation of the French throne and so separated the two crowns. Charles III, already king in Naples and Sicily, became king of Spain in 1759. Bourbons ruled Naples from 1734 to 1806, Sicily from 1735 to 1816 and the Two Sicilies from 1816 to 1861.

The Spanish branch has been overthrown and restored several times, reigning 1700 to 1808, 1813 to 1868, 1875 to 1931 and again from 1975. Since 1733 the Bourbons have been the only surviving legitimate branch of the House of Capet.
house-of-commons-of-the-united-kingdom: The House of Commons of England began to evolve in the 13th and 14th centuries; the first English parliament was called in 1236. In 1707, after the political union with Scotland, it became the House of Commons of Great Britain, with 45 Scottish members added. The Acts of Union 1800 added 100 Irish members at Westminster. In 1922, after the independence of the Irish Free State, it became the House of Commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

The chamber's shape comes from St Stephen's Chapel, which housed the Commons until a fire destroyed it in 1834. Benches face one another across the floor as the chapel's choir stalls did, an arrangement that favours adversarial debate.

The Commons went through important reform in the 19th century. Constituency boundaries had not changed since 1660, so declining towns still elected two members each. Among these rotten boroughs were Old Sarum, which had only six voters for two MPs, and Dunwich, largely lost to coastal erosion, while large cities such as Manchester had no separate representation.

In 1909 David Lloyd George, as Chancellor of the Exchequer, introduced the People's Budget, which proposed a new tax on wealthy landowners. The Conservative House of Lords rejected it. After a further election in December 1910 the government of H. H. Asquith secured a bill curbing the Lords, after threatening to create 500 new Liberal peers. Under the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949 the Lords' power to reject legislation was reduced to a delaying power.

The government is responsible solely to the Commons. The House does not formally elect the prime minister, but by convention the monarch appoints the person who commands its support, normally the leader of the largest party, and the prime minister holds office only while keeping the confidence of a majority. The House scrutinises ministers through committees and weekly Prime Minister's Questions.

At the start of each term the House elects one of its members as Speaker, whose election needs the Sovereign's approval as a formality. Its symbol is a portcullis topped by St Edward's Crown, a badge of the Tudors and a favourite of Henry VII.
house-of-hohenzollern: The family came from the area around Hechingen in Swabia in the late 11th century and took its name from Hohenzollern Castle, on an 855-metre mountain in the Swabian Alps. Its first ancestor mentioned is Burkhard I, Count of Zollern, who according to Berthold of Reichenau was born before 1025 and died in 1061. A founder named Tassilo, said to be a grandson of Charlemagne, was invented in 1560 by the historian Johann Basilius Herold, and his existence was disproved in the 19th century.

The Zollerns received the title of count from Emperor Henry V in 1111, and the county was called Hohenzollern from 1218. The family split into a Catholic Swabian branch and a Protestant Franconian branch, the latter founded by Conrad I, Burgrave of Nuremberg.

The Franconian Hohenzollerns supported Hohenstaufen and Habsburg rulers and were rewarded with territory, adding Ansbach in 1331 and Kulmbach in 1340. In 1411 Frederick VI, Burgrave of Nuremberg, was appointed governor of Brandenburg, and at the Council of Constance in 1415 King Sigismund made him Elector and Margrave as Frederick I; in 1417 he bought Brandenburg for 400,000 Hungarian guilders. In 1525 Albert of Prussia, last Grand Master of the Teutonic Knights, became the first Duke of Prussia as a fief of the King of Poland.

Brandenburg and Prussia were ruled together from 1618. John Sigismund turned from Lutheranism to Calvinism, taking communion in the Calvinist rite on 25 December 1613, but strong protest forced him in 1615 to give up forcing his subjects to follow, making Brandenburg-Prussia a bi-confessional state. In 1701 Frederick I took the title King in Prussia with the assent of Emperor Leopold I. In 1871 the German Empire was proclaimed, and William I, as German Emperor and King of Prussia, ruled it until the revolution that followed Germany's defeat in 1918 ended the German and Prussian monarchy.

The Swabian branch, founded by Frederick IV, Count of Zollern, ruled Hechingen, Sigmaringen and Haigerloch and became princes in 1623. Troops of the Swabian League destroyed Hohenzollern Castle in 1423. This branch ruled until 1849. In 1866 Prince Charles of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen became prince of Romania, and king as Carol I in 1881; his line reigned until 1947.

From a minor princely family the Franconian line became one of the most important dynasties of Europe by marriage and by purchasing neighbouring lands. In 1870 the candidacy of Leopold, Prince of Hohenzollern, for the Spanish throne, and Bismarck's altered Ems telegram, led to the Franco-Prussian War. Since 1949 Germany's Basic Law recognises no Hohenzollern claim to royal or imperial prerogatives. Hohenzollern Castle still belongs to the family.
house-of-medici: The Medici came from the agricultural Mugello region north of Florence and are first mentioned in a document of 1230. The origin of the name is uncertain; medici is the plural of the Italian word for doctors. Members of the family rose in the early 14th century in the wool trade, though they were far less notable than the Albizzi or the Strozzi. Involvement in a plot in 1400 banned all but two branches of the family from Florentine politics for twenty years.

In 1397 Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici founded the Medici Bank in Florence and became one of the city's richest men. He never held political office. The bank, which lasted until 1494, was the largest in Europe in the 15th century, and was among the earliest businesses to use double-entry bookkeeping.

Giovanni's son Cosimo the Elder was exiled by the Albizzi in 1433, but in 1434 a pro-Medici signoria was elected and he returned. Cosimo, his son Piero and his grandson Lorenzo dominated Florentine government through most of the 15th century without abolishing it, rarely holding official posts. When Lorenzo died in 1492 his son Piero proved unable to meet the French invasion, and within two years he and his supporters were exiled. The family returned in 1512, and Florence was in other hands again between 1527 and 1530.

The senior line ended with the assassination of Alessandro de' Medici, first Duke of Florence, in 1537; power passed to the junior branch, beginning with Cosimo I. The family held the title Duke of Florence from 1532 and the Grand Duchy of Tuscany from 1569. Two Medici popes, Leo X and Clement VII, ruled in the 16th century, and Catherine de' Medici and Marie de' Medici became queens of France.

Cosimo II is remembered as patron of Galileo Galilei, who dedicated his Sidereus Nuncius of 1610 to him. By 1705 the grand ducal treasury under Cosimo III was nearly bankrupt. The last Medici grand duke, Gian Gastone, died in 1737.

Their chief accomplishments were in sponsoring art and architecture. Giovanni di Bicci aided Masaccio and commissioned Filippo Brunelleschi to rebuild the Basilica of San Lorenzo in 1419. Cosimo the Elder's circle included Donatello and Fra Angelico, and Lorenzo invited the young Michelangelo to study the family's collection of antique sculpture and was patron to Leonardo da Vinci for seven years. Contemporaries and later writers disagreed about the family, some calling it corrupt, while Machiavelli's The Prince was in the end dedicated to Lorenzo di Piero de' Medici.
house-of-plantagenet: The house originated in the French county of Anjou. The later counts of Anjou descended from Geoffrey II, Count of Gâtinais, and his wife Ermengarde of Anjou, who in 1060 inherited the title through cognatic kinship from an Angevin family descended from a noble named Ingelger, whose recorded history dates from 870. Plantegenest was a twelfth-century nickname of Geoffrey, Count of Anjou and Duke of Normandy. One theory derives it from the blossom of the common broom, called genista in medieval Latin. In the fifteenth century Richard of York, 3rd Duke of York, adopted Plantagenet as his family name.

Henry II was born in 1133, and his grandfather Henry I is reported to have been delighted, calling the boy the heir to the kingdom. The first three Plantagenet kings, Henry II, Richard I and John, ruled extensive territories in France and are sometimes called the Angevins, though some historians use that term for the whole dynasty.

Henry's marriage to Eleanor, who had already had two daughters by her first husband, King Louis, produced eight children in thirteen years. When Richard I left no heir, a succession crisis arose between supporters of his nephew Arthur and of John. John won a significant victory at the Battle of Mirebeau, but he lost Anjou and most of his other French territories, which made England rather than France the centre of the realm. His son Henry III, king for most of the thirteenth century, faced baronial conflict that helped establish Parliament, and the kings were often forced to accept compromises such as Magna Carta.

Edward I enforced his claims in Britain, and the Statute of Rhuddlan established England's authority over Wales. In 1328 Charles IV of France died without a male heir, and Philip of Valois became king over Queen Isabella's claim on behalf of her son Edward III. By the end of Edward III's reign the dynasty had adopted Middle English as the language of governance. Richard II, who came to the throne as a boy, faced the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 after poll taxes were levied to pay for military campaigns.

After the deposition of Richard II in 1399, two cadet branches, Lancaster and York, ruled England. Henry V won a near total victory at Agincourt and secured the Treaty of Troyes, but his son Henry VI, who succeeded at nine months old, lost the Hundred Years' War. The rivalry of Lancaster and York brought about the Wars of the Roses, which ended at the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485, when Richard III died. Henry VII, a Lancastrian through his mother, then married Elizabeth of York, and the Tudor dynasty began.
house-of-romanov: The Romanovs share their origin with about two dozen other Russian noble families. Their earliest common ancestor is Andrei Kobyla, attested about 1347 as a boyar in the service of Simeon, prince of Moscow. Later genealogies gave him a distinguished pedigree, including descent from an Old Prussian prince, a legend contested by another version that derives the family from a boyar line of Novgorod. His descendants took the names Koshkin, Zakharin and Zakharin-Yuriev, and the grandchildren of Roman Yurievich Zakharyin-Yuriev took the name Romanov.

The family rose when Roman's daughter Anastasia Zakharyina married Ivan IV on 3 (13) February 1547 and was crowned the first tsaritsa of Russia. After Boris Godunov's party prevailed in 1598, he accused Feodor Nikitich Romanov of treason in 1600 and had the family deported to remote parts of the north and the Urals, where most died; Feodor was forced to become a monk with the name Filaret.

The Rurik dynasty ended with Feodor I in 1598, and the Time of Troubles followed. On 21 February 1613 the Zemsky Sobor elected Michael Romanov as tsar. His son Alexei succeeded him in 1645, and after Alexei's death in 1676 his children by two marriages struggled for the throne.

Peter I, who ruled from 1682 to 1725, proclaimed the Russian Empire in 1721 and, through wars and reforms, made Russia a major European power. The direct male line ended when Elizabeth died childless in 1762. Her nephew Peter III, of the House of Holstein-Gottorp, succeeded and kept his mother's house name, so later monarchs are sometimes called Holstein-Gottorp-Romanov. His wife overthrew him and reigned as Catherine the Great.

Her son Paul I issued the Pauline Laws, which set semi-Salic primogeniture and required the Orthodox faith. He was murdered in 1801. After Alexander I came Nicholas I in 1825, whose accession met the Decembrist revolt, and Alexander II, who freed the serfs in 1861. The February Revolution of 1917 led to Nicholas II's abdication on 15 March [O.S. 2 March] 1917, ending 304 years of Romanov rule.

After the abdication Nicholas II and his family were held at the Alexander Palace, sent to Tobolsk in August 1917 and moved to Yekaterinburg in April 1918. On the night of 16 to 18 July 1918 the Bolsheviks executed the entire family and several retainers. Of the house's 65 members, 47 survivors went into exile. In 1924 Grand Duke Kirill Vladimirovich claimed the headship of the defunct imperial house. Living descendants of other members of the imperial house remain.
house-of-savoy: The house was established in 1003 in the historical region of Savoy, which was originally part of the Kingdom of Burgundy and now lies mostly in south-eastern France. It descended from Humbert I, Count of Savoy, called Biancamano or White Hand, who ruled from 1003 to 1047 or 1048. His ancestry is uncertain, since contemporary documents do not mention his father. The family was traditionally believed to have come from Saxony, but more recent research points to the County of Vienne, where Humbert and his relatives held extensive possessions. Through marriages and diplomacy the family expanded its territory and influence, first as counts of a small Alpine county north-west of Italy.

Amadeus VIII was raised by the Holy Roman Emperor Sigismund to Duke of Savoy in 1416. In 1536 Francis I of France invaded Savoy and Piedmont and took Turin, and Duke Charles III fled to Vercelli. In April 1655, on perhaps false reports of resistance by the Protestant Waldensians to a plan to resettle them, Charles Emmanuel II ordered their general massacre, known as the Piedmontese Easter. It aroused indignation across Europe and prompted John Milton's sonnet On the Late Massacre in Piedmont.

The house gained the crown of Sicily, but in 1720 was forced to exchange it for the Kingdom of Sardinia after the War of the Quadruple Alliance. Charles Emmanuel III gained lands at the expense of the Austrian-controlled Duchy of Milan. In 1796 Napoleon beat Piedmont-Sardinia, and in 1798 French troops occupied Turin and forced Charles Emmanuel IV to abdicate. The kingdom was restored in 1814 and enlarged with the former Republic of Genoa by the Congress of Vienna.

By 1861 the House of Savoy, through its cadet branch Carignano, led the unification of Italy and ruled the Kingdom of Italy until 1946. Its Italian kings were Victor Emmanuel II, Umberto I, Victor Emmanuel III and Umberto II. Victor Emmanuel III appointed Mussolini prime minister on 28 October 1922, and his failure to move against the regime later led to much criticism. Umberto II reigned for only a few weeks before being deposed after the 1946 Italian institutional referendum, when the Italian Republic was proclaimed. The residences of the royal house in and around Turin are a World Heritage Site.
house-of-stuart: The house was originally spelled Stewart, from the office of High Steward of Scotland, first held by the family's progenitor Walter fitz Alan, around 1150. The family's probable ancestry goes back to Alan fitz Flaad, a Breton who went to England soon after the Norman Conquest and was rewarded by Henry I with lands in Shropshire. His son Walter followed David I of Scotland north after the civil war known as the Anarchy, received lands in Renfrewshire, and held the lordship of the High Steward for life; Malcolm IV later made the office hereditary.

The sixth High Steward, Walter Stewart, married Marjorie, daughter of Robert the Bruce. Their son Robert inherited the Scottish throne as Robert II when his uncle David II died childless in 1371. Mary, Queen of Scots, who was brought up in France, adopted the French spelling Stuart.

In 1503 James IV married Margaret Tudor, daughter of Henry VII, which brought the Stewarts into the line of descent to the English throne. When Elizabeth I of England died without issue in 1603, James VI of Scotland, the son of Mary, Queen of Scots, and Lord Darnley, became king of England and Ireland as James I. This was a personal union: the three kingdoms shared a monarch but kept separate governments, churches and institutions. It did not prevent the Bishops' Wars of 1639, part of the cycle of conflict that marked the reign of Charles I and culminated in the War of the Three Kingdoms.

The trial and execution of Charles I by the English Parliament in 1649 began eleven years of republican government, the English Interregnum. Charles II, whose mother was French, left no legitimate children. His brother James II, who had converted to Catholicism, was deposed by Parliament in favour of his Protestant daughters Mary II and Anne, after the birth of a son to be raised as a Catholic.

Neither daughter had a child who survived to adulthood, so after the death of Queen Anne in 1714 the crown passed to the House of Hanover under the Act of Settlement of 1701. Under the Acts of Union, which came into effect on 1 May 1707, Anne had become queen of Great Britain. The descendants of James II, known as Jacobites, long tried to regain the throne. The royal house became extinct with the death of Cardinal Henry Benedict Stuart, brother of Charles Edward Stuart, in 1807.
house-of-tudor: The Tudors descended from Ednyfed Fychan and the Welsh noble family of Penmynydd, and from Catherine of Valois. Owen Tudor abandoned the Welsh patronymic custom and took a fixed surname, choosing that of his grandfather, Tudur ap Goronwy. His son Edmund Tudor, half-brother of Henry VI, married Margaret Beaufort on 1 November 1455. Her line came from John Beaufort, born to John of Gaunt and his mistress Katherine Swynford before they married in 1396; the Beauforts were declared legitimate, but Henry IV's proclamation barred them from the throne.

The Tudor name itself was hardly used in the sixteenth century. Monarchs stressed continuity with the English and French royal families rather than their descent from a Welsh adventurer, and the surname was not used in official publications. When Richard III called his rival Henry Tudor, it was to stress his Welshness and unfitness to rule.

Henry VII took the throne by right of conquest after defeating Richard III at the Battle of Bosworth Field on 22 August 1485. On 18 January 1486 he married Elizabeth of York, daughter of Edward IV, which symbolically united Lancaster and York; the Tudor rose joined the red and white roses. He faced Yorkist risings, among them the one in support of Lambert Simnel, defeated at the Battle of Stoke Field in 1487, and Perkin Warbeck's landing in Cornwall in 1497, ending in Warbeck's execution in 1499.

Henry VIII succeeded on 22 April 1509 and married Catherine of Aragon, his brother Arthur's widow. The Tudors achieved the full union of England and Wales in 1542 and asserted English authority over Ireland. When Henry died on 28 January 1547 his nine-year-old son succeeded as Edward VI, and nobles struggled for influence during the regency. Edward named Lady Jane Grey as heir, but public support went to his half-sister Mary, and Jane was beheaded on 12 February 1554.

Mary I's planned marriage to Philip, son of Charles V, was unpopular and provoked Thomas Wyatt the Younger's rebellion; Mary lost Calais in 1558. Elizabeth I reigned for 44 years, the longest of the dynasty, after the short, troubled reigns of her siblings. She chose William Cecil as chief minister. On her death without children, James VI of Scotland succeeded her on 24 March 1603.

Royal succession, including marriage and the succession rights of women, and the English Reformation were the leading political themes of the period. The Tudor rose has been used as a royal badge by every English, and later British, monarch since Henry VII. The Scottish House of Stuart, which followed, descended from Henry VII's daughter Margaret, who married James IV of Scotland in 1503.
house-of-valois: The Valois descended from Charles, Count of Valois (1270-1325), the second surviving son of King Philip III of France. Philip IV left three sons, Louis, Philip and Charles, who each became king in turn and each died young without a surviving male heir. When Charles IV died in 1328 three candidates had a plausible claim: Philip, Count of Valois, the closest heir in the male line; Joan of Navarre, daughter of Louis X; and Edward III of England, son of Isabella of France. The French magnates rejected a claim passing through a woman and chose Philip of Valois as Philip VI. Joan received the Kingdom of Navarre.

Philip VI confiscated the Duchy of Aquitaine in 1337, and Edward III claimed the French throne himself, which helped launch the Hundred Years' War. The French were defeated at Crécy in 1346 and at Poitiers in 1356, where John II was captured.

Under Charles V they recovered most of their territory, leaving the English only Calais, Bordeaux and Bayonne by 1380. Charles VI's madness let rivalry between the dukes of Burgundy and Orléans grow into the Armagnac-Burgundian Civil War, and after Agincourt in 1415 the Treaty of Troyes made Henry V of England heir to the throne. Joan of Arc raised the siege of Orléans in 1429 and had Charles VII crowned at Reims. By 1453, after the English defeat at Castillon, only Calais remained to them.

Charles VII created France's first standing army since Roman times. Louis XI subdued the great nobles, who had formed the League of the Public Weal against him in 1465, by intrigue and diplomacy, and after Charles the Bold of Burgundy died in 1477 he seized the duchy of Burgundy. Charles VIII invaded Italy in 1494 to press an Angevin claim to Naples, beginning the Italian Wars, and died in 1498 without heirs, ending the senior line. His cousin Louis XII, then Francis I, who was captured at Pavia in 1525, and Henry II continued the wars, which ended with the Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis in 1559.

Henry II died in a jousting accident in 1559, and his sons Francis II, Charles IX and Henry III ruled through the French Wars of Religion, in which the House of Guise led the Catholic League against the Huguenots. The St Bartholomew's Day massacre took place in 1572. Henry III had the Duke of Guise assassinated, and was himself killed by an assassin in 1589. With his death the male line of the Valois was extinct after 261 years on the throne. Henry of Navarre, as head of the House of Bourbon, the senior surviving Capetian branch, became Henry IV. Junior Valois lines held Orléans, Anjou, Burgundy and Alençon.
howard-florey: Howard Walter Florey was born on 24 September 1898 in Malvern, a southern suburb of Adelaide, the only son of Joseph Florey, a bootmaker from Oxfordshire who had emigrated to South Australia. He graduated from the University of Adelaide and decided to pursue medical research, which required study overseas. Selected as South Australia's Rhodes Scholar, he began at the University of Oxford in January 1922, and later studied in the United States on a fellowship from the Rockefeller Foundation.

He held posts at the London Hospital, at the University of Cambridge and at the University of Sheffield, where he revitalised the pathology department. In 1935 he was appointed Professor of Pathology at the Sir William Dunn School of Pathology at Oxford and became a fellow of Lincoln College.

At the Dunn School Florey assembled a multidisciplinary staff. Ernst Chain, who had read Alexander Fleming's paper on the antibacterial effects of the Penicillium notatum mould while studying the enzyme lysozyme, joined him in a large project on antibacterial substances made by micro-organisms. Fleming first observed the antibiotic properties of the mould, but it was Chain and Florey who developed penicillin into a useful treatment, with crucial technical contributions from Heatley. They developed techniques for growing, purifying and manufacturing the drug and tested it on animals.

In 1941 they used it to treat a police constable from Oxford, who began to recover but died because not enough penicillin could then be made. Commercial production from a pilot plant of Imperial Chemical Industries became available in January 1942, and later trials in Britain, the United States and North Africa were highly successful. Florey went to North Africa in 1943 and to the Soviet Union in 1944, and was knighted in June 1944. He shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1945 with Chain and Fleming.

After the war Florey's team studied further antibiotic substances, and he took part in founding the Australian National University and its John Curtin School of Medical Research in Canberra. He was elected a fellow of the Royal Society in 1941 and served as its president from 1960 to 1965. In 1962 he became provost of The Queen's College, Oxford, and from 1965 until his death on 21 February 1968 he was chancellor of the Australian National University. His discoveries are estimated to have saved over 80 million lives.
hua-guofeng: Hua Guofeng was born Su Zhu on 16 February 1921 in Jiaocheng, Shanxi, the fourth son of a family from Fan County in Henan, and lost his father at the age of seven. He joined the Chinese Communist Party in 1938, during the Second Sino-Japanese War, and took the name Hua Guofeng from the title of a patriotic vanguard organisation. In 1948 he went with the People's Liberation Army to Hunan, where he stayed until 1971. In 1952 he became secretary of the Xiangtan Special District, which included Mao Zedong's hometown of Shaoshan, and built a memorial hall dedicated to Mao there.

Hua supported the Cultural Revolution and led it in Hunan, becoming chairman of the provincial Revolutionary Committee and first secretary of the party's Hunan committee in December 1970. In 1973 he joined the Politburo, and Mao named him Minister of Public Security and vice premier. After Zhou Enlai died on 8 January 1976 Mao made him acting premier, passing over Zhang Chunqiao, and after the Tiananmen Incident of 1976 he became first vice chairman of the party and premier.

Mao died on 9 September 1976. With Marshal Ye Jianying and the security chief Wang Dongxing, Hua decided to use force, and the Gang of Four were arrested on 6 October. The next day he was appointed chairman of the party and of the Central Military Commission, the first to hold the offices of party leader, premier and commander-in-chief together. He ended the constant ideological campaigns and rehabilitated more than 4,600 disgraced cadres, and in 1977 the first national college entrance examination since the Cultural Revolution was authorised. He held to a command economy and a ten-year plan of heavy industry and imported technology, soon scrapped for a cheaper five-year plan. His slogan, the Two Whatevers, committed the leadership to follow whatever Mao had decided.

Deng Xiaoping and his allies forced Hua from power between December 1978 and June 1981; Zhao Ziyang replaced him as premier in September 1980, and Hu Yaobang as chairman. The Historical Resolution of 27 June 1981 said that he had removed the Gang of Four but then committed serious errors. He remained a member of the Central Committee until 2002 and died in Beijing on 20 August 2008.

His legacy is often reduced to the Two Whatevers, though Isabella Weber argues that this is overemphasised, and Andrew B. Kennedy calls him essentially a pragmatic problem solver. His break with Cultural Revolution economic policy and the opening of China's first Special Economic Zone are seen as paving the way for the reform and opening up led by Deng. His ousting also set a precedent in which disgraced party members were stripped of posts but not jailed.
hubei: Hubei borders Henan to the north, Anhui and Jiangxi to the east, Hunan to the south, and Chongqing and Shaanxi to the west. Its name means 'north of the lake', referring to Dongting Lake. The Jianghan Plain takes up most of central and southern Hubei, while the west is mountainous. The Yangtze enters from the west through the Three Gorges and the Han River from the northwest, and the two meet at the centre of Wuhan. Thousands of lakes give the province the name Province of Lakes.

The region was home to sophisticated Neolithic cultures. By the Spring and Autumn period it formed part of the powerful State of Chu, which blended northern and southern culture and controlled much of the middle and lower Yangtze. In the Warring States period Chu lost land to Qin, and in 278 BCE it lost its heartland, which corresponds to modern Hubei. The Han dynasty set up the province of Jingzhou in what is now Hubei and Hunan. After the death of the warlord Liu Biao in 208, Liu Bei and Sun Quan drove Cao Cao out of Jingzhou at the Battle of Red Cliffs, and the Wu kingdom then held it for decades.

The Song reunified the region in 982, the Mongols conquered it in 1279 and created the province of Huguang, and the Qing split it into Hubei and Hunan after 1644. Zhang Zhidong, Viceroy of Huguang from 1889 to 1907, made Wuhan a prosperous centre of commerce and industry. The Wuchang Uprising of 1911 in Wuhan began the Xinhai Revolution that overthrew the Qing dynasty. In 1927 Wuhan became the seat of a left-wing Kuomintang government led by Wang Jingwei, and in the Second World War Japan occupied eastern Hubei.

The province suffered severely from the Yangtze floods of 1954, and large dams followed: the Gezhouba Dam near Yichang was built from 1970 to 1988, and work on the Three Gorges Dam began in 1993. Authorities resettled millions of people from western Hubei to make way for it.

Hubei is a province of Central China with its capital at Wuhan, a major political, cultural and economic hub. The Huazhong University of Science and Technology and Wuhan University are among its institutions. The Wudang Mountains building complex has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1994, and the Hubei Provincial Museum in Wuhan is regarded as one of the best places to learn about the ancient state of Chu.
hudson-bay: Hudson Bay is a body of saltwater of about 1,230,000 square kilometres, about 1,370 kilometres long and 1,050 kilometres wide. It is shallow, with an average depth of about 100 metres, and lies north of Ontario, west of Quebec and south-east of Nunavut. Its southern arm is James Bay, and the Hudson Strait links it to the Labrador Sea. Its water is less salty than the ocean's, and it is largely frozen from mid-December to mid-June. The Eastern Cree call it Wînipekw or Wînipâkw, meaning muddy or brackish water.

The bay is named after Henry Hudson, an Englishman sailing for the Dutch East India Company, who explored it from 2 August 1610 on the Discovery. The ship was trapped in ice over the winter, and on 22 June 1611 the crew mutinied and left Hudson and others adrift in a small boat. Their fate is unknown. In 1668 the ship Nonsuch reached the bay and traded for beaver pelts, which led to the Hudson's Bay Company. In 1670 the English Crown granted it a charter and a trading monopoly over the drainage basin, known as Rupert's Land.

France contested the grant with several military expeditions but gave up its claim in the Treaty of Utrecht, signed on 11 April 1713. The company built forts and trading posts at the mouths of the major rivers, among them York Factory, Fort Severn and the Prince of Wales Fort, where Indigenous peoples brought furs. The monopoly ended in 1870, when the Deed of Surrender ceded Rupert's Land to Canada as part of the Northwest Territories. Churchill, Manitoba, became a deep-sea port for wheat exports in 1929.

The bay is politically entirely part of Nunavut, as are its islands. Its coast is very sparsely populated, with only about a dozen communities, many of them now almost wholly Cree and Inuit. Churchill holds the only deep-water port on the bay. The western shore is the Hudson Bay Lowlands, Canada's largest continuous peatland.
hudson-river: The Hudson rises at Henderson Lake in the Adirondack Mountains, though the nearby Lake Tear of the Clouds is more commonly named as its source. It flows south largely through eastern New York to New York Bay and the Atlantic, and marks the border between New York and New Jersey. The lower half is a tidal estuary occupying the Hudson Fjord, an inlet carved by glaciers, and the tide reaches as far north as the Federal Dam at Troy.

Before Europeans arrived the river ran through the homelands of the Munsee Lenape, the Mohican and the Mohawk. The Mohicans called it Mahicannittuk, the river that flows two ways, a name that refers to its tides. Giovanni da Verrazzano, sailing for Francis I of France, entered New York Harbor in 1524 but left without sailing up the river. Henry Hudson, an Englishman employed by the Dutch East India Company, explored it in 1609 and gave it his name. The Dutch called it the North River, and it formed the spine of the colony of New Netherland. As the gateway to the interior of America, it was the subject of years of competition between the English and the Dutch.

In the American Revolutionary War the British saw that the river would let their navy control the water route from Montreal to New York City. General John Burgoyne planned the Saratoga campaign to control it and cut New England off from the other colonies, and many battles were fought along it. The Erie Canal, completed in 1825, linked Albany on the Hudson to Buffalo on Lake Erie, joining New York to the Great Lakes and becoming a route for western settlers. The valley inspired Washington Irving and the Hudson River School of landscape painting.

The river is navigable by large steamers up to Troy and by ocean-going vessels to the Port of Albany. A 30-mile stretch on the east bank is the Hudson River Historic District, a National Historic Landmark, and the river was designated an American Heritage River in 1997. Landmarks along it include the home and presidential library of Franklin D. Roosevelt and the United States Military Academy. Industrial contamination grew sharply in the mid-twentieth century, but water quality has improved since the Clean Water Act of 1972.
hue: The Perfume River passes through the centre of Huế, which lies roughly in the middle of Vietnam on the transition between the north central and south central regions. The area includes the Tam Giang–Cau Hai lagoon, 68 km long, and has about 128 km of coastline. Mountains line its western and south-western borders, and the climate is tropical monsoon, with most rain falling from September to December.

The oldest ruins in the area belong to the kingdom of Lâm Ấp and date to the 4th century CE. The region, called Thuận Hóa, was ceded by Champa to Đại Việt in 1306: the Cham king Chế Mân gave two prefectures in exchange for marriage with a Vietnamese princess, Huyền Trân.

In the 16th century Nguyễn Hoàng asked to govern Thuận Hóa, then the southernmost region of Vietnam. After he pacified it, he and his heir Nguyễn Phúc Nguyên made it loyal to the Nguyễn family and rose against the Trịnh lords, and Vietnam divided between two ruling clans. The Nguyễn lords moved their palace to Kim Long in 1636 and based themselves at Phú Xuân, the future Huế, in 1687. The Trịnh captured it in 1775, and the Tây Sơn, whose rebellion had broken out in 1771, defeated the Trịnh garrison in 1786 and took Phú Xuân.

Nguyễn Ánh, a successor of the Nguyễn lords, recaptured Phú Xuân and unified the country. He rebuilt the citadel entirely and, as Emperor Gia Long, made Huế the national capital. After the French conquest Phú Xuân was officially renamed Huế in 1899, and the city remained capital of Annam within French Indochina. The imperial court stayed there until Emperor Bảo Đại abdicated in 1945.

Huế became a centrally governed city of Vietnam in 2025, when it was merged with the rest of Thừa Thiên Huế province. Its complex of imperial palaces, tombs and temples is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, including the Imperial City and the Forbidden Purple City, once the emperor's home. The tombs of emperors such as Minh Mạng, Khải Định and Tự Đức lie along the Perfume River, and the Thiên Mụ Temple, the largest pagoda in the city, is its official symbol.
huelva: Huelva lies in the south-west of the Iberian Peninsula on the Gulf of Cádiz, facing the Atlantic. It stands on the estuary formed where the Odiel and Tinto rivers meet, between the two rivers. In ancient times the estuary was rather wide, and it has progressively silted up.

Historians long held that Huelva began as a native Tartessian settlement. Finds of Phoenician material at the Méndez Núñez-Las Monjas site led to the Phoenician chronology being reassessed, and the evidence now favours seeing Huelva as a very early Phoenician colony, founded roughly in the 9th century BCE, though a 10th-century date has also been argued. The Phoenicians called it ʿunʿu baʿl, 'Baal's fort', which Greek texts corrupted to Onoba. The outpost exported silver, copper, purple dye and salted fish and was a node on routes linking the Atlantic and the Mediterranean. The Tartessian world entered a crisis in the 6th century BCE, and the town passed slowly to the Turdetani.

Under Rome it was Onoba or Onuba and had a mint. Musa ibn Nusayr's troops seized it by April 712, and its name became Walba. It was a short-lived independent taifa from 1012 to 1051, was then annexed by Seville and was occupied by the Almoravids in 1091. Alfonso X of Castile took it in 1262.

Huelva was a leading fishing town of Andalusia in the 16th century, became a provincial capital in 1833 and a city by royal decree on 17 September 1876. Mining by Rio Tinto, the main company from about 1873, sent copper and pyrite to its port. On 4 February 1888 soldiers fired on demonstrators against ore-smelting pollution at Rio Tinto, and historians estimate 100 to 200 deaths.

Huelva is the capital of its province in Andalusia, with a population of 149,410 at the 2010 census. Its port still handles copper and pyrite from mines inland. Recreativo de Huelva, founded in 1889 by workers of Rio Tinto, is the oldest football club in Spain, and the Fiestas Colombinas honour Christopher Columbus's departure from the port on 3 August 1492.
huesca: Huesca lies on a plateau in northern Aragon at an elevation of 488 metres, close to the Sierra de Guara, which reaches 2,077 metres. It is the capital of the Spanish province of the same name and one of the smallest provincial capitals in Spain, 71 kilometres from Zaragoza. Its coat of arms carries a block with a V-shaped notch, commonly said to represent the Salto de Roldán, or Roland's Leap, a rock formation about 25 kilometres to the north.

The city dates from before the Roman period, when it was called Bolskan in the Iberian language. As Osca it became a Roman colony under Quintus Sertorius, who made it his base. It minted its own coinage and had a school, founded by Sertorius, where young Iberians were taught Latin and Roman customs. Augustus made it a municipium in 30 BCE. The Arabs conquered the city in the late 8th century and called it Washqah. Part of the Upper March of the Emirate of Córdoba, it was repeatedly troubled by rebellion as the Banu Qasi, Banu Amrus and Banu al-Tawil clans and the Arista dynasty of Pamplona struggled for control. In 1018 it became part of the Taifa of Zaragoza.

In 1094 Sancho Ramírez built the Castle of Montearagón nearby in order to besiege the city, but was killed by a stray arrow as he reached its walls. Peter I of Aragon conquered it in 1096 and moved the royal capital there from Jaca. Peter IV of Aragon founded the University of Huesca in 1354; it was abolished in 1845. Huesca had one of the most important Jewish communities in Aragon, which flourished until the expulsion of 1492. During the Spanish Civil War the city was held by the Nationalists and besieged by the Republicans, among them George Orwell, but did not fall.

Huesca had 52,059 inhabitants in 2009, almost a quarter of the province's population. Its Gothic cathedral was begun by James I of Aragon around 1273, on the foundations of a mosque. The Abbey of San Pedro el Viejo, built between 1100 and 1241, is one of the oldest Romanesque structures in the Iberian Peninsula. The city celebrates the Fiestas de San Lorenzo from 9 to 15 August, in honour of Saint Lawrence, a native of Huesca martyred in 268 CE.
hugh-capet: Hugh was the son of Hugh the Great, Duke of the Franks, and Hedwige of Saxony, daughter of the German king Henry the Fowler. Through his mother he was a nephew of Otto I, and through his paternal grandmother he descended from Charlemagne. His family, the Robertians, were powerful landowners in the Île-de-France, and two of them, Odo I and Robert I, had been chosen as kings in place of Carolingians. When his father died in 956 Hugh, the eldest son, was about fifteen, and his neighbours took advantage: Theobald I of Blois took Chartres and Châteaudun.

In 960 King Lothair agreed that Hugh should have his father's margraviate of Neustria and the title Duke of the Franks. In 978, when Otto II invaded France and besieged Lothair in Paris, a relief army under Hugh helped force him to lift the siege on 30 November, and Otto's rearguard was destroyed crossing the flooded Aisne. The victory restored Hugh's position as the first noble of the kingdom.

Lothair's son Louis V died in a riding accident while hunting in the forest of Senlis on 22 May 987, leaving no children. Charles, Duke of Lower Lorraine, a Carolingian claimant, was accused of having made himself a vassal of the emperor. Adalberon, Archbishop of Reims, argued that the throne was not acquired by hereditary right. Hugh was crowned rex Francorum at Noyon on 1 June and again in Paris on 3 July 987, and he had his son Robert crowned on 25 December that year.

Charles of Lorraine took Laon, and Hugh and Robert twice besieged it without success. Adalberon, Bishop of Laon, then seized Charles in his sleep and delivered him to Hugh, who imprisoned him at Orléans until his death. Hugh's power was narrow. He held towns and estates between Paris and Orléans of about 400 square miles, and a plot of 993 to hand him to Otto III went unpunished, which shows how tenuous his hold was. He had to seek military aid from Richard I of Normandy, though his unanimous election gave him moral authority.

Hugh died on 24 October 996 and was buried at the Basilica of Saint-Denis. His son Robert continued to reign, and the direct Capetians ruled France from 987 to 1328, with cadet branches after that until 1848.
hugo-chavez: Hugo Rafael Chávez Frías was born on 28 July 1954 in the rural village of Sabaneta, in Barinas State, in his paternal grandmother's three-room house. His family was of Amerindian, Afro-Venezuelan, Spanish and Italian descent, and his parents were schoolteachers. At 17 he entered the Venezuelan Academy of Military Sciences in Caracas, where a curriculum known as the Andrés Bello Plan brought in civilian professors to teach the cadets. He served as a communications officer in a counterinsurgency unit and, after fighting a Marxist–Hoxhaist insurgency in Anzoátegui in 1977, began to doubt the army.

Chávez formed a secret cell within the military, later the Revolutionary Bolivarian Movement-200 (MBR-200), inspired by Simón Bolívar, Simón Rodríguez and Ezequiel Zamora. Dissatisfied with a political system based on the Puntofijo Pact, he led it in an unsuccessful coup against President Carlos Andrés Pérez in 1992 and was imprisoned. President Rafael Caldera freed him in 1994. He then founded the Fifth Republic Movement and won the 1998 presidential election with 56.2 per cent of the vote. He took office on 2 February 1999 and was re-elected in 2000, 2006 and 2012.

With the high oil revenues of the 2000s his government nationalised key industries, created Communal Councils and ran the Bolivarian missions to widen access to food, housing, healthcare and education. Poverty and inequality fell between about 2003 and 2007, though structural inequalities remained. Critics point to his packing of the Supreme Court, pressure on the media and rising murder and kidnapping rates. Deficit spending and price controls later proved unsustainable, and shortages and inflation grew.

In June 2011 Chávez announced from Havana that he had had operations, including the removal of a tumour with cancerous cells. He won a fourth election on 7 October 2012, but his inauguration was cancelled because of his treatment, and he died in Caracas on 5 March 2013, aged 58. His ideas form the basis of Chavismo, close to Bolivarianism. He supported regional bodies such as the Union of South American Nations and the television network TeleSUR, and he is regarded across the political spectrum as one of the most influential and controversial figures in the modern history of Venezuela and Latin America.
hugo-grotius: Hugo Grotius, also called Hugo de Groot, was born in Delft on 10 April 1583, during the Dutch Revolt, into a patrician family. His father, who had studied with Justus Lipsius, translated Archimedes and gave his son a humanist education. Grotius entered Leiden University at eleven, and at sixteen published an edition of Martianus Capella's work on the seven liberal arts, which remained a reference for centuries. In 1603 his cousin Captain Jacob van Heemskerk captured the Portuguese carrack Santa Catarina off present-day Singapore, and the Company he served asked Grotius to defend the seizure. His treatise of 1604 to 1605, later called De Jure Praedae, grounded it in natural justice and was not published in full in his lifetime.

Grotius advanced as an associate of Johan van Oldenbarnevelt, becoming Pensionary of Rotterdam in 1613. A theological dispute between the followers of Jacobus Arminius, the Remonstrants, and the strongly Calvinist followers of Franciscus Gomarus divided the Republic. Grotius drafted for the States of Holland an edict of toleration, which held that only the tenets needed for civil order should be enforced. When Maurice of Nassau moved against Oldenbarnevelt, Grotius was imprisoned at Loevestein Castle. He escaped hidden in a chest of books and fled to Paris.

In France, where he lived almost continuously from 1621 to 1644, he published in 1625 De jure belli ac pacis, On the Law of War and Peace, dedicated to Louis XIII. Begun in prison, it was an effort to restrain conflict on the basis of a broad moral consensus. In 1634 Sweden named him ambassador to France, a post he kept for ten years.

In the summer of 1645 he left Sweden, was shipwrecked and washed up near Rostock ill, and died there on 28 August 1645. His body was laid in the Nieuwe Kerk in Delft. His thought on natural law influenced Samuel Pufendorf and John Locke, and along with the earlier works of Francisco de Vitoria and Alberico Gentili his writings laid foundations for international law. His influence declined with the rise of positivism, but revived after the First World War.
huguenots: The term Huguenot was in common use by around 1550 and was originally a term of derision whose source is unclear. One hypothesis links it to Besançon Hugues, a burgomaster who defended Geneva against Catholic Savoy. The Huguenots called themselves reformés. Their numbers grew rapidly between 1555 and 1561, chiefly among nobles and city dwellers, and they held their first national synod in Paris in 1558. They were concentrated in the south and west of France, whereas the Protestants of Alsace, Moselle and Montbéliard were mainly Lutherans.

Eight civil wars between 1562 and 1598 took on a dynastic character, as a feud between the Houses of Bourbon and Guise. The Huguenots were led by Jeanne d'Albret, her son, the future Henry IV, and the princes of Condé. On the eve of the St Bartholomew's Day massacre of 1572 the community made up as much as 10 per cent of the French population. Catholics killed thousands of Huguenots in Paris between 24 August and 3 October 1572, and similar massacres followed in Aix, Bordeaux, Lyon, Rouen, Toulouse and other towns. Henry IV, who had converted to Catholicism to gain the crown, issued the Edict of Nantes in 1598, giving Protestants equality under the crown and a degree of religious and political freedom.

Rebellions in the 1620s cost the Huguenots their political and military privileges. Louis XIV first sent missionaries, then closed Huguenot schools, excluded them from favoured professions and billeted troops in their homes in the dragonnades. In 1685 the Edict of Fontainebleau revoked the Edict of Nantes and made Protestantism illegal. Some converted, others emigrated, chiefly to the Dutch Republic, England, Brandenburg-Prussia and Switzerland. Persecution ended officially with the Edict of Versailles in 1787, and the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen of 1789 gave Protestants equal rights.

The exodus drained France of people who had held important places in society, and the kingdom did not fully recover for years. In England some 40,000 to 50,000 settled, and they founded the silk industry there. In Brandenburg-Prussia, Frederick William granted them privileges by the Edict of Potsdam of 1685. In South Africa many Afrikaners bear French surnames. In 2013 the Reformed Church of France merged with the Evangelical Lutheran Church to form the United Protestant Church of France. In 1985 President François Mitterrand announced a formal apology to the descendants of the Huguenots.
hulagu-khan: Hulagu, also written Hulegu or Hülegü, was born around 1217 to Tolui, a son of Genghis Khan, and Sorghaghtani Beki, an influential Keraite princess. He was a brother of Möngke Khan, Kublai Khan and Ariq Böke. Little is known of his childhood. His mother, a Christian of the Church of the East, arranged for all her sons to become Mongol leaders, and Hulagu was friendly to Christianity; his favourite wife, Doquz Khatun, and his closest friend and general, Kitbuqa, were also Christians.

Möngke, installed as Great Khan in 1251, charged Hulagu with conquering or destroying the remaining Muslim states of south-western Asia, including the Abbasid Caliphate. Two-tenths of the empire's fighting men were gathered for his army in 1253. The Lurs were destroyed and the Assassins surrendered their fortress of Alamut in early 1256. He chose Azerbaijan as his base.

The army set out for Baghdad in November 1257, and the Mongols laid siege on 29 January 1258. The city surrendered on 10 February, and the Mongols entered on 13 February and began a week of destruction, including that of the Grand Library. Death counts vary widely, from a low estimate of about 90,000 to a million. In 1260 the Mongols took Aleppo and Damascus, but Hulagu then withdrew most of his force and left for Mongolia over the succession after Möngke's death. At the Battle of Ain Jalut in 1260 the Mamluks of Qutuz and Baybars destroyed the Mongol force left behind.

After Kublai became Great Khan, Hulagu returned to his lands by 1262. He was drawn into war with Berke Khan of the Golden Horde, a Muslim convert who had allied with the Mamluks, and suffered a severe defeat north of the Caucasus in 1263. He sent letters to Europe seeking an alliance, among them one of 10 April 1262 to Louis IX of France, but never gained one. He fell ill in January 1265 and died on 8 February 1265; he was buried on Shahi Island in Lake Urmia, and his tomb has never been found.

He founded the Ilkhanate. He employed Shams al-Din Juvayni as sahib-divan, while Ata-Malik Juvayni governed Baghdad and helped repair it, and he patronised Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, for whom the Maragheh observatory was built.
huldrych-zwingli: Zwingli was born on 1 January 1484 at Wildhaus in the Toggenburg valley, the third of eleven children in a farming family. His father Ulrich was the chief local magistrate. At ten he was sent to Basel for secondary schooling. He studied at the University of Vienna and then at Basel, where he received his Master of Arts in 1506. He served as a pastor in Glarus and later in Einsiedeln, and the writings of Erasmus influenced him.

On 1 January 1519 Zwingli gave his first sermon as people's priest of the Grossmünster in Zurich. Instead of preaching on the Sunday's set Gospel, he read through Matthew verse by verse, and went on through the rest of the New Testament and the Old. In Lent 1522 he and about a dozen others ate sausages in breach of the fast, and the Affair of the Sausages is considered the start of the Reformation in Switzerland. After the first Zurich disputation, on 29 January 1523, the city council allowed him to go on preaching. Zurich severed its ties with the bishop of Constance in 1524 and replaced the Mass with a new communion liturgy in 1525.

Zwingli clashed with the Anabaptists, and after a public debate on 17 January 1525 the council ordered those who refused to have their children baptised to leave Zurich. A Christian Civic Union of Reformed cities was formed in 1528. At the Marburg Colloquy in 1529 he and Martin Luther agreed on many points but not on the Real Presence in the Eucharist, which Zwingli took to be symbolic.

In 1531 the Reformed alliance's food blockade of the Catholic cantons failed. The cantons attacked when Zurich was ill-prepared, and Zwingli died on the battlefield on 11 October 1531. The Zurich council chose Heinrich Bullinger as his successor, who defended him as a prophet and martyr and consolidated his reforms. Zwingli's legacy lives on in the confessions, liturgy and church orders of the Reformed churches.
humayun: Humayun was born Nasir al-Din Muhammad on 6 March 1508, the son of Babur and his favourite wife Māham Begum. On 26 December 1530 he succeeded his father at 22, an inexperienced ruler. His half-brother Kamran Mirza inherited Kabul and Kandahar, and the two became bitter rivals. Babur had divided his lands between sons, a Central Asian practice since Genghis Khan, and not all nobles saw Humayun as the rightful successor.

Humayun's first campaign was against Sher Shah Suri in Bihar, but he broke it off to annex Gujarat, Malwa and the fort of Mandu. While he was there, Sher Shah invaded Bengal and besieged its capital Gaur, and its wealth gave him a war chest. At the battle of Kannauj on 17 May 1540 Humayun was soundly defeated and retreated to Lahore. Kamran offered to join Sher Shah against him, but Humayun refused to kill his brother, citing Babur's last words: do nothing against your brothers, even though they may deserve it.

He withdrew across the Thar Desert, where his wife Hamida Bano, eight months pregnant, was left without a horse; he later called it the lowest point of his life. He crossed the Indus on 11 July 1543 and fled with a small party to the Safavid Shah Tahmasp I, who received him as a royal guest at Herat. With 14,000 Persian soldiers he besieged Kandahar from 21 March 1545 and entered Kabul on 18 November 1545. At the Battle of Sirhind on 22 June 1555 his general Bairam Khan decisively defeated Sikandar Shah Suri, and the Mughal Empire was re-established.

On 24 January 1556 Humayun was descending the staircase of his library, Sher Mandal, with his arms full of books when the muezzin called the prayer. Trying to kneel, he caught his foot in his robe, fell several steps and struck his temple on a stone edge. He died three days later.

He was buried at last in Humayun's Tomb in Delhi, commissioned by his chief wife Bega Begum, the first very grand garden tomb of Mughal architecture, which set the precedent for the Taj Mahal. His return from Persia brought Persian noblemen to the Mughal court and changed its culture, and he left a substantial legacy to his son Akbar.
humayuns-tomb: Humayun died on 27 January 1556. His body was first buried in his palace in the Purana Quila at Delhi, then taken to Sirhind in Punjab by Khanjar Beg. His widow and chief consort, Bega Begum, devoted herself to building a memorial that would be the grandest mausoleum in the Mughal empire. According to the Ain-i-Akbari she supervised the work after returning from the Hajj. Construction began in 1565 and ended in 1572, and the whole cost of 1.5 million rupees was paid by her. The emperor Akbar visited the tomb in 1571, when it was nearly complete.

The site beside the Yamuna was chosen for its nearness to the Nizamuddin Dargah, the shrine of the Sufi saint Nizamuddin Auliya, whom the rulers of Delhi revered. Abd al-Qadir Bada'uni, one of the few contemporary historians to mention the building, says the Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas, whom the empress chose and brought from Herat, designed it. His son Sayyid Muhammad completed it.

The tomb is built of rubble masonry and red sandstone, clad in white marble, which is also used for the floors, lattice screens, door frames, eaves and the main dome. It stands on a vaulted terrace eight metres high and is essentially square, with chamfered corners that make it look octagonal. A high rubble wall encloses the complex, entered through two double-storeyed gateways 16 metres high. The terrace holds fifty-six cells with over 100 graves.

It stands at the centre of a 30-acre charbagh, a Persian-style garden divided into four squares by paved walkways and two crossing water channels that recall the four rivers of paradise. Each square is divided again into smaller gardens, 32 in all. It was the first such garden on this scale in South Asia, and the first structure to use red sandstone on such a scale. The tomb was modelled on Gur-e Amir, the tomb of Timur at Samarkand.

The tomb marked a leap in Mughal architecture and set a precedent for later royal mausolea, which reached their height in the Taj Mahal at Agra. Beside Humayun it holds the graves of Bega Begum, Dara Shikoh and several later Mughals, among them Jahandar Shah, Farrukhsiyar and Alamgir II. When William Finch visited in 1611 he described the central chamber richly furnished with carpets.

The last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, took refuge here with three princes during the Indian Rebellion of 1857, and was captured by Captain Hodson and exiled to Rangoon. The tomb became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993. The Aga Khan Trust for Culture and the Archaeological Survey of India restored the gardens and water channels between about 1999 and 2003.
humboldt-university-of-berlin: The university arose during the Prussian Reform Movement on the initiative of the philosopher and linguist Wilhelm von Humboldt, with Johann Gottlieb Fichte and Friedrich Schleiermacher, under King Frederick William III. It was housed in the palace built for Prince Henry of Prussia, brother of Frederick the Great, on Unter den Linden. Humboldt met great resistance and submitted his resignation to the King in April 1810, so he was absent when it opened.

The first students were admitted on 6 October 1810 and the first semester began on 10 October, with 256 students and 52 lecturers in faculties of law, medicine, theology and philosophy. The university keeps 15 October 1810 as its opening date. It set up the world's first academic chair in history. From 1828 to 1945 it was named the Royal Friedrich Wilhelm University of Berlin.

In the 19th century the university grew to take in many new disciplines, and modern research facilities aided the natural sciences. Researchers such as the physicist Hermann von Helmholtz and the physicians Rudolf Virchow and Robert Koch built its fame. It absorbed other Berlin colleges, among them the Charité, which became its medical campus by 1829. Its principle of uniting teaching and research served as a model elsewhere, for institutions such as Johns Hopkins University.

After 1933 the Nazi regime affected the university like all German universities. Under the Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service, 250 Jewish professors and employees were dismissed in 1933-1934, and nearly a third of the staff was fired in all. On 10 May 1933 some 20,000 books were taken from libraries to be burned in the Opernplatz, now Bebelplatz.

After the Second World War the university lay in East Berlin and reopened in 1946 under the Soviet Military Administration, which required lectures to be approved by Socialist Unity Party officials. The Free University of Berlin was founded in West Berlin in 1948. Because the old name had monarchic origins, the university was renamed in 1949 after the brothers Alexander and Wilhelm von Humboldt.

After German reunification it was restructured by commissions led by West German professors. Alumni and faculty include Hegel, Karl Marx, Friedrich Engels, Otto von Bismarck, W. E. B. Du Bois, Albert Einstein, Max Planck and the Brothers Grimm.
hunan: Hunan lies on the south bank of the Yangtze River, about halfway along its length, and its name means south of the lake, the lake being Dongting. Mountains and hills cover more than 80 per cent of the province. The Wuling, Xuefeng, Nanling and Luoxiao ranges enclose it on the west, south and east, and the Xiang, Zi, Yuan and Li rivers converge on Lake Dongting in the north. The lake and the Xiaoxiang area figure prominently in Chinese poetry and painting, particularly in the Song dynasty, when they were associated with officials who had been unjustly dismissed. The area was under Chinese rule as far back as 350 BCE.

The forests were first occupied by the ancestors of the Miao, Tujia, Dong and Yao peoples. After Qin conquered Chu in 278 BCE the region came under Qin, and under the Han it formed the Changsha Kingdom. For hundreds of years Han Chinese settlers came from the north, displacing and assimilating the original inhabitants, clearing forests and farming rice in the valleys and plains. Migration was especially heavy when the north was ruled by non-Han groups and in disorder. In the Tang dynasty Changsha was a ceramics district, mass-producing tea bowls and ewers for export; the Belitung Shipwreck, an Arab dhow dated to the 830s, carried more than 60,000 pieces of such wares.

During the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period Hunan had its own independent regime, Ma Chu. Under the Yuan it was joined with Hubei in the province of Huguang, and the Red Turban Rebellions first rose up in Hunan in the 14th century. Hunan province was created in 1664 from Huguang and renamed in 1723. The Yuelu Academy at Changsha made it a centre of Confucian learning, and its grain surpluses fed many parts of China. By the 19th century it was overcrowded and prone to uprisings, among them the Miao Rebellion of 1795 to 1806. A Hunanese army under Zeng Guofan marched into Nanjing to put down the Taiping Rebellion in 1864.

A famine in 1920 killed an estimated 2 million people and led to the Autumn Harvest Uprising of 1927, led by the Hunan native Mao Zedong. Communists held a guerrilla army along the Hunan and Jiangxi border until 1934, when the Long March began. Changsha fell to the Japanese in 1944.

Hunan has a population of just over 66 million at the 2020 census, and Changsha is its capital and largest city. Han Chinese are the majority, with Tujia and Miao among the minorities. Wulingyuan, noted for its quartzite sandstone pillars, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1992. Mount Heng at Hengyang is one of the Five Great Mountains of China.
hundred-years-war: The tension between the two crowns went back to the Norman Conquest of 1066, which put the Duke of Normandy, a vassal of the king of France, on the English throne. English kings thereafter held lands in France, and the status of those fiefs was a lasting source of conflict.

The immediate cause was dynastic. After Louis X died in 1316, the French crown passed through his brothers, and when Charles IV died, Edward III claimed the succession through his mother Isabella, Charles's sister. In May 1337 Philip VI took Aquitaine back into his hands, since Edward was in breach of his obligations as a vassal. Edward answered by challenging Philip's right to the throne, and in 1340 he formally took the title of king of France.

Historians usually divide the war into three phases, separated by truces. In the Edwardian phase, to 1360, Edward III and his son Edward the Black Prince won at Crécy in 1346 and at Poitiers in 1356, where King John II of France was taken prisoner. The Black Death, which spread through Europe between 1347 and 1351, killed 6 to 12 million people in France, over a third of the population, and 2 to 3 million in England.

In the Caroline phase, under Charles V and the commander Bertrand du Guesclin, the French reconquered most of the lands ceded to Edward at the Treaty of Brétigny in 1360; Charles created a professional standing army, the first in post-Roman western Europe. After the Truce of Leulinghem of 1389, Henry V of England used the madness of Charles VI and the civil war between Armagnacs and Burgundians to renew the war. He won at Agincourt in 1415, where about 40 per cent of the French nobility was killed, and at Verneuil in 1424. In April 1429 Joan of Arc entered the besieged city of Orléans, and the English lifted the siege.

When the war ended, England had lost its continental possessions apart from Calais, which it held until 1558. The French and English monarchies stayed separate, although English sovereigns styled themselves kings of France until 1802. Historians point to the war's lasting effects on European warfare: professional armies replaced feudal levies, artillery became important, and stronger national identities took root in both kingdoms.
hungary: Hungary is a landlocked country in Central Europe that spans much of the Carpathian Basin. It is bordered by Slovakia to the north, Ukraine to the northeast, Romania to the east and southeast, Serbia to the south, Croatia and Slovenia to the southwest, and Austria to the west. The whole country lies within the drainage basin of the Danube, which flows north to south through its centre. Its traditional divisions are Transdanubia, the land between the Danube and the Tisza, and the land beyond the Tisza.

Transdanubia is mostly hilly, with the eastern edge of the Alps in the west and Lake Balaton, the largest lake in Central Europe. The Great Hungarian Plain covers most of the east and southeast. Kékes, at 1,014 metres, is the tallest mountain, in the foothills of the Carpathians near the Slovak border.

The Roman Empire took the land west of the Danube in 16 to 15 BCE, and Pannonia was recognised as Roman in 14 BCE. The province of Dacia, which included the east of present-day Hungary, was formed in 106 CE and remained under Roman rule until 271. Later arrivals included the Hunnic Empire (c. 370 to 469), the Gepids, and the Avars, who founded the Avar Khaganate in the 560s. The Franks under Charlemagne defeated the Avars in a series of campaigns during the 790s.

Statehood began in the late ninth century with the Principality of Hungary, which became a Christian kingdom under King Stephen I in 1000. After the Battle of Mohács in 1526 the kingdom was divided into three regions for over 150 years, until it was reunited under Habsburg rule before the turn of the 18th century. The Treaty of Trianon in 1920 set Hungary's modern borders and cost it 71% of its historical territory; a third of ethnic Hungarians were left outside the new borders.

The Hungarian People's Republic was established in 1949 as a satellite state inside the Warsaw Pact. The Hungarian Revolution of 1956 was unsuccessful, and during the Revolutions of 1989 the country moved peacefully to a democratic parliamentary republic. Parliament has 199 members.

The population was 9,689,000 in 2021, down from a peak of 10.8 million in 1980, and around 70% of the population lives in cities and towns, and a quarter of Hungarians live in the Budapest metropolitan area. About 5 million Hungarians live outside the country.
huns: The Huns left no sources of their own, and their origins and links to other steppe peoples remain uncertain. They probably came from Central Asia. Roman writers equated them with earlier steppe peoples, calling them Massagetae, Scythians or Cimmerians. In the 18th century Joseph de Guignes proposed that they were descended from the Xiongnu. Scholars still dispute the connection, though recent archaeogenetic studies show some Hun-era individuals with DNA similar to ancient Mongolian populations.

The Romans became aware of the Huns in 376, when their invasion of the Pontic steppes drove thousands of Goths to seek refuge on the Lower Danube. In 395 they began their first large-scale attack on the Eastern Roman Empire, striking Thrace, Armenia, Cappadocia and Syria. From 434 the brothers Attila and Bleda ruled together, and in 435 they forced the Eastern Roman Empire to sign the Treaty of Margus, which gave the Huns trade rights and annual tribute. Theodosius II gave in to their demands in the Peace of Anatolius in 443. Bleda died in 445 and Attila ruled alone.

In 451 the Huns invaded Gaul and fought a combined army of Romans and Visigoths at the Battle of the Catalaunian Fields, and in 452 they invaded Italy. After Attila's death in 453 his empire faced a struggle between its Germanic vassals and the Hunnic rulers. At the Battle of Nedao, around 454, the Gepid king Ardaric led a Germanic coalition against Attila's son Ellak, and the Huns lost many of their vassals.

The Huns practised pastoral nomadism, and their main method of warfare was mounted archery. Under Attila their economy depended heavily on plunder and tribute from the Roman provinces. Their government is debated: Peter Heather sees a loose confederation, and Hyun Jin Kim argues for a far more centralised system. They ruled many peoples, among them Gepids, Sarmatians, Heruli, Rugii, Suebi and Sciri, whose own kings often remained in place.

Very few archaeological remains are firmly Hunnic. Large copper cauldrons are attributed to them, and between 50 and 80 per cent of burials in the Carpathian basin in the Hun period show artificial cranial deformation. Almost nothing is known of their religion, though divination is attested. Medieval Hungarian chronicles claimed descent from them, a claim mainstream scholarship has dismissed.
hurrem-sultan: No document records Hürrem's life before she entered the harem, and her birth name is unknown. Legends of her origins arose in literature, and she has been claimed as Ukrainian, Russian or Polish. Many sources place her in Ruthenia, then part of the Polish Crown. The ambassador Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, in his Turkish Letters, published in 1581, called her Roxelana after Roxolania, the name often given to that territory. According to accounts, Crimean Tatars kidnapped her in a slave raid between 1512 and 1520, and she may have been taken first to Kaffa, a major centre of the Ottoman slave trade, before reaching Constantinople.

Her rise from slave to legal wife attracted jealousy in the harem and among the general population. No law forbade the marriage, but custom was strong and astonished the court. The wedding probably took place around 1533. She bore at least six children, five of them sons, which broke the old custom that a concubine gave the sultan only one son. Her daughter Mihrimah married Rüstem Pasha, later grand vizier, on 26 November 1539.

Suleiman spent nearly ten years of his reign on campaign, and from the 1530s Hürrem wrote to him about the capital and the statesmen. She is known as the first woman in Ottoman history to concern herself with state affairs. Two of her letters to King Sigismund II Augustus of Poland survive, one congratulating him on his accession in 1548, and during her lifetime the empire's relations with Poland were generally peaceful. Her patronage of public buildings extended to Jerusalem, though the full list of works is unknown.

Hürrem died on 15 April 1558 of an unknown illness. The French ambassador Jean de la Vigne reported that Suleiman's grief was so great that he seemed to have aged. Her funeral prayers were led by the chief mufti Ebu Suud, and she was buried in a domed mausoleum decorated with Iznik tiles beside the Süleymaniye Mosque, where Suleiman was laid eight years later. Her son Selim II ascended the throne on 30 September 1566. European artists, barred from the harem, created a largely imagined image of her.
