The French author Gabriel Bounin wrote the tragedy La Soltane in 1561, and she has since inspired paintings, Haydn's Symphony No. 63, plays and novels.
hurrians: Some historians believe the Hurrians originated in the Armenian highlands or the Caucasus and migrated south into the Fertile Crescent. Several scholars have proposed the Kura-Araxes culture as their ancestor. Excavations at Tell Mozan, ancient Urkesh, show Hurrian artefacts with affinities to Kura-Araxes, though Antonio Sagona finds a connection hard to demonstrate. Others suggest the Hurrians were native to Mesopotamia, linked to the prehistoric Tell Halaf or Samarra cultures, while Igor Diakonoff thought them newcomers who arrived in the third millennium BCE. Their language is agglutinative and related to Urartian, together forming the Hurro-Urartian family; wider connections are disputed.

The Khabur River valley became the heart of Hurrian lands for a millennium. The first known Hurrian kingdom arose around Urkesh in the third millennium BCE. The king Tupkish had a queen named Uqnitum, Akkadian for "girl of lapis lazuli", and there is evidence that the Hurrians were allied with the Akkadian Empire by the reign of Naram-Sin. By 1725 BCE they were found in northern Syria, at places such as Alalakh. The mixed Amorite-Hurrian kingdom of Yamhad struggled with the early Hittite king Hattusilis I around 1600 BCE, and Hurrians settled in Kizzuwatna in southern Anatolia.

The Hurrians who entered northern Syria at the end of the 17th century BCE brought political and cultural change, establishing feudal states led by a chariot-warrior aristocracy. The Mitanni Empire, which first rose to power before 1550 BCE, was bounded by the Hittites to the north, the Egyptians to the south-west, the Kassites to the south-east and later the Assyrians to the east. Egyptian records of Thutmose I and Thutmose III mention it, usually as Naharin. After an internal succession crisis Mitanni fell to the Hittites and later came under Assyrian control. The kingdom of Shupria, north of the upper Tigris, survived until Assyria conquered it in 673-672 BCE, and by the Early Iron Age the Hurrians had been assimilated into other peoples.

Knowledge of Hurrian culture comes from excavations at Nuzi and Alalakh and from cuneiform tablets, mainly from Hattusa, the Hittite capital. The Hurrians adopted the Akkadian language and cuneiform script about 2000 BCE. They were skilled potters, and their Khabur ware and Nuzi ware were valued as far away as Egypt. They may have been the first in Mesopotamia to recognise the full potential of the horse, and with the Hittites the first in the Near East to use the horse-drawn chariot in war. Hurrian texts from Ugarit hold the oldest known written music, from about 1400 BCE.

Their religion influenced the Hittites, spreading from the cult centre at Kummanni in Kizzuwatna. Teshub was the weather god and Hebat his wife; Kumarbi was the father of Teshub. The Hurrian myth The Songs of Ullikummi, preserved among the Hittites, parallels Hesiod's Theogony.
husayn-ibn-ali: Most narrations report that Husayn was born in Medina on 11 January 626, the younger son of Ali and Fatima, both of the Banu Hashim clan of the Quraysh. He was still a child when his grandfather Muhammad died. During the caliphate of Ali he accompanied his father in the campaigns of the First Fitna. After Ali's assassination he obeyed his elder brother Hasan in accepting the Hasan–Mu'awiya treaty, and the two withdrew to Medina and kept aloof from politics under Mu'awiya I.

Mu'awiya named his son Yazid as successor, which Husayn held to violate that treaty, and Husayn withheld allegiance. After Mu'awiya died on 22 April 680, Yazid ordered the governor of Medina to secure Husayn's allegiance, by force if necessary. Husayn refused and went to Mecca. There letters came from Kufa, where many resented Umayyad rule, asking him to lead them. He sent his cousin Muslim ibn Aqil to assess the situation, but the new governor Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad crushed the revolt and Ibn Aqil was killed. Husayn was advised against going, but held to his decision.

With a retinue of about 72 men, he was intercepted by a force of 1,000 and driven north to the plain of Karbala, where he camped on 2 October. A larger Umayyad army, put at some 4,000 or 30,000 in different accounts, arrived soon after. Ibn Ziyad refused him safe passage unless he submitted, and Husayn declined. Battle was joined on 10 October 680. Husayn was killed with most of his relatives and companions, and his surviving family were taken prisoner.

Karbala gave the pro-Alid party a distinct religious identity with its own rituals and collective memory. Kufans mounted two campaigns of vengeance during the Second Fitna, one by the Penitents and one by Mukhtar al-Thaqafi. For Shia Muslims Husayn is the third Imam, and his martyrdom is a symbol of sacrifice for justice and truth. Sunni Muslims regard the event as a tragedy and Husayn and his companions as martyrs. The battle is commemorated over ten days of Muharram, ending on Ashura. His tomb at Karbala, about 90 kilometres south-west of Baghdad, was at first marked by a simple sign and later given a monument.
hussein-badreddin-al-houthi: Hussein al-Houthi was born on 20 August 1959 in the Marran area of northern Yemen, the ancestral home of the Houthi tribe; some sources give 1956 as the year. His father, Badreddin al-Houthi, was a prominent Zaydi cleric. According to a disciple, he lived for part of his life in Qom, in Iran, with his family, including his father and his younger brother Abdul-Malik; the same disciple claimed that he was close to Ali Khamenei, Supreme Leader of Iran, and to Hassan Nasrallah of Hezbollah.

He sat in the Yemeni parliament from 1993 to 1997 for Al-Haqq, the Party of Truth, a party of Zaydi and Shafi'i membership. When the party supported South Yemeni separatism it became a target of the government, and he fled, allegedly to Syria and then to Iran. After his return he broke with Al-Haqq. In 1990 or 1992 he founded the Believing Youth movement to teach young people about Zaydi Islam and its history and so to revive Zaydism in Saada Governorate.

The government of Ali Abdullah Saleh accused him of trying to set himself up as an imam, of opening unlicensed religious centres, of creating an armed group called Ansarallah and of staging violent protests against the United States and Israel. His followers held that the government was too closely allied with the United States.

On 18 June 2004 police arrested 640 of his followers who were demonstrating in front of the Great Mosque of Sanaa, and two days later the government offered a bounty of 55,000 US dollars for his capture and began an operation against him. In July the army killed 25 of his supporters and raised the bounty to 75,500 dollars. On 10 September the interior and defence ministries announced that he had been killed with 20 of his aides in Marran.

His father briefly took control of the movement after his death. The government buried him at the central prison of Sanaa so that his grave would not become a shrine. After Saleh stepped down, the new government handed his remains to his family on 28 December 2012, and on 5 June 2013 tens of thousands attended his reburial in Saada. His brothers Abdul-Malik, Yahia and Abdul-Karim are leaders of the movement.
hussein-of-jordan: Hussein was born in Amman on 14 November 1935, the eldest child of Crown Prince Talal and Princess Zein al-Sharaf, in the Hashemite dynasty. His baby sister Asma died of pneumonia in a cold winter, which shows how poor the family then was: they could not afford heating. After Talal became king in 1951, he named Hussein crown prince on 9 September 1951. Less than thirteen months into his reign Parliament forced Talal to abdicate because of his mental state, which doctors had diagnosed as schizophrenia. Hussein was proclaimed king on 11 August 1952, three months before his 17th birthday; a regency council acted until he was enthroned in 1953.

The young king inherited a poor country that also held the West Bank, annexed in 1950, whose annexation had made Palestinians two-thirds of the population. Hussein allowed an elected government in 1956 but forced it to resign within months, declared martial law and banned political parties. In 1958, when Egypt and Syria formed the United Arab Republic, he and his cousin King Faisal II of Iraq set up the Arab Federation. He survived dozens of assassination attempts; a bomb killed his prime minister Hazza' Majali, and a second explosion twenty minutes later was meant for the king.

In the Six-Day War, begun on 5 June 1967, misleading information from Cairo led the Jordanian army to attack around Jerusalem, and Jordan lost the West Bank. In 1970 Hussein expelled Palestinian militants from Jordan in what became known as Black September. In 1988 he renounced Jordan's ties to the West Bank, and in 1989 he lifted martial law and reintroduced elections after riots over price rises. In 1994 he became the second Arab head of state to sign a peace treaty with Israel.

In 1998 Hussein, a heavy smoker, was diagnosed at the Mayo Clinic with Non-Hodgkin lymphoma and received six courses of chemotherapy over five months while his brother Hassan, crown prince since 1965, acted as regent. He died on 7 February 1999, aged 63, and was succeeded by his eldest son, Abdullah II. He married four times. Admirers saw him as a regional peacemaker who pardoned political opponents and gave them senior posts, while critics noted that he left a Jordan dependent on foreign aid from British, American, Gulf and Iraqi sources. He was a keen amateur radio operator with the call sign JY1.
hvar: Hvar lies in the Adriatic off the Dalmatian coast, between the islands of Brač, Vis and Korčula. It is about 68 kilometres long and at most 10.5 kilometres wide, a high east-west ridge of limestone and dolomite that was part of the mainland until about 11,000 years ago. The landscape is karst, with little surface water, so farming depends on cisterns, dry-stone walls and terracing. Unusually for the area the island has a large fertile coastal plain and freshwater springs. Its position on the Adriatic sailing routes made it a base for commanding trade.

The first inhabitants were Neolithic people whose pottery gave its name to the Hvar culture, dated from 3500 to 2500 BCE, and later the Illyrians. Greeks from Paros colonised the island from the 4th century BCE, and in 384 BCE the colonists of Pharos defeated Iadasinoi warriors whom the natives had invited against them. Rome took the island in 219 BCE and renamed it Pharia. Later it came under the Byzantine Empire, and the Narentines took it in the first half of the 7th century. In the 11th century it joined the Kingdom of Croatia.

Venice became its long-term owner, and under Venetian rule the town of Hvar became a major naval base, with one of the first public theatres in Europe. The island was a centre of Croatian Renaissance literature, with writers such as Petar Hektorović, who designed Tvrdalj Castle at Stari Grad, and Hanibal Lucić. In the 16th century the Hvar Rebellion and raids by pirates and the Ottoman army led to fortified buildings on the northern shore. The fall of the Venetian Republic in 1797 gave the island to the Habsburg monarchy by the Treaty of Campo Formio, and after French and British occupation it returned to Austria in 1815.

Hvar is part of Split-Dalmatia County in Croatia, with two towns, Hvar and Stari Grad, and two municipalities, Jelsa and Sućuraj. Stari Grad stands on the site of Pharos, and its Plain preserves the field divisions laid out by the Greeks, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Tourism, begun with the Hygienic Association of Hvar in 1868, supports much of the economy, along with lavender, fishing and wine, including red wines from the Plavac Mali grape.
hyderabad: Hyderabad occupies about 650 square kilometres on the Deccan Plateau along the Musi River, in the northern part of South India. The ground is mostly sloping granite dotted with small hills, and the city has numerous artificial lakes, among them Hussain Sagar, built in 1562 near the centre. The climate is tropical wet and dry, with hot, dry summers from March to June. Megalithic burial sites found in 1851 by Philip Meadows Taylor show that the region has been inhabited since the Stone Age.

The region was ruled by the Chalukya dynasty from 624 to 1075 and then by the Kakatiya dynasty from 1158, whose ruler Ganapatideva (1199–1262) built the hilltop outpost later known as Golconda Fort. Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah of the Qutb Shahi dynasty established Hyderabad in 1591 to extend the capital beyond the fortified Golconda. The name means Haydar's City, after Caliph Ali Ibn Abi Talib, and the city was first called Baghnagar, city of gardens. The Mughals annexed it in 1687.

In 1724 Asaf Jah I, the Mughal viceroy of the Deccan, defeated Mubariz Khan at the Battle of Shakar Kheda and established his autonomy, founding the Asaf Jahi dynasty, whose rulers are known as the Nizams of Hyderabad. Hyderabad remained their capital until 1948, and as capital of the princely state it housed the British Residency and cantonment until Indian independence in 1947. After a flood of the Musi in 1908 the city was expanded and civic monuments were built, particularly under Mir Osman Ali Khan, the seventh Nizam. The Indian Union annexed Hyderabad in 1948.

Hyderabad is the capital and largest city of the Indian state of Telangana, with 6.9 million inhabitants within the city limits at the 2011 census. Until the 19th century it was known as the City of Pearls and was the only trading centre for Golconda diamonds in the world. The Charminar has come to symbolise the city, and UNESCO lists Hyderabad as a creative city of gastronomy.
hydroelectricity: The use of water to generate mechanical energy can be traced back to 203 BCE in Han dynasty China. In the late 18th century hydraulic power supplied the energy for the start of the Industrial Revolution. In the mid-1700s the French engineer Bernard Forest de Bélidor published Architecture Hydraulique, describing vertical- and horizontal-axis hydraulic machines, and in 1771 Richard Arkwright's combination of water power, the water frame and continuous production played a significant part in the growth of the factory system. In the 1840s hydraulic power networks were developed to generate and transmit hydro power to users.

On 30 September 1882 the first Edison hydroelectric power station, the Vulcan Street Plant, began operating in Appleton, Wisconsin, with an output of about 12.5 kilowatts. By 1886 there were 45 hydroelectric power stations in the United States and Canada. By 1920, 40 per cent of the power produced in the United States was hydroelectric, and the Federal Power Act created the Federal Power Commission to regulate stations on federal land and water.

As stations grew, their dams took on further purposes, including flood control, irrigation and navigation, and large projects needed federal funding, such as the Tennessee Valley Authority (1933) and the Bonneville Power Administration (1937). Hoover Dam's 1,345 MW power station was the world's largest in 1936 and was surpassed by the 6,809 MW Grand Coulee Dam in 1942. Itaipu, opened in 1984, was surpassed in 2008 by the Three Gorges Dam. Hydropower was called white coal.

Most hydroelectric power comes from the potential energy of dammed water driving a turbine and generator. The power extracted depends on the volume of water and on the height difference between source and outflow, called the head; a large pipe, the penstock, delivers water from the reservoir to the turbine. Pumped-storage schemes move water between reservoirs at different elevations, pumping it up when demand is low and releasing it through a turbine when demand is high. Run-of-the-river stations have little or no reservoir, so that only the water arriving from upstream is available. Tidal power stations use the daily rise and fall of ocean water.
hymn-to-liberty: The Hymn to Liberty is a Greek poem written by Dionysios Solomos in 1823 and set to music by Nikolaos Mantzaros in 1828. It was printed in Messolonghi a year after it was written, and in October 1824 the Philhellenic Committee published it in London. An Italian translation appeared at about the same time in the Messolonghi newspaper Ellinika Chronika.

Mantzaros, a Corfiot operatic composer, wrote a choral version in 24 parts and dedicated it to Otto, the first king of Greece, who rewarded him with the Silver Cross of the Order of the Redeemer. During Otto's reign, from 1832 to 1862, however, an anthem based on God Save the King with a text praising Otto was used instead.

Solomos wrote the hymn, inspired by the Greek War of Independence, to honour the struggle of the Greeks against centuries of Ottoman rule. It tells of their misery under the Ottomans and their hope of freedom. It describes events of the war, among them the execution of Patriarch Gregory V of Constantinople, the reaction of the Great Powers and, at length, the Siege of Tripolitsa, and it stresses the Christian character of the struggle.

After Otto was ousted in 1862, the hymn was adopted in 1864 as the national and royal anthem of Greece, using its first two stanzas. It remained the royal anthem from 1864 to 1924 and again from 1935 to 1973, each time until the monarchy was abolished. An adapted version served the short-lived Cretan State as its anthem.

Cyprus adopted the hymn as its national anthem in 1966 by order of its Council of Ministers, after an anthem by the Cypriot composer Solon Michaelides, shared with Turkish Cypriots, was abandoned in 1963 during intercommunal conflicts. The hymn is performed at every closing ceremony of the Olympic Games to honour Greece as their birthplace, usually in an instrumental version. The arrangement played by military bands is by Lieutenant Colonel Margaritis Kastellis.
hyogo-prefecture: Hyōgo covers about 8,400 square kilometres and borders Kyoto Prefecture to the east, Osaka Prefecture to the south-east and Okayama and Tottori prefectures to the west. It has coasts on the Sea of Japan to the north and the Seto Inland Sea to the south, and on Awaji Island it also meets the Pacific. The north is sparsely populated, apart from Toyooka, and the central highlands hold only tiny villages. Most people live on the southern coast, part of the Osaka–Kobe–Kyoto metropolitan area. The north gets abundant snow in winter.

The prefecture includes the former provinces of Harima, Tajima and Awaji and parts of Tanba and Settsu. In 1180, near the end of the Heian period, Emperor Antoku, Taira no Kiyomori and the imperial court moved briefly to Fukuhara, in what is now Kobe, and the capital stayed there for five months. In 1995 the Great Hanshin earthquake, of magnitude 6.9, devastated southern Hyōgo, destroying large parts of Kobe and Awaji as well as Nishinomiya and Ashiya and killing nearly 6,500 people.

Kobe is the capital and largest city, and other major cities are Himeji, Nishinomiya and Amagasaki. Kobe Port is one of the largest in Japan, and since 1975 prefectural law has kept it free of nuclear weapons. Hyōgo belongs to the Hanshin Industrial Region and holds two Riken research institutes, at Kobe and Harima, as well as the SPring-8 synchrotron at Harima. Its cultural sites include several National Treasures, the preservation districts of Izushi and Sasayama, the hot springs of Arima and the Takarazuka Revue. In 1963 Hyōgo became the first Japanese prefecture to enter a sister state relationship with an American state, Washington.
hypatia: Hypatia was the daughter of Theon of Alexandria, whose main achievement was a new edition of Euclid's Elements correcting scribal errors made over nearly 700 years of copying; it became the most widely used edition for centuries. Like her father, Hypatia rejected the teachings of Iamblichus and embraced the original Neoplatonism of Plotinus. Alexandria was regarded as second only to Athens as the philosophical capital of the Greco-Roman world, and she taught students from all over the Mediterranean. According to Damascius, she lectured on Plato and Aristotle, and walked through the city in a tribon, a cloak associated with philosophers, giving impromptu public lectures.

Hypatia was probably more a teacher and commentator than an innovator. No evidence shows that she published independent philosophical works, but scholars of her time preserved and commented on classical mathematical texts rather than publishing new ones. She is now known to have edited Book III of Ptolemy's Almagest; its title in Theon's commentary describes an edition revised by his daughter Hypatia, the philosopher. Her contribution is thought to be an improved tabular method for the long divisions needed in astronomical computation. She also wrote a commentary on Diophantus's Arithmetica, which may survive in part, and one on the conic sections of Apollonius of Perga, which has not survived.

A letter of her pupil Synesius, the future bishop of Ptolemais, says she taught him to construct a silver plane astrolabe as a gift for an official. Ancient sources record that she was widely loved by pagans and Christians alike.

According to Socrates Scholasticus, in March 415, during Lent, a mob of Christians led by a lector named Peter seized Hypatia's carriage as she travelled home, dragged her into the Kaisarion, a former pagan temple turned church, and killed her. Her body was torn apart and burned. Although no firm evidence linked the bishop Cyril to the murder, it was widely believed that he had ordered it, and the Alexandrian council sent an embassy to Constantinople; the advisers of Theodosius II began an investigation. Her death shocked the empire, and Neoplatonists such as Damascius grew more fervent in their opposition to Christianity.

Neoplatonism survived in Alexandria for centuries afterwards. In the Middle Ages she was part of the basis for the legend of Saint Catherine of Alexandria. Charles Kingsley's novel Hypatia of 1853 called her the last of the Hellenes. Some modern portrayals link her death to the destruction of the Library of Alexandria, although the library no longer existed in her lifetime.
